questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). IT register kept apart
questions.question: A hotel group's IT department keeps its own register of 60 risks, none of which appear in the enterprise register the executive committee reviews. What should the risk practitioner recommend as the BEST approach?

options.A: Bring the separate IT risk register to the executive committee
options.B: Have the CIO accept the IT risks on the enterprise's behalf
options.C: Bring IT risks into the enterprise register in its categories
options.D: Identify the security standard each IT risk relates to

questions.key_concept: IT risk is business risk: it belongs in the enterprise register, in enterprise categories and scales, so leaders can compare and prioritize it.
questions.pre_read: Notice who reviews which register. Ask what executives need to compare IT risk with everything else.
questions.correct_explanation: IT risk is business risk, so leaders must see it beside every other enterprise risk, rated on the same categories and scales. Bringing the 60 risks into the enterprise register lets the executive committee compare, prioritize and fund them alongside other exposures. Bringing the separate IT register to the committee is the runner-up: it adds visibility, but it keeps IT risk in IT's own terms and leaves the comparison undone.

wrong_explanations.A: A separate IT register shows the risks in IT's own terms and volume, so executives still cannot weigh them against other enterprise risks.
wrong_explanations.B: The CIO can own risks to IT objectives, but accepting risks to business objectives for the enterprise takes the decision from the business owners.
wrong_explanations.D: Matching risks to security standards helps control design, but it keeps them in technical terms instead of linking them to enterprise objectives.

tips: Eliminate: B lets the CIO accept risk for business owners, and D keeps the risks in technical rather than business terms.
Final two: C beats A because leaders need IT risk in the enterprise's terms beside other risks, not a second register in IT's terms.
Exam cue: one enterprise view, one taxonomy, one set of scales; IT risk feeds ERM rather than running beside it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-03 (cybersecurity risk management activities and outcomes are included in enterprise risk management processes); NIST IR 8286 Rev. 1 Section 3.8 (Creating and Maintaining an Enterprise-Level Cybersecurity Risk Register)

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). Framework in practice
questions.question: A year after an engineering firm's executive committee approved a new risk management framework, what would give the risk practitioner the BEST evidence that it is embedded?

options.A: The executive committee's minutes approving the framework
options.B: Unit managers' self-assessments of framework compliance
options.C: A crosswalk from the framework to COBIT 2019 and NIST CSF
options.D: Unit risk assessments that use the framework's methods

questions.key_concept: A framework is embedded when business units use its methods in their own risk work; approval gives authority but does not show use.
questions.pre_read: Separate evidence that leaders adopted the framework from evidence that business units now work by it.
questions.correct_explanation: A framework is embedded when units actually use it, so the strongest evidence is their own risk assessments applying its methods, scales and taxonomy. The approval minutes are the runner-up: approval by senior management gives the framework authority across units, which matters, but it shows that leaders adopted it a year ago, not that the units now work by it.

wrong_explanations.A: Approval gives the framework its authority, but it records a decision made a year ago, not how units assess risk today.
wrong_explanations.B: Self-assessments are managers' own claims of compliance. They are weaker than the assessments themselves, which show the methods in use.
wrong_explanations.C: A crosswalk shows how the framework's design relates to other frameworks. It says nothing about whether business units apply it.

tips: Eliminate: C maps the framework's design to others, and B relies on managers' own claims of compliance.
Final two: D beats A because approval gives authority, while the units' assessments show the framework in actual use.
Exam cue: evidence of use beats evidence of intent; look for the framework in work products, not in sign-offs.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 EDM01 (Ensured Governance Framework Setting and Maintenance); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-06 (a standardized method for calculating, documenting, categorizing and prioritizing cybersecurity risks is established and communicated)

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. Overlapping assurance
questions.question: A bank's internal audit and second-line risk team both test the same 40 key controls yearly, while neither tests its cloud controls. What should the risk practitioner recommend as the BEST approach?

options.A: Agree a combined assurance map with internal audit
options.B: Have internal audit take over testing of the 40 controls
options.C: Stop the second line's testing of the 40 key controls
options.D: Ask the cloud team to self-assess its cloud controls

questions.key_concept: Combined assurance coordinates what each line tests, removing duplication and closing gaps while each line keeps its role.
questions.pre_read: Notice both problems in the stem. Check which option leaves each line in its proper role.
questions.correct_explanation: Combined assurance maps which line tests which risks, so the lines can rely on each other's work, remove duplicate testing and close gaps such as the untested cloud controls. Agreeing the map with internal audit fixes both problems while each line keeps its role. A cloud self-assessment is the runner-up: first-line checking is useful, but it closes only part of the cloud gap and leaves the duplication.

wrong_explanations.B: Internal audit gives independent assurance; taking over routine testing would replace second-line oversight and still leave the cloud controls uncovered.
wrong_explanations.C: Stopping second-line testing removes the duplication by dropping oversight, and the cloud controls remain untested by anyone.
wrong_explanations.D: First-line self-assessment adds some cloud coverage, but it is not independent challenge, and the duplicated testing of the 40 controls stays.

tips: Eliminate: B turns the third line into routine testers, and C removes second-line oversight while the cloud gap stays open.
Final two: A beats D because a combined assurance map fixes the duplication and the gap; self-assessment covers part of one.
Exam cue: when lines overlap in one place and leave gaps in another, coordinate coverage across the lines instead of moving work to one line.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Journal 2018 Volume 4 (Roles of Three Lines of Defense for Information Security and Governance); COBIT 2019 APO12 (Managed Risk)

CRISC D1 round 2.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. Second line running a control
questions.question: For the past year, a logistics firm's second-line risk team has run the monthly firewall rule reviews because the network team is short-staffed. What should concern the risk practitioner MOST?

options.A: The risk team lacks the network team's firewall expertise
options.B: Internal audit will need to widen its review testing
options.C: The risk team cannot objectively challenge a control it runs
options.D: Rule changes made between monthly reviews go unchecked

questions.key_concept: A second line that runs a first-line control loses its ability to challenge it, and the first line stops owning it.
questions.pre_read: Think about what each line of defense is for. Ask what changes when the overseer performs the control.
questions.correct_explanation: The second line oversees and challenges first-line controls. After a year of running the firewall reviews itself, the risk team is checking its own work, and the network team no longer owns the control, so a key control has lost both its owner and its challenger. Lack of firewall expertise is the runner-up: it matters, but skills can be added, while the conflict in roles remains.

wrong_explanations.A: Expertise matters for good reviews, but it can be supplied or trained. The lasting problem is that the team meant to challenge the control now runs it.
wrong_explanations.B: Audit may adjust its plan, but wider audit testing is a consequence. It does not restore first-line ownership or second-line challenge.
wrong_explanations.D: Monthly reviews can suit the firm's risk, and nothing in the scenario shows the interval is wrong. The problem is who performs them.

tips: Eliminate: B describes a knock-on effect on audit planning, and D questions an interval the scenario gives no reason to doubt.
Final two: C beats A because skills can be added, but a team that runs a control cannot also challenge it objectively.
Exam cue: if the second line performs a first-line control, flag the lost challenge and ownership, and plan a hand-back.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Journal 2018 Volume 4 (Roles of Three Lines of Defense for Information Security and Governance); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. Control credited in the profile has failed
questions.question: Internal audit reports that an airline's access recertification control, credited in three risks the profile shows within appetite, has not operated for six months. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the control owner to restart the recertifications
options.B: Reassess the three risks without credit for the control
options.C: Keep the profile as reported until its next update
options.D: Ask the control owner to assess the control again next quarter

questions.key_concept: Current risk credits only controls that are in place and working; when a credited control fails, the affected risks are re-rated without it.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the profile credits and what audit found. Ask what the three ratings now claim that is no longer true.
questions.correct_explanation: Current risk counts only controls that are in place and working. With recertification stopped for six months, the three ratings overstate protection, and the risks may now sit above appetite. Reassessing them without the control shows the true position to the owners and leaders. Asking the control owner to restart is the runner-up: it is needed, but it does not show how exposed the airline is now.

wrong_explanations.A: Restarting the control is the owner's job and will be needed, but it does not tell the risk owners or leaders how exposed the three risks are today.
wrong_explanations.C: Holding the profile leaves leaders relying on ratings that credit a control that has not worked for six months.
wrong_explanations.D: The audit finding already shows the control has not operated. Its owner assessing it again next quarter leaves the profile overstated in the meantime.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves a known-wrong rating in the profile, and D waits to retest a failure that is already established.
Final two: B beats A because the practitioner first needs the true exposure; restarting the control is the owner's fix, not a rating.
Exam cue: a control earns credit in a rating only while it works; when it fails, re-rate the risk without it at once; the owner's fix runs alongside, not first.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. AI exposure in the profile
questions.question: Several business units at a retailer adopted generative AI tools this year. Which of the following would BEST show senior management how this changes the enterprise risk profile?

options.A: AI risks mapped to the objectives and categories they affect
options.B: A count of AI tools in use for each business objective
options.C: The AI acceptable use policy and its approval date
options.D: Vendor assurance reports for each AI service in use

questions.key_concept: AI enters the risk profile as risks mapped to the objectives and categories they affect, so leaders can weigh AI exposure against appetite.
questions.pre_read: Ask what senior management uses a risk profile for. Compare each option with that purpose.
questions.correct_explanation: A risk profile shows exposure in terms leaders can weigh against appetite. Mapping the AI risks in the register to the objectives and risk categories they affect shows senior management where AI has raised exposure and how it sits against appetite. A count of tools per objective is the runner-up: it shows where AI is used, but the volume of use says little about the size of the risk.

wrong_explanations.B: Counting tools shows how far AI has spread, but ten low-risk tools can matter less than one model making credit or pricing decisions.
wrong_explanations.C: A policy states how AI may be used. It shows intent and approval, not how much risk the business units now carry.
wrong_explanations.D: Vendor reports describe suppliers' controls. They are inputs to analysis, not a view of the enterprise's own exposure.

tips: Eliminate: C shows intent rather than exposure, and D covers suppliers' controls rather than the enterprise's own risk.
Final two: A beats B because the profile reports exposure by objective; counting tools measures adoption, not risk.
Exam cue: report changes to the profile as risks to objectives against appetite, never as inventories or counts.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. Exposure well below appetite
questions.question: For two years, a SaaS provider's risk profile has shown technology risk well below appetite in every category, while rivals release features faster. What should the risk practitioner recommend as the BEST action?

options.A: Lower the risk appetite to match the current profile
options.B: Have owners add controls to stay well below appetite
options.C: Have risk owners cut controls in low-rated categories
options.D: Report the gap below appetite to senior management

questions.key_concept: Exposure far below appetite is a finding too: it may mean excess control cost or missed opportunity, and leaders decide whether to rebalance.
questions.pre_read: Notice which way the gap runs. Ask who decides how much risk the provider should take.
questions.correct_explanation: Exposure far below appetite can mean the provider spends more on control than its risk warrants and passes up opportunities its appetite allows, a real cost when rivals move faster. Senior management should see that gap and decide whether to rebalance. Having risk owners cut controls is the runner-up: it may be part of the answer, but whether to use the unused appetite is for senior management to decide first.

wrong_explanations.A: Appetite reflects strategy and is set by the board and senior management. Lowering it to fit today's profile moves the limit to match the result.
wrong_explanations.B: More controls from the owners would push risk further below appetite and add cost, widening a gap that may already be slowing the business.
wrong_explanations.C: Relaxing some controls may be right, but a gap in every category, tied to how fast the firm competes, is senior management's call; cutting controls everywhere settles it first.

tips: Eliminate: A moves the appetite to fit the profile, and B has owners add cost where risk is already low.
Final two: D beats C because a gap below appetite across every category is a decision for leaders; owners cutting controls everywhere settles it before they see it.
Exam cue: being well below appetite is also a finding; report it so leaders can weigh control cost and missed opportunity.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Input for a downtime tolerance
questions.question: Senior management asks the risk practitioner to help set a tolerance for order-system downtime at a food distributor. Which of the following inputs is MOST important?

options.A: The order system's uptime over the past year
options.B: The IT team's estimate of acceptable downtime
options.C: The business impact of outages of different lengths
options.D: The cost of moving to a high-availability platform

questions.key_concept: A tolerance reflects how much variation an objective can bear, so it rests on business impact data, not on what the system already achieves.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a tolerance is meant to express. Then compare each input with that purpose.
questions.correct_explanation: A tolerance sets how much variation the business will accept around its objectives, so it rests on what downtime of different lengths would do to orders, customers and contracts. Past uptime is the runner-up: it shows what the system achieves, which helps later to judge whether it meets the tolerance, but setting the limit from it records capability rather than need.

wrong_explanations.A: Past uptime shows capability. Setting the tolerance from it would accept whatever the system already does, whether or not the business can bear it.
wrong_explanations.B: IT can say what the system can deliver, but how much downtime is acceptable depends on harm to orders, customers and contracts, which the business judges.
wrong_explanations.D: Upgrade cost matters when choosing a response to a gap. It comes after the tolerance is set, not as the basis for it.

tips: Eliminate: B lets IT judge what the business can bear, and D prices a response before the limit it must meet is known.
Final two: C beats A because a tolerance reflects what the business can bear; past uptime only shows what the system delivers.
Exam cue: limits come from impact on objectives; capability is then compared with the limit, never used to set it.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Tolerance beyond capacity
questions.question: While helping draft tolerances for an online broker, the risk analyst finds the proposed loss limit for trading-platform failures exceeds the firm's risk capacity. What should the analyst recommend as the BEST approach?

options.A: Keep the proposed limit and have the risk owner track losses
options.B: Propose a limit within capacity for senior management approval
options.C: Have the trading risk owner accept the excess over capacity
options.D: Raise the firm's stated risk capacity to match the proposed limit

questions.key_concept: Risk capacity is the outer bound; any tolerance that crosses it must be brought inside it before senior management approves it.
questions.pre_read: Place capacity, appetite and tolerance in order. Ask what a limit beyond capacity would mean for the firm.
questions.correct_explanation: Capacity is the most loss the broker can absorb, so a tolerance above it would accept failures that could threaten the firm itself. The analyst helps by proposing a limit inside capacity, consistent with appetite, for senior management to approve. Owner acceptance is the runner-up, because owners do accept residual risk, but no owner can accept losses beyond what the enterprise can survive.

wrong_explanations.A: The owner would be tracking losses the firm could not survive. The flaw is in the limit itself, and it must be fixed before approval.
wrong_explanations.C: Risk owners accept residual risk within appetite. Losses beyond capacity threaten the whole firm, which no single owner has the authority to accept.
wrong_explanations.D: Capacity reflects the firm's finances, capital and regulatory limits. It is a fact to respect, not a setting to raise so that a limit fits.

tips: Eliminate: D treats capacity as adjustable, and A has the owner track losses against a limit the firm could not survive.
Final two: B beats C because no owner can accept losses beyond capacity; the limit itself has to move inside it.
Exam cue: capacity is the outer bound; appetite and every tolerance must sit inside it, so flag any limit that crosses it.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Running above tolerance for a time
questions.question: A water utility's operations director owns telemetry outage risk and wants to run above the tolerance set by the board's risk committee for 90 days while radios are replaced. Who is the MOST appropriate approver?

options.A: The operations director who owns the outage risk
options.B: The chief engineer who leads the radio replacement
options.C: The risk analyst who reports against the tolerance
options.D: The board risk committee that approved the limit

questions.key_concept: The risk owner decides within set limits; carrying risk above a tolerance, even temporarily, needs approval from the level that set it.
questions.pre_read: Notice the roles the stem names. Ask what kind of decision the director is asking for.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk owners decide responses within the limits leadership sets. Running above a tolerance for 90 days is a temporary acceptance beyond that limit, so it needs approval from the body that set it, the board's risk committee, with the director's plan and interim measures. The director is the runner-up: they own the risk and should request the acceptance, but they cannot approve going beyond a limit set above them.

wrong_explanations.A: The director owns the risk and should make the case, with interim measures, but approving operation above a board-set limit is beyond their authority.
wrong_explanations.B: The chief engineer delivers the fix and can confirm its timing, but has no authority over the board's limits or over the risk itself.
wrong_explanations.C: The analyst monitors the risk against tolerance and reports breaches. Approving a breach would turn the second line into the decision-maker.

tips: Eliminate: B leads the fix without authority over limits, and C monitors the tolerance rather than deciding on breaches of it.
Final two: D beats A because only the level that set a tolerance can approve exceeding it; the owner requests the exception.
Exam cue: within limits, the owner decides; beyond them, take the decision to whoever set the limit.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. Supplier SLA short of the RTO
questions.question: During renewal of an online grocer's warehouse software contract, the risk analyst finds its restoration SLA is 24 hours, against an 8-hour business RTO for dispatch. What is the BEST recommendation?

options.A: Have the contract owner negotiate an SLA that meets the RTO
options.B: Accept the SLA and rely on service credits for missed targets
options.C: Change the dispatch RTO to 24 hours to match the contract
options.D: Propose a right-to-audit clause to the contract owner

questions.key_concept: Supplier SLAs must meet business recovery needs; service credits shift part of the cost, while the impact and accountability stay with the enterprise.
questions.pre_read: Compare the two numbers and ask which one should give way. Then ask what each option does to the gap.
questions.correct_explanation: Supplier terms should meet the business's recovery need, and renewal is when the grocer has leverage to fix them. The contract owner should negotiate restoration within the 8-hour RTO; if the provider cannot meet it, the business owner decides on a workaround or accepts the gap. Relying on service credits is the runner-up: credits repay part of the fee, but dispatch still stops and the grocer keeps the impact.

wrong_explanations.B: Service credits repay part of the fee after a miss. They do not restore dispatch within 8 hours, and the grocer still bears the lost orders.
wrong_explanations.C: The RTO reflects how long dispatch can be down before harm becomes unacceptable. Moving it to fit the contract hides the gap instead of closing it.
wrong_explanations.D: Audit rights help verify the provider's controls, but they leave the 24-hour restoration target unchanged and the gap open.

tips: Eliminate: C bends the business need to fit the contract, and D adds oversight without changing the restoration target.
Final two: A beats B because credits shift part of the cost, not the impact; the contract must meet the business's recovery need.
Exam cue: supplier SLAs serve business recovery targets; outsourcing moves the work, never the accountability for the outcome.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. Adopting a framework
questions.question: A 60-person marketing analytics firm asks its risk practitioner how to adopt NIST CSF 2.0. Which of the following is the BEST advice?

options.A: Implement the framework's outcomes as written
options.B: Copy the profile and objectives of its largest customer
options.C: Tailor the outcomes to its own risks and objectives
options.D: Address first the outcomes that auditors test most

questions.key_concept: Frameworks are starting points: NIST CSF 2.0 is tailored through Organizational Profiles built from the firm's own mission, risks and requirements.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a framework is for in a small firm. Compare each option with the firm's own risks.
questions.correct_explanation: Frameworks are starting points. NIST CSF 2.0 expects an organization to build Organizational Profiles from its own mission, risks and requirements, with a Target Profile setting the outcomes it prioritizes. Adopting every outcome as written is the runner-up, because it looks thorough, but a small firm would spend effort on outcomes that matter little to it and still not focus on its own top risks.

wrong_explanations.A: Applying every outcome unchanged looks complete, but it spreads a small team across low-value work and sets no priorities from the firm's own risks.
wrong_explanations.B: A customer's profile reflects the customer's mission and threats. It may inform requirements, but the firm's priorities must come from its own risks.
wrong_explanations.D: Audit attention is one input, but priorities set by what auditors test drift toward compliance rather than toward the firm's largest risks.

tips: Eliminate: B adopts another organization's priorities, and D lets audit attention set them in place of risk.
Final two: C beats A because frameworks are starting points to tailor; adopting every outcome unchanged spreads effort without priorities.
Exam cue: choose a framework, then tailor it to objectives, risks, size and obligations, and have senior management approve the result.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 Section 3.1 (CSF Profiles: a Current Profile describes outcomes being achieved and a Target Profile the outcomes selected for risk management objectives); COBIT 2019 EDM01 (Ensured Governance Framework Setting and Maintenance)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: Round 2, 31 Oct 2026: authored from notes 1B5.1 (Choosing and Tailoring a Framework: frameworks are starting points; CSF 2.0 tailoring through Current and Target Profiles); original small analytics firm adopting CSF 2.0 scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. New AI law
questions.question: A staffing agency plans to screen applicants with an AI model, and a law taking effect in nine months will class that use as high-risk. What is the risk practitioner's BEST course of action?

options.A: Ask the vendor to certify that the model meets the law
options.B: Assess the law's impact on the planned screening use
options.C: Wait for the regulator's guidance before assessing it
options.D: Recommend that the agency cancel the screening project

questions.key_concept: A new legal obligation is a source of risk: assess its impact on the planned use before its effective date, before relying on vendor assurance.
questions.pre_read: Notice how much time remains before the law applies. Ask what the agency must know before choosing any response.
questions.correct_explanation: A new obligation is a source of risk, and nine months is the time to understand it. Assessing the law's impact on the planned screening use shows which duties fall on the agency, such as oversight, testing or records, and who should own them. A vendor certificate is the runner-up: it can be useful evidence, but many duties fall on the system's user, and the agency cannot judge a certificate until it knows them.

wrong_explanations.A: A vendor's certificate covers the model, not how the agency will use it. The agency first needs to know its own duties as the user of a high-risk system.
wrong_explanations.C: Guidance may refine details, but waiting shortens the time left to meet duties that are already known. The impact assessment can start now.
wrong_explanations.D: Canceling is an avoidance response chosen before the risk is analyzed. The business decides once the impact and options are clear.

tips: Eliminate: C delays analysis the effective date makes pressing, and D chooses avoidance before the risk is known.
Final two: B beats A because the agency must know its own duties as the user before a vendor's certificate can show they are met.
Exam cue: a new law or rule triggers an impact assessment before its effective date; apply the principle, not a quoted clause.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 1.1 (legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood, managed and documented); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-03 (legal, regulatory and contractual requirements, including privacy obligations, are understood and managed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: Round 2, 31 Oct 2026: authored from notes 1B5.2 (Compliance Obligations as a Source of Risk: new rules trigger an impact assessment before their effective date; trap, relying on the AI vendor's statement); original staffing agency AI applicant screening under a new law scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. Gauging risk culture
questions.question: Which of the following would give the risk practitioner the BEST insight into a freight forwarder's risk culture?

options.A: The share of staff who completed this year's awareness course
options.B: The number of risk policies senior management approved this year
options.C: The share of reported control failures that managers follow up
options.D: The share of staff who signed the code of conduct this year

questions.key_concept: Risk culture shows in behavior, especially whether leaders act when problems are reported, not in counts of training or policies.
questions.pre_read: Ask which option shows how people behave when risk comes to the surface.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk culture is the values and beliefs people share about risk and the behavior they drive, so the best sign is what happens when risk surfaces. The share of reported control failures that managers follow up shows whether raising an issue leads to action, which decides whether staff keep raising them. Course completion is the runner-up: it shows that people sat the training, not whether they speak up or are heard when they do.

wrong_explanations.A: Completion shows attendance, not behavior. Staff can finish the course and still hide problems if raising them is punished.
wrong_explanations.B: A count of approved policies measures paperwork. Culture shows in how people act on risk, which policies alone do not change.
wrong_explanations.D: A signature shows acknowledgment, not conduct. Staff can sign the code and still stay silent about failures.

tips: Eliminate: B and D measure documents and signatures, which show that rules exist, not how people behave around risk.
Final two: C beats A because follow-up of reported failures shows the culture in action, while course completion only shows attendance.
Exam cue: to judge risk culture, look for behavior when risk surfaces, such as reporting and how leaders react, over counts of courses or policies.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (risk culture); NIST SP 800-39 Section 2.7 (Organizational Culture)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A3.1 (Risk Culture and Tone at the Top: culture is assessed through reporting behavior and how leaders respond; trap, awareness training as the main lever). Key unchanged (C).

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Strategy, goals and objectives. Late IT goal
questions.question: A university's IT department made rollout of a new identity platform its top goal, and the rollout is now four months late. How should the risk practitioner BEST express this risk to senior management?

options.A: As the delay's effect on the goals the platform serves
options.B: As the project milestones the rollout has missed so far
options.C: As the security goals the new platform has not yet reached
options.D: As the budget the rollout has spent against plan

questions.key_concept: Risk to an IT goal is expressed through its effect on the enterprise goals it serves, not through project or technical measures.
questions.pre_read: Ask which description leaders could weigh against risks elsewhere in the enterprise.
questions.correct_explanation: In the COBIT 2019 goals cascade, alignment goals (the IT goals) serve enterprise goals, so a late IT goal matters through what it puts at risk above it, such as student access to systems or research data protection. Expressed that way, senior management can weigh it against other business risks and appetite. Unmet security goals are the runner-up: closer to impact than milestones, but still alignment-level measures until tied to enterprise goals.

wrong_explanations.B: Missed milestones describe project progress. They do not tell leaders what the delay puts at risk for the university.
wrong_explanations.C: Security goals are alignment-level means. Leaders can weigh a shortfall only once it is tied to the enterprise goals it supports.
wrong_explanations.D: Spend against plan is a project measure. Overspending matters, but it says nothing about which business goals the delay threatens.

tips: Eliminate: B and D are project measures of schedule and spend that say nothing about what the delay threatens.
Final two: A beats C because security goals are alignment-level means in the goals cascade; leaders weigh risk through the enterprise goals above them.
Exam cue: when an IT goal or project slips, report it through the enterprise goal it serves, not through milestones or technical targets.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO02 (Managed Strategy); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-01 (the organizational mission is understood and informs cybersecurity risk management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A1.2 (The Goals Cascade and Strategic Change: IT goals are means, assessed and reported through the enterprise goals they serve; trap, IT goals pursued for their own sake). questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. Unrecorded AI training data
questions.question: A retailer's data science team built a three-year sales dataset to train the pricing department's AI model, but it is missing from the asset inventory. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Assess the dataset's exposure where it is stored
options.B: Record the data science team as the business owner
options.C: Encrypt the storage that holds the dataset
options.D: Identify a business owner for the dataset

questions.key_concept: AI training datasets are assets: give each a business owner first, since classification and risk decisions depend on ownership.
questions.pre_read: Sort the options into steps, then find the one the other steps rely on.
questions.correct_explanation: Classification, valuation and risk acceptance all depend on who owns an asset, so the first step for an unrecorded dataset is to identify its business owner, likely in the pricing department the model serves. With an owner, the dataset can be classified, recorded and assessed. Assessing exposure is the runner-up: without an owner to set the data's classification, there is no agreed basis for rating the exposure and no one to decide on it.

wrong_explanations.A: Exposure can be rated once the dataset is classified, and its owner is the one who classifies it and decides on the risk.
wrong_explanations.B: Building a dataset makes the data science team its developer or custodian, not its owner. Ownership sits with the business that relies on it.
wrong_explanations.C: Encryption is a control chosen before the data is classified or its risk analyzed, so it may not fit what the data needs.

tips: Eliminate: B confuses the team that built the dataset with its business owner, and C picks a control before the data is classified or analyzed.
Final two: D beats A because the owner classifies the dataset and decides on its risk; rating the exposure needs that basis first.
Exam cue: for an asset missing from the inventory, AI datasets included, establish the business owner first; classification and risk rating follow.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM-07 (inventories of data and corresponding metadata for designated data types are maintained); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 1.6 (mechanisms are in place to inventory AI systems)

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. Blocked risk reporting
questions.question: At a retailer, the CRO reports to the CFO, who has twice cut high-rated finance system risks from reports bound for the board. What is the BEST structural change for the risk practitioner to recommend?

options.A: Move the risk function under internal audit
options.B: Give the CRO direct access to the board risk committee
options.C: Update reporting to have the CFO sign off each rating
options.D: Have internal audit vet each report before the board

questions.key_concept: The second line sits within management but needs an escalation route to the board that executives cannot block.
questions.pre_read: Notice who controls the risk function's reporting line today.
questions.correct_explanation: The second line sits within management but needs an escalation route that management cannot block. Direct access from the CRO to the board risk committee lets significant risks reach the board even when a senior executive objects, which removes the cause of the omissions. Having internal audit vet each report is the runner-up: it adds a check, but approving management's reports is a management duty that would weaken audit's independence.

wrong_explanations.A: Placing the risk function under internal audit merges the second and third lines, so audit would be assuring work it runs.
wrong_explanations.C: A CFO sign-off makes official the very filter that removed the risks, giving the CFO more control over what the board sees.
wrong_explanations.D: Vetting management's risk reports is a management duty. Audit would lose independence, and the CRO would still have no route of its own.

tips: Eliminate: A merges the second line into internal audit, and C makes the CFO's filter official instead of removing it.
Final two: B beats D because the second line needs its own escalation route to the board; vetting reports pulls internal audit into management work.
Exam cue: when management can block the second line's reporting, look for a direct escalation path to the board, not another approval step.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Journal 2018 Volume 4 (Roles of Three Lines of Defense for Information Security and Governance); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B2.2 (Independence, Challenge and Coordination Across Lines: the second line sits within management with its own reporting line to the CRO and access to the board; independence is the third line's defining need). questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. Procedure change against a standard
questions.question: At a bank, the access control standard requires quarterly access reviews, and the team that owns the review procedure wants to rewrite it to run the reviews yearly. What is the risk practitioner's BEST advice?

options.A: Accept a yearly cycle if the team logs an exception
options.B: Leave the review frequency to the procedure's owner
options.C: Approve the yearly cycle as a procedure update
options.D: Refer the change to the standard's owner to decide

questions.key_concept: A procedure carries out a standard and cannot relax it; changing a mandatory requirement is a decision for the standard's owner.
questions.pre_read: Place each document in the policy hierarchy before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: A procedure sets out the steps for meeting a standard, so it cannot relax what the standard requires. Moving from quarterly to yearly reviews changes the standard itself, which its owner decides, informed by the practitioner's analysis of what a longer cycle would add to risk. Leaving the frequency to the procedure's owner is the runner-up: the team owns its steps, but not the mandatory requirement those steps exist to meet.

wrong_explanations.A: An exception covers a specific, time-limited gap approved by the risk owner. It is not a way to rewrite a requirement, and the practitioner does not accept it.
wrong_explanations.B: Procedure owners control how the steps are done, not the mandatory requirement. A yearly cycle would quietly override the standard.
wrong_explanations.C: Approving a change to a mandatory requirement is not the practitioner's role, and a procedure update cannot relax the standard it carries out.

tips: Eliminate: A uses an exception to make a permanent change, and C has the practitioner approve a change that a procedure cannot make.
Final two: D beats B because procedures must conform to standards; a team can change its steps but not the requirement they meet.
Exam cue: a lower layer of the policy hierarchy cannot override a higher one; a change to a requirement goes to the owner of that layer.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (procedure); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.PO-01 (policy for managing cybersecurity risks is established based on organizational context, cybersecurity strategy and priorities and is communicated and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A4.1 (The Policy Hierarchy: standards make policy measurable and are mandatory, procedures give the steps to meet a standard and are owned by the teams that perform them; trap, guidelines treated as mandatory). Round 3, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario of a bank team rewriting its access review procedure written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. Key unchanged (D).

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). Same risk in two categories
questions.question: At a retail group, one unit files card-data theft under technology risk and another under compliance, so the profile splits the exposure. Which of the following should the risk practitioner recommend as the BEST fix?

options.A: Merge the two units' entries by hand at each group roll-up
options.B: Have IT own the card-data risks filed under technology
options.C: Report each unit's categories to the board as filed
options.D: Propose one group taxonomy for senior management approval

questions.key_concept: A shared risk taxonomy, approved by senior management, lets units record the same risk the same way so it rolls up whole.
questions.pre_read: Ask why the exposure splits, not only how to repair this one case.
questions.correct_explanation: The exposure splits because units sort the same risk into different categories, so the cause is a missing shared taxonomy. A group taxonomy, approved by senior management as part of the risk framework, lets every unit file the risk the same way and the profile show its full size. Merging entries by hand is the runner-up: it repairs this one risk at each roll-up but leaves the cause, and the next mismatch, in place.

wrong_explanations.A: A manual merge treats the symptom. Each roll-up depends on someone spotting mismatches, and other risks split the same way go unnoticed.
wrong_explanations.B: Ownership follows the affected objective, not a category label. Card-data theft hits business and compliance objectives, so IT is not its natural owner.
wrong_explanations.C: Reporting categories as filed passes the split to the board, which then sees the exposure understated in each category.

tips: Eliminate: B lets a category label decide ownership, and C passes the inconsistent categories straight to the board.
Final two: D beats A because a shared taxonomy removes the cause of the split; merging by hand repairs it one roll-up at a time.
Exam cue: when units' risks cannot be combined or compared, look for a common taxonomy or scale approved by senior management.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-06 (a standardized method for calculating, documenting, categorizing and prioritizing cybersecurity risks is established and communicated); NIST IR 8286 Rev. 1 Section 3.8 (Creating and Maintaining an Enterprise-Level Cybersecurity Risk Register)

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Organizational structure, roles and responsibilities. Two accountable names
questions.question: A university's RACI chart lists both the CIO and the registrar as accountable for the risk of exam results being released in error. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Keep the CIO and the registrar jointly accountable
options.B: Name the registrar accountable and the CIO responsible
options.C: Name the CIO accountable and the registrar consulted
options.D: Make the academic board accountable for the risk

questions.key_concept: A RACI chart has one accountable person per activity: the business manager whose objective is at risk, with IT responsible.
questions.pre_read: Recall how many people a RACI chart allows to be accountable for one activity.
questions.correct_explanation: A RACI chart has one accountable person per activity, and accountability for a risk sits with the business manager whose objective it affects. Releasing correct results is the registrar's objective, so the registrar is accountable, while the CIO is responsible for the system controls that support it. Making the CIO accountable is the runner-up: IT runs the platform, but running a system does not make IT the owner of the business risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Joint accountability blurs who decides. When two people are accountable, each can assume the other will act.
wrong_explanations.C: The CIO runs the platform but does not own the outcome. The risk falls on the registrar's objective of releasing correct results.
wrong_explanations.D: A board or committee oversees but cannot be the single accountable person. Accountability needs one named manager with authority.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps two accountable people, and D gives accountability to a body; a RACI chart needs one named accountable person.
Final two: B beats C because the risk hits the registrar's objective; the CIO is responsible for the platform's controls, not accountable for the outcome.
Exam cue: one activity, one accountable person, and it is the business manager whose objective is at risk; IT is usually responsible.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced); ISACA Glossary (risk owner)

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Business processes and resilience. Process spanning three teams
questions.question: An online pharmacy's order fulfillment runs through customer service, IT and the warehouse, and each team's continuity plan covers only its own steps. What should the risk practitioner recommend as the BEST improvement?

options.A: Update the three plans as one document kept by IT
options.B: Test the three fulfillment teams' plans together
options.C: Have each team's plan owner review the other plans
options.D: Name one owner for the end-to-end fulfillment process

questions.key_concept: A critical process that spans teams needs one end-to-end owner accountable for its recovery needs and plans.
questions.pre_read: Compare what each option changes: the plans, the testing or how the process is run.
questions.correct_explanation: Each team plans for its own steps, so no one answers for orders getting through from end to end, and gaps at the handoffs go unowned. Naming one process owner gives fulfillment someone accountable for its recovery needs and for a plan that joins the steps up. A joint test is the runner-up: it could expose handoff gaps, but without a process owner no one is accountable for setting the requirement or closing them.

wrong_explanations.A: Combining documents is clerical work. A single file kept by IT with no process owner still leaves the handoffs between teams unowned.
wrong_explanations.B: A joint test may reveal gaps, but someone must own the process to set recovery needs and fix what the test finds.
wrong_explanations.C: Peer review spreads the work across the same three silos. It adds checks but no one accountable for the whole process.

tips: Eliminate: A treats the gap as a document task for IT, and C keeps three separate plan owners checking one another.
Final two: D beats B because a test can only find gaps; a process owner is needed to set recovery needs and close them.
Exam cue: when a critical process spans teams and each plans alone, look for one accountable process owner before more testing or paperwork.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 DSS04 (Managed Continuity); NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 2.2 (Types of Plans: Business Continuity Plan and Disaster Recovery Plan)

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Appetite for AI uses
questions.question: An insurer's board has a low appetite for harm to policyholders, and units want generative AI in claims and customer service. Which of the following should the risk practitioner propose to BEST apply that appetite?

options.A: Allowed, review-needed and prohibited tiers of AI use
options.B: A minimum accuracy level for each AI model in use
options.C: A ban on customer-facing AI until regulators publish rules
options.D: CISO approval of each AI use case before launch

questions.key_concept: AI appetite becomes usable when it sorts uses into allowed, review-needed and prohibited tiers that owners can apply.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a business owner would need in hand when the next AI request arrives.
questions.correct_explanation: A broad appetite statement guides AI decisions once it says which uses fit. Tiers of allowed, review-needed and prohibited uses turn a low appetite for harm to policyholders into a rule owners can apply to each new use case, with closer review where harm is likelier. A minimum accuracy level is the runner-up: it is measurable, but accuracy is one property of a model and says nothing about which uses the insurer will accept.

wrong_explanations.B: Accuracy is one measure of a model, not an expression of appetite. A highly accurate model can still be used where harm is unacceptable.
wrong_explanations.C: Low appetite is not zero appetite. A ban chooses avoidance for every use before its risk is analyzed, including low-harm uses.
wrong_explanations.D: The CISO covers security, while decisions on harm to policyholders sit with business owners within the board's appetite. One technical approver does not express appetite.

tips: Eliminate: C treats low appetite as zero and bans every use, and D gives decisions on harm to policyholders to a security approver.
Final two: A beats B because tiers say which AI uses the insurer accepts; an accuracy level measures a model, not the insurer's appetite for harm.
Exam cue: to make appetite usable, look for statements that tell owners which activities fit, need extra review or are out of bounds.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-02 (risk appetite and risk tolerance statements are established, communicated and maintained); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 1.3 (processes, procedures and practices are in place to determine the needed level of risk management activities based on the organization's risk tolerance)

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. Praise for a skipped review
questions.question: A fintech's CEO publicly praised a team that launched by skipping the required security review, and two more teams plan to skip it. What is the risk practitioner's MOST effective recommendation to stop the trend?

options.A: Retrain product teams on the security review process
options.B: Ask the CEO to restate support for the review
options.C: Tighten the security review policy for launches
options.D: Have the security team review the launched product

questions.key_concept: Tone at the top drives behavior: when a leader rewards a skipped control, the fix starts with that leader restating the rule.
questions.pre_read: Look for what is driving the other teams' plans.
questions.correct_explanation: Staff take their cue from what leaders reward, and the CEO's praise told teams that skipping the review pays. The trend stops when the same leader restates that the review is required, which changes the signal at its source. Retraining is the runner-up: the teams already know the review exists, since they plan to skip it, so more training cannot outweigh a public reward from the CEO.

wrong_explanations.A: The teams know the review is required; they plan to skip it anyway. Training cannot outweigh a reward signal from the top.
wrong_explanations.C: A stricter policy restates intent, but the CEO's praise rewarded working around it; teams will keep doing so while that signal stands.
wrong_explanations.D: Reviewing the launched product deals with one product's risk but leaves the signal that is driving the other teams' plans.

tips: Eliminate: C tightens a rule the teams already work around, and D treats one product's risk while the trend continues.
Final two: B beats A because the teams already know the rule; the CEO's praise is the cause, so the fix starts with the same leader.
Exam cue: fix the leadership signal in the form it was sent: praise for skipping a control is answered by the leader restating it, an exemption by the leader following it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-01 (organizational leadership is responsible and accountable for cybersecurity risk and fosters a culture that is risk-aware, ethical and continually improving); NIST SP 800-39 Section 2.7 (Organizational Culture)

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. Request to send the full register
questions.question: A shipping company's CIO proposes sending the board the full IT risk register of 240 entries in place of the risk profile, so nothing is hidden. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: Send the full register, ranked from highest rating down
options.B: Keep the profile, traceable to the register entries
options.C: Send the register's high-rated entries in its place
options.D: Send the profile with the full register attached

questions.key_concept: The board decides from the aggregated risk profile; keeping it traceable to the register answers the worry that detail is hidden.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the board needs in order to decide, and what the risk team needs in order to manage.
questions.correct_explanation: The register is the detailed working record; the profile aggregates and prioritizes it into the view leaders need to decide, set against appetite. Keeping the profile, with each item traceable to the register entries behind it, gives the board focus and a way to drill down, so nothing is hidden. Sending both documents is the runner-up: it adds 240 entries to every board pack and buries the few decisions the board must make.

wrong_explanations.A: A ranked register of 240 entries is detail for owners and the risk team. The board needs aggregated exposure against appetite to decide.
wrong_explanations.C: A list of high-rated entries, with no aggregation or comparison against appetite, misses combined exposure and how each category sits against appetite.
wrong_explanations.D: Adding the full register to each pack buries the decisions. Traceability lets the board ask for any detail without receiving all of it.

tips: Eliminate: A and C both send register entries, ranked or filtered, which lack the aggregated view against appetite that the board needs.
Final two: B beats D because a traceable profile keeps the board's pack focused while still letting it drill into any entry.
Exam cue: boards decide from the risk profile against appetite; the register is the working record behind it, available on request.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286 Rev. 1 Section 4.1 (Applying the Enterprise Risk Register and Developing the Enterprise Risk Profile); ISACA Glossary (IT risk profile)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B3.1 (Risk Register Versus Risk Profile: the register is the practitioner's working record, the profile the leaders' decision view, kept traceable to the register; trap, send the board the full register so nothing is left out). questions.subtopic: 1A1 Strategy, goals and objectives. Growth goal against a control
questions.question: A bank's director who owns account opening wants two-minute sign-ups for growth, using an automated ID check that meets regulatory rules but misses more forgeries than staff review. What is the risk practitioner's BEST approach?

options.A: Recommend the design that keeps the manual ID check
options.B: Support the two-minute design that the director prefers
options.C: Ask compliance to set the appetite for ID checks
options.D: Give the director each design's risk against appetite

questions.key_concept: When objectives pull against a control, the practitioner analyzes each option's risk against appetite and the owner of the objective decides.
questions.pre_read: Notice who owns the process and which goals are pulling against each other.
questions.correct_explanation: The trade-off between growth and fraud control belongs to the director who owns account opening, within the appetite leaders have set. Both designs meet regulatory rules, so the choice turns on fraud risk: giving the director each design's fraud exposure against appetite lets them choose with the risk in view. Recommending the manual check is the runner-up: it may prove right, but it settles the trade-off before each design's risk is analyzed.

wrong_explanations.A: Keeping the manual check may be the outcome, but recommending it before each design's fraud risk is analyzed decides the trade-off for the owner and may give up growth needlessly.
wrong_explanations.B: Backing the two-minute design favors growth before its fraud risk is known, and the choice is the director's to make.
wrong_explanations.C: Appetite is set by the board and senior management, not by compliance. Compliance is consulted on the obligations a design must meet.

tips: Eliminate: B backs the faster design before its fraud risk is analyzed, and C gives compliance an appetite-setting role that belongs to leadership.
Final two: D beats A because the owner makes the trade-off; the practitioner shows each design's risk against appetite instead of picking one.
Exam cue: when a business goal and a control conflict, analyze each option against appetite and take it to the owner of the objective.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 EDM03 (Ensured Risk Optimization); ISACA Glossary (risk owner)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A1.1 (Risk in Service of Business Objectives: risk is the effect of uncertainty on objectives, and the executive accountable for the affected goal chooses the treatment) and 1A2.2 (the practitioner brings options with cost and benefit to the owner). questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. Most shares at the top class
questions.question: An engineering firm's new business owners classified 38 of its 40 project file shares as restricted, the top level, so IT cannot tell which need the strongest protection. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Keep the classifications the owners have set
options.B: Update the shares' classes from IT's scan of contents
options.C: Have the owners reapply the scheme's criteria
options.D: Apply the restricted controls to the 40 shares

questions.key_concept: Owners classify assets against the scheme's criteria; when nearly everything lands at the top level, the scheme no longer shows what needs most protection.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a classification scheme is for, then look at what this result does to it.
questions.correct_explanation: Classification exists to show which assets need the strongest protection. With 38 of 40 shares marked restricted it no longer does, so the owners, who hold the decision, should reapply the scheme's criteria to each share. Keeping the owners' labels is the runner-up: classification is their call, but the practitioner challenges a result that defeats the scheme's purpose, and here protection can no longer be prioritized.

wrong_explanations.A: Owners do classify, but a result that puts nearly everything at the top level gives IT no basis to prioritize protection; the practitioner challenges it rather than accepting it.
wrong_explanations.B: IT is the custodian: it applies the protection a class calls for, but deciding the class is the owner's decision.
wrong_explanations.D: Top-level protection for every share spends the strongest controls on data that does not need them and leaves the classification meaningless.

tips: Eliminate: B gives the owner's decision to the custodian, and D spends top-level protection on every share.
Final two: C beats A because owners classify against agreed criteria; the practitioner challenges labels that no longer separate what needs most protection.
Exam cue: classification is the owner's call, made against the scheme's criteria; when almost everything is top level, send it back to the owners.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM-05 (assets are prioritized based on classification, criticality, resources and impact on the mission); ISACA Glossary (data owner)

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. Client notice term
questions.question: A payroll software provider has signed a bank client's contract requiring breach notice within 24 hours, but its incident procedure allows 72 hours. What should the risk practitioner recommend as the BEST action?

options.A: Have the procedure's owner meet the 24-hour term
options.B: Ask the bank to accept the 72-hour procedure instead
options.C: Note the gap for the owner's next policy review
options.D: Rely on cyber insurance to cover late-notice penalties

questions.key_concept: A signed customer contract term is an obligation in force; internal procedures must be aligned so it can be met.
questions.pre_read: Notice whether the contract is proposed or already in force.
questions.correct_explanation: A signed contract term is an obligation the provider has already accepted, so its incident procedure must be able to meet it. Having the procedure's owner bring notice within 24 hours closes the gap before a breach tests it. Asking the bank to accept 72 hours is the runner-up: renegotiation is possible, but the term binds from signing, so any breach handled before a change is agreed would put the provider in default.

wrong_explanations.B: The term binds from signing. Until the bank agrees a change, a breach handled under the 72-hour procedure would breach the contract.
wrong_explanations.C: The obligation applies now. Waiting for that review leaves months in which any breach would be reported late.
wrong_explanations.D: Insurance may cover some costs, but it does not meet the term or protect the client relationship. Accountability stays with the provider.

tips: Eliminate: C waits for a scheduled review while the term already applies, and D treats insurance as if it moved the obligation.
Final two: A beats B because the signed term binds now; aligning the procedure meets it, while renegotiating leaves the gap open meanwhile.
Exam cue: commitments in customer contracts become obligations with owners; close gaps between contract terms and internal procedures.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-03 (legal, regulatory and contractual requirements, including privacy obligations, are understood and managed); COBIT 2019 MEA03 (Managed Compliance With External Requirements)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B5.3 (Contractual Requirements and Service Level Agreements: customer contracts can require breach notice times, which become obligations with owners). questions.subtopic: 1A2 Organizational structure, roles and responsibilities. Owner asks the analyst to choose
questions.question: A distributor's operations director, who owns the warehouse robot outage risk, asks the risk analyst to pick whichever of three treatment options the analyst thinks best. What is the analyst's BEST response?

options.A: Choose the option that cuts the risk the most
options.B: Refer the option choice to the risk committee
options.C: Recommend one option with its cost and benefit
options.D: Choose the cheapest option that meets appetite

questions.key_concept: The practitioner recommends with costs and benefits; the risk owner decides the response, even when asked to hand it over.
questions.pre_read: Notice who owns the risk, and who is being asked to decide.
questions.correct_explanation: The owner decides the response, even when they would rather not. The analyst's job is to recommend, so presenting a preferred option with its cost, benefit and resulting risk lets the director make an informed choice and record it. Referring the choice to the risk committee is the runner-up: a committee oversees and challenges, but handing it the choice moves the decision away from the director who is accountable for the risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Picking the strongest option makes the analyst the decision-maker and may spend more than the risk warrants. The choice belongs to the owner.
wrong_explanations.B: A committee oversees and may challenge, but choosing the response for an owned risk shifts accountability away from the director.
wrong_explanations.D: Even within appetite, choosing and recording the response is the owner's act. The analyst recommends; the director decides.

tips: Eliminate: A and D have the analyst choose the response, which is the risk owner's decision however the choice is made.
Final two: C beats B because the director owns the risk; the analyst recommends to the owner instead of moving the decision to a committee.
Exam cue: when an owner asks the practitioner to decide, recommend with costs and benefits and leave the decision with the owner.

questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A2.2 (Risk Owner, Control Owner and Risk Practitioner: the owner accepts, mitigates, transfers or avoids; the practitioner brings options with cost and benefit to the owner). questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). Framework after major change
questions.question: A media group approved its risk management framework four years ago and has since moved most systems to the cloud and bought two firms. What should the risk practitioner check FIRST in reviewing it?

options.A: Whether its rating scales match those of peer media groups
options.B: Whether internal audit has rated the framework effective
options.C: Whether its scope and roles still cover the whole group
options.D: Whether each unit's register uses its current methods

questions.key_concept: After major change, a framework review starts by checking that its scope and roles still cover the enterprise as it now is.
questions.pre_read: Ask which check the rest of the review depends on.
questions.correct_explanation: After major change, the first question is whether the framework still reaches the group as it now is. Cloud services and two acquired firms may sit outside its scope and roles, so checking coverage shows what the revision must add before senior management approves it. Checking how units use its methods is the runner-up: adoption matters, but it can only be judged inside the existing scope, which may leave out the new firms.

wrong_explanations.A: Peer comparison may inform the scales, but it does not show whether the group's own changes are covered.
wrong_explanations.B: An audit rating describes the framework as it was. It does not show whether the new firms and cloud services fall inside it.
wrong_explanations.D: Checking use of the methods tests adoption within the current scope; the acquired firms and cloud services may not be in that scope at all.

tips: Eliminate: A benchmarks against peers and B relies on a past audit rating; neither shows whether the group's changes are covered.
Final two: C beats D because the changes in the stem are about reach; adoption can only be checked inside a scope that may omit the new firms.
Exam cue: after a merger, acquisition or platform shift, check first that the framework's scope and roles reach the changed enterprise.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. Request for loss figures
questions.question: An industry peer group asks a bank's risk analyst for the bank's ransomware loss figures to build a sector benchmark. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Share the figures under the group's confidentiality promise
options.B: Share the figures once system names are removed
options.C: Decline to take part in the sector benchmark
options.D: Seek the bank's approval before sharing the figures

questions.key_concept: Information gained at work is released only with the organization's approval or under legal authority, so ask before sharing it.
questions.pre_read: Ask who has the right to decide what happens to the figures.
questions.correct_explanation: The ISACA Code of Professional Ethics asks members to keep information gained in their work confidential and not release it to inappropriate parties. The loss figures belong to the bank, so the first step is to seek approval from whoever can authorize their release, who may agree, set conditions or refuse. Declining is the runner-up: it protects the data, but it makes the bank's decision for it and may give up a useful benchmark.

wrong_explanations.A: A peer group's promise does not authorize release. The figures are the bank's information, and only the bank can decide who receives them.
wrong_explanations.B: Removing system names may reduce harm, but the loss figures are still the bank's confidential information, released without its approval.
wrong_explanations.C: Declining protects the data but decides for the bank, which may choose to share approved figures if the benchmark serves it.

tips: Eliminate: A treats an outsider's promise as permission, and B assumes that removing names makes the bank's data the analyst's to release.
Final two: D beats C because release is the bank's decision; the analyst seeks approval instead of refusing on the bank's behalf.
Exam cue: information gained at work stays confidential unless its owner, or the law, authorizes release; ask before sharing.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Business processes and resilience. Exercise gap with a planned fix
questions.question: A broadcaster's continuity exercise showed its backup studio cannot run playout remotely, and the head of playout approved a fix due in six months. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation for the continuity plan?

options.A: A tested workaround for playout until the fix is live
options.B: A longer recovery time objective for playout until then
options.C: A note that remote playout arrives in six months
options.D: A repeat of the same exercise once the fix is done

questions.key_concept: When an exercise exposes a continuity gap with a fix months away, the plan needs a tested interim workaround so the process can continue meanwhile.
questions.pre_read: Ask what would happen if a disruption came next week.
questions.correct_explanation: For six months, a disruption would find the backup studio unable to run playout remotely, and the approved fix does nothing until it is live. The plan needs an interim workaround, such as staff working on site at the backup studio, agreed with the head of playout and tested. Repeating the exercise after the fix is the runner-up: it proves the fix, but leaves the six months before it uncovered.

wrong_explanations.B: The recovery time objective reflects how long the business can be without playout; lengthening it to fit the gap moves the target, not the exposure.
wrong_explanations.C: A note about a future capability says what will exist, not how to keep playout running if a disruption comes first.
wrong_explanations.D: Retesting proves the fix once it exists; it does not cover a disruption in the six months before then.

tips: Eliminate: B lengthens the recovery objective to fit the gap, and C records a capability that does not exist yet.
Final two: A beats D because a disruption could come before the fix; a retest proves the fix but covers nothing until then.
Exam cue: a continuity plan must work with what exists today; when a fix is months away, add a tested workaround and retest after the fix.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. Tools found at each count
questions.question: Each yearly asset count at an architecture firm finds cloud tools bought on staff expense cards that no one listed. Which of the following is the BEST fix for the risk practitioner to recommend?

options.A: Run the asset count each quarter instead of yearly
options.B: Record new tools at expense and purchase approval
options.C: Have IT scan the office network for new devices
options.D: Have IT block new cloud sign-ups from company laptops

questions.key_concept: Keep the inventory current by linking it to purchasing and change processes, not by more frequent clean-up counts.
questions.pre_read: Ask how these tools enter the firm without being recorded.
questions.correct_explanation: The tools are missed because they enter through expense claims, a route the inventory process does not watch, so the cause is a process gap. Recording each new tool when its expense or purchase is approved captures it, with an owner, as it arrives. A quarterly count is the runner-up: it finds the tools sooner, but it still relies on clean-up after the fact instead of recording them when they are bought.

wrong_explanations.A: A more frequent count shortens the gap but keeps the same cause. Tools still arrive unrecorded and are found only later.
wrong_explanations.C: Network scans find devices on the firm's network. Cloud subscriptions bought on cards run on the provider's systems and are easily missed.
wrong_explanations.D: Blocking sign-ups stops tools staff may need and is a control chosen before the risk is analyzed; it does not fix how tools are recorded.

tips: Eliminate: C looks for devices when the missing assets are cloud subscriptions, and D blocks tools instead of fixing how they are recorded.
Final two: B beats A because recording tools at purchase removes the cause; counting more often only finds them sooner.
Exam cue: when an inventory keeps missing the same kind of asset, fix the process that lets it in unrecorded, not how often it is counted.
