questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. Unchallenged self-assessments
questions.question: Business units at an insurer rate their own controls in yearly self-assessments, and the risk team passes the ratings to the board unchanged. What should the risk practitioner recommend as the BEST change?

options.A: Have internal audit check each self-assessment first
options.B: Have business units rate one another's controls
options.C: Have the risk team challenge ratings before reporting them
options.D: Replace the self-assessments with the risk team's ratings

questions.key_concept: The second line reviews and challenges first-line self-assessments before they are reported; internal audit assures independently.
questions.pre_read: Match each option to the line of defense it would put to work.
questions.correct_explanation: Self-assessment by the first line is a sound start, but the second line's job is to review and challenge it before it reaches the board. Having the risk team test the ratings against evidence, and question those that look optimistic, gives the board ratings it can rely on. Having internal audit check each one is the runner-up: audit gives periodic independent assurance, but routine challenge of first-line ratings is second-line work.

wrong_explanations.A: Internal audit assures on a risk-based plan; checking each unit's self-assessment every year does the second line's routine oversight for it.
wrong_explanations.B: Peer rating still leaves first-line managers marking first-line work. It adds no independent oversight or challenge.
wrong_explanations.D: Replacing the units' ratings takes risk and control ownership away from the first line, which must own and assess its own controls.

tips: Eliminate: B keeps the rating inside the first line, and D has the second line take over ratings that the first line owns.
Final two: C beats A because challenging first-line ratings is the second line's routine role; internal audit gives periodic independent assurance.
Exam cue: the first line self-assesses, the second line challenges, the third line assures; match each fix to the line whose job it is.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Journal 2018 Volume 4 (Roles of Three Lines of Defense for Information Security and Governance)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B2.1 (The Three Lines and Their Jobs: first line owns and runs controls, second line monitors, challenges and reports, third line gives independent assurance; trap, the second line owns the risks it monitors). Round 3, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario of an insurer's control self-assessments passed to the board unchallenged written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Strategy, goals and objectives. Approving AI pilots
questions.question: A hotel group's AI steering group receives about a dozen requests for generative AI pilots each quarter. Which of the following should the risk practitioner propose as the MOST important criterion for approving each pilot?

options.A: The accuracy objective the tool met in its maker's tests
options.B: The business savings the vendor projects for it
options.C: The business objective the pilot is meant to serve
options.D: The data science team's capacity to support the pilot

questions.key_concept: AI initiatives start from a business objective, which gives value, risk and ownership something to be judged against.
questions.pre_read: Ask which criterion the other criteria would be measured against.
questions.correct_explanation: AI initiatives start from a business purpose: without a defined objective there is nothing to measure benefit or risk against, and no clear owner. Requiring each pilot to name the objective it serves lets the hotel group judge its value and risk through that objective and assign the manager who owns it. Vendor-projected savings are the runner-up: they look like business value, but they are the vendor's claim, not a goal the group has set.

wrong_explanations.A: The maker's test accuracy describes the tool, not why the group needs it. A precise tool can still serve no goal worth its risk.
wrong_explanations.B: Projected savings are the vendor's estimate, not a business goal. They can be judged only against an objective the group has set.
wrong_explanations.D: Support capacity matters for delivery, but it ranks pilots by what the team can handle, not by what the business needs.

tips: Eliminate: A judges the tool's technical quality, and D ranks pilots by team capacity; neither says why the business needs the pilot.
Final two: C beats B because savings claimed by a vendor are judged against an objective the group sets; the objective comes first.
Exam cue: for new technology, AI included, the first gate is the business objective it serves; value, risk and ownership follow from it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MAP 1.3 (the organization's mission and relevant goals for AI technology are understood and documented); COBIT 2019 APO02 (Managed Strategy)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A1.2 (The Goals Cascade and Strategic Change: AI initiatives start from a business purpose, with a risk owner and appetite fit agreed before they scale; trap, a new AI tool is only a technology project). Round 3, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario of a hotel group setting a gate for generative AI pilots written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Appetite change and IT thresholds
questions.question: A telecom's executive committee lowered its appetite for customer data risk, but IT's thresholds for the related KRIs still reflect the old level. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Keep IT owners' thresholds until the KRI review cycle
options.B: Have the executive committee set each IT KRI threshold
options.C: Have the IT owners accept the gap to the new appetite
options.D: Propose thresholds that match the new appetite

questions.key_concept: Enterprise appetite decisions flow down: KRI thresholds are recalibrated to a changed appetite, proposed by the practitioner.
questions.pre_read: Trace how a decision at the top reaches the indicators IT watches.
questions.correct_explanation: Appetite set at the top only works when it flows down into the limits that trigger action. Proposing KRI thresholds that match the lower appetite, for the risk owners to agree, means IT warnings fire at the level leaders now accept. Asking the executive committee to set each threshold is the runner-up: the committee sets appetite, but detailed operating thresholds are agreed below it by the risk owners, with the practitioner proposing them.

wrong_explanations.A: A change in appetite is a reason to recalibrate now. Old thresholds let exposure the committee no longer accepts pass without warning.
wrong_explanations.B: The committee sets appetite; detailed KRI thresholds are agreed below it by the risk owners, with the practitioner proposing values.
wrong_explanations.C: Accepting exposure above appetite is beyond an IT owner's authority and goes against the committee's decision to lower appetite.

tips: Eliminate: A leaves thresholds at a level leaders no longer accept, and C has owners accept exposure above the new appetite.
Final two: D beats B because leaders set appetite and risk owners agree the thresholds beneath it; the practitioner proposes them.
Exam cue: when appetite changes, expect the thresholds, KRIs and policies below it to be recalibrated; decisions at the top flow down.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-02 (risk appetite and risk tolerance statements are established, communicated and maintained); NIST IR 8286C Rev. 1 Section 5.1 (Key CSRM Mechanisms: risk tolerance is translated into security controls, KPIs and KRIs)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B4.2 (Setting and Expressing Risk Appetite: appetite is built into KRI thresholds) and 1B1.1 (IT Risk Within Enterprise Risk: enterprise leaders set appetite, and decisions on IT risk flow back down as guidance so local teams act within enterprise appetite). Round 3, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario of a telecom lowering appetite while IT KRI thresholds lag written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. Review fixes 4 Nov 2026 (standards audit and concept review): correct_explanation, wrong B and tip 2 no longer call threshold-setting 'management's work' (the executive committee is senior management): risk owners agree the thresholds below appetite, with the practitioner proposing them. Re-lettered: key D (was C), options C and D swapped, to break the run of three C keys at crisc_d1_065 to 067. Cross-domain fixes 4 Nov 2026: retagged from 1B1 to 1B4, since it tests the appetite to tolerance to threshold cascade; the provenance now names 1B4.2 first so the practice link moves with it. Cue pass 12 Nov 2026 (fixed periods): option A dropped an incidental period word.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. Combined exposure above appetite
questions.question: The risk practitioner's aggregation shows an airport operator's 12 supplier risks, each within its own tolerance, together exceed the board's appetite for supplier risk. What should the practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Escalate the combined exposure to the board
options.B: Have each owner accept their own risk on record
options.C: Ask each owner to cut their risk by an equal share
options.D: Hold the finding for the next board profile review

questions.key_concept: Combined exposure can breach appetite while each risk is within tolerance; escalate the breach to the level that set appetite.
questions.pre_read: Separate the limits that apply to single risks from the limit that applies to the total.
questions.correct_explanation: Tolerances limit each risk, but appetite limits the total, so exposure can breach appetite while every risk stays inside its own limit. A breach of the board's appetite goes to the board, which can direct treatment, accept the position for a time or revisit the limit. Asking each owner to cut an equal share is the runner-up: owners may well act, but the practitioner would be choosing the response to a board-level breach.

wrong_explanations.B: Each owner could accept a risk within its own tolerance, but together the risks exceed the board's appetite, and no single owner can accept that breach.
wrong_explanations.C: An equal cut is a response chosen by the practitioner. The board that set the appetite decides how the breach is handled, and cuts should follow the risk.
wrong_explanations.D: A breach of appetite is a governance event. Waiting for that review leaves the board unaware of exposure above its limit.

tips: Eliminate: B has each owner accept their own risk when the breach is of the board's limit on the total, and D holds a breach until a scheduled review.
Final two: A beats C because a breach of the board's appetite goes to the board; the practitioner does not choose the response on its behalf.
Exam cue: aggregate exposure can breach appetite even when each risk is within tolerance; escalate to whoever set the limit that was breached.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 3.2 Task 2-6 (Determine Risk: several moderate-level risks can aggregate to a higher level of risk); ISACA Glossary (risk aggregation); ISACA Glossary (risk appetite)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B3.2 (Aggregation and Keeping the Profile Current: aggregate related risks, report against appetite) and 1B4.3 (a breach is escalated to the risk owner and the level that set the limit). Round 3, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario of an airport operator's supplier risks breaching appetite only in combination written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. Cross-domain fixes 4 Nov 2026 (round 6): option B is now owner acceptance on record of risks each within tolerance, a stated reason acceptance is wrong (the total breaches the board's appetite), as a counter-example to the within-appetite acceptance cue; why-B and the Eliminate tip follow (cross-domain gate). Cue pass 12 Nov 2026 (fixed periods): option D dropped an incidental period word.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. Policy behind a business change
questions.question: A manufacturer's device policy, due for review in 18 months, predates letting staff read work email on personal phones, a risk the risk analyst rates above appetite. What is the analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Ask the policy owner to review the policy now
options.B: Keep the policy until the owner's scheduled review
options.C: Issue staff a guideline on using personal phones
options.D: Have IT publish a personal phone standard

questions.key_concept: Significant change triggers a policy review through the policy owner; the standards beneath the policy then follow it.
questions.pre_read: Notice what changed and whether the policy has kept up.
questions.correct_explanation: Policies are reviewed on schedule and after significant change, and allowing personal phones, with a risk above appetite, is such a change. Asking the policy owner to review now starts the route by which the policy is updated and approved by senior management, so the standards beneath it can follow. Having IT publish a phone standard is the runner-up: a standard may well be needed, but without the policy behind it, it lacks management's direction.

wrong_explanations.B: Scheduled reviews are a minimum. Significant change triggers a review in its own right, especially when the risk is above appetite.
wrong_explanations.C: A guideline is advisory, so staff may set it aside. It cannot bring a risk above appetite back within limits.
wrong_explanations.D: Standards carry out policy. An IT standard issued ahead of the policy lacks management's direction and may not fit the business decision.

tips: Eliminate: B waits for the schedule despite a significant change, and C answers a risk above appetite with advisory guidance.
Final two: A beats D because the policy states management's intent and comes first; the standards beneath it then follow that direction.
Exam cue: when new technology or a business decision outpaces policy, go through the policy owner for an event-driven review.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.PO-02 (policy for managing cybersecurity risks is reviewed, updated, communicated and enforced to reflect changes); ISACA Glossary (policy)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A4.3 (Policy Review and AI Acceptable Use: each policy has an owner and a review cycle plus a review after major change; gaps go to the policy owner, who proposes changes for senior management approval). Round 3, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario of a manufacturer allowing work email on personal phones ahead of its policy written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. Risk handed to a provider
questions.question: A charity's HR director, who owns payroll outage risk, wants it deleted from the register now that a provider with a strong SLA runs payroll. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: Delete the risk and have the HR director track SLA reports
options.B: Keep the risk in the register under the HR director
options.C: Name the provider's account manager as the risk's owner
options.D: Close the risk and log the SLA in the contract register

questions.key_concept: Outsourcing and SLAs move work, not accountability: the risk stays in the register with an internal owner, re-rated for the SLA.
questions.pre_read: Ask who would feel the impact if the provider failed.
questions.correct_explanation: Outsourcing can transfer or share part of the risk, as the ISACA Glossary notes, but not the accountability: if payroll fails, the charity's staff go unpaid whatever the contract says. Keeping it in the register under the HR director keeps it owned, re-rated for the SLA and monitored. Deleting it and tracking SLA reports is the runner-up: the monitoring is right, but the remaining risk would drop out of rating and reporting.

wrong_explanations.A: Tracking SLA reports is monitoring, but deleting the risk takes the exposure that stays with the charity out of the register, so it is no longer rated or reported.
wrong_explanations.C: An outside account manager cannot own the charity's risk. Accountability for the effect on staff stays with the charity's HR director.
wrong_explanations.D: An SLA is a response that may lower the risk, not remove it. Closing the entry hides the exposure that remains with the charity.

tips: Eliminate: C gives the charity's risk to an outside party, and D closes the risk as if the SLA had removed it.
Final two: B beats A because the remaining risk must stay in the register to be rated and reported; SLA reports monitor it but do not replace the entry.
Exam cue: contracts and SLAs move work or cost, never accountability; the risk stays in the register with an internal owner.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.SC-07 (the risks posed by a supplier, their products and services and other third parties are understood, recorded, prioritized, assessed, responded to and monitored); ISACA Glossary (risk transfer)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B5.3 (Contractual Requirements and Service Level Agreements: handing a task to a supplier does not hand over accountability; trap, once a supplier signs an SLA the risk of its outages is transferred to it). Round 3, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario of a charity HR director asking to delete payroll outage risk after outsourcing written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. Review fixes 4 Nov 2026 (standards audit and concept review): correct_explanation now says outsourcing can transfer or share part of the risk, as the cited Glossary entry on risk transfer does, but not the accountability; the delete-the-risk option now names the HR director, so the stem's 'HR director' no longer appears only in the key (blind test), and its explanation and tip 2 now rest on the risk leaving the register rather than on having no owner. questions.subtopic: 1A1 Strategy, goals and objectives. Objective with no target
questions.question: A city council's deputy chief executive sponsors an objective of 'faster resident services' with no target, and asks the risk practitioner to rate the IT risks to it. What should the practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Assess each IT risk by its technical severity score
options.B: Help the sponsor define how success will be measured
options.C: Give the sponsor a target from IT's current response times
options.D: Rate the risks against the council's overall appetite

questions.key_concept: Risk to an objective can be rated only once the objective has a measure, which its owner defines with the practitioner's help.
questions.pre_read: Read what the sponsor's objective says, and what it leaves out.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk is rated by its effect on an objective, and 'faster' gives nothing to measure that effect against, so ratings would be guesses. Helping the sponsor define the measure, such as days to resolve a request, lets each IT risk be rated by how far it could set that target back. A target taken from IT's current response times is the runner-up: measurable, but it records what IT achieves today, not what residents need.

wrong_explanations.A: Severity scores rate technical flaws, not their effect on resident services; without a measure for the objective, risks cannot be ranked by business impact.
wrong_explanations.C: IT's current times describe capability, not need. The sponsor who owns the objective decides what 'faster' must mean for residents.
wrong_explanations.D: Appetite says how much risk leaders accept; it cannot show how far an IT risk would slow services that have no measure yet.

tips: Eliminate: A assesses technical severity instead of effect on the objective, and D compares risks with appetite before their impact can be measured.
Final two: B beats C because the objective's sponsor sets what success means; a target copied from IT's current performance records capability, not need.
Exam cue: when an objective has no measure, help its owner define one before rating the risks to it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-01 (the organizational mission is understood and informs cybersecurity risk management); COBIT 2019 APO02 (Managed Strategy)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A1.1 (Risk in Service of Business Objectives: start from measurable objectives and express each risk by its effect on them) and 1A1.2 (an objective's owner gives it a measure so risk to it can be rated). Round 4, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario (a city council objective of faster resident services with no target) written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. Cue pass 5 Nov 2026: A now opens with 'Assess' (the assess family was keyed about half the time).

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Organizational structure, roles and responsibilities. Role of the chief risk officer
questions.question: Which of the following is the MOST appropriate role for a bank's chief risk officer (CRO)?

options.A: Running the risk function and reporting the risk profile
options.B: Approving the enterprise risk appetite for the board
options.C: Giving independent assurance on risk management
options.D: Running the bank's security operations for the CIO

questions.key_concept: The CRO runs the second-line risk function and reports the profile; the board sets appetite with senior management, and internal audit gives independent assurance.
questions.pre_read: For each option, ask which role or body normally holds that decision.
questions.correct_explanation: The CRO heads the second-line risk function: keeping the framework working, challenging ratings and reporting the risk profile to senior management and the board. Approving appetite is the runner-up because CROs draft and explain it, but appetite expresses how much risk the enterprise chooses to take, so the board, with senior management, sets and approves it; the CRO then monitors against it.

wrong_explanations.B: The CRO proposes and monitors appetite. Setting it reflects strategy and stakeholder expectations, which the board, with senior management, decides.
wrong_explanations.C: Independent assurance over risk management is internal audit's role. The CRO runs the risk function, so the CRO cannot give an independent view of it.
wrong_explanations.D: Security operations is first-line IT work under the CIO or CISO; a CRO running it could no longer challenge it.

tips: Eliminate: C is internal audit's third-line assurance role, and D is first-line security work the risk function should challenge, not run.
Final two: A beats B because the CRO runs the risk function and reports; approving appetite is the board's decision, with senior management, on the CRO's analysis.
Exam cue: the CRO proposes, monitors and reports; the board sets appetite, business managers own the risks and internal audit assures.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced); ISACA Glossary (risk appetite)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A2.1 (Board, Senior Management and the Risk Committee: the CRO runs the risk function and reports the profile; trap, the CRO approves appetite). questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. Own error in a reported rating
questions.question: A risk analyst confirms that a formula error in their own model understated a data-loss risk the board saw last month as within appetite; corrected, it exceeds appetite. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Correct the rating in next quarter's board report
options.B: Ask the risk owner whether to report the correction
options.C: Report the corrected rating to the owner and board
options.D: Record the error and its fix in the model's change log

questions.key_concept: Due care and disclosure of significant facts apply to the practitioner's own errors: correct them promptly with those who relied on them.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the board saw last month with what is true now.
questions.correct_explanation: The board relied on a wrong rating, and the corrected risk is above its appetite, a significant fact it needs to decide. Due care and the duty to disclose significant facts mean reporting the correction promptly to the risk owner and the board, with its cause. Correcting it in next quarter's report is the runner-up: the record ends up right, but the board would carry an unknown breach of its appetite for months.

wrong_explanations.A: The correction is right, but waiting a quarter leaves the board unaware that a risk it reviewed is above its appetite.
wrong_explanations.B: The owner decides the response, not whether facts are reported. A confirmed error the board relied on must be corrected with those who relied on it.
wrong_explanations.D: Recording the fix keeps the model's history accurate, but it tells no one that a risk the board reviewed now exceeds its appetite.

tips: Eliminate: B lets the owner decide whether facts are reported, and D records the fix without telling those who relied on the rating.
Final two: C beats A because a risk the board thinks is within appetite now exceeds it; disclosing significant facts cannot wait for the next scheduled report.
Exam cue: when your own error changed what leaders relied on, correct it promptly with those who relied on it.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Code of Professional Ethics (inform appropriate parties of all significant facts); ISACA Code of Professional Ethics (objectivity, due diligence and professional care)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A3.3 (Professional Ethics and Ethical AI Use: inform the right parties of all significant facts, including the practitioner's own errors once found). Round 4, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario (an analyst's own model error that hid an appetite breach from the board) written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. Review fixes 4 Nov 2026 (standards audit and concept review): distractor D (review the model's other ratings first) replaced, since checking a formula error's reach before reporting could be defended; D now records the fix in the model's change log, which tells no one who relied on the rating. Wrong explanation D and the Eliminate tip rewritten to match.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. Encryption left in a guideline
questions.question: A SaaS provider's cloud guideline recommends encrypting storage buckets, and the risk analyst finds 40% unencrypted, a risk rated above appetite. What should the analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Strengthen the guideline's wording on bucket encryption
options.B: Ask teams to record why they departed from the cloud guideline
options.C: Log encryption exceptions for the buckets, with expiry dates
options.D: Make bucket encryption a requirement in the cloud standard

questions.key_concept: Guidelines advise and allow departures; a control needed to keep risk within appetite belongs in a mandatory standard.
questions.pre_read: Check which layer of the policy hierarchy the encryption rule sits in now.
questions.correct_explanation: A guideline only advises, so teams may depart from it: acceptable for good practice, but not for a control whose absence leaves risk above appetite. Moving encryption into the mandatory cloud standard, through the standard's owner, makes the control required and checkable. Asking teams to record their reasons is the runner-up: it suits a guideline, but documented departures would still leave 40% of buckets exposed beyond appetite.

wrong_explanations.A: Stronger wording is still advice: teams may depart from a guideline, so the exposure above appetite can remain.
wrong_explanations.B: Recorded reasons suit advisory guidance, but they keep encryption optional while the analyzed risk is above appetite.
wrong_explanations.C: Exceptions are departures from a mandatory requirement. While encryption is only recommended, there is nothing to grant an exception from.

tips: Eliminate: A only strengthens advice that teams may still depart from, and C grants exceptions to a rule that is not mandatory.
Final two: D beats B because a control needed to keep risk within appetite belongs in a mandatory standard; recorded reasons suit advisory guidance only.
Exam cue: if a practice must be followed, put it in a standard or procedure; guidelines advise and allow departures.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (guideline); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.PO-01 (policy for managing cybersecurity risks is established based on organizational context, cybersecurity strategy and priorities and is communicated and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A4.1 (The Policy Hierarchy: guidelines advise; a practice that must be followed belongs in a standard; every layer traces to appetite). Round 4, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario (a SaaS provider's encryption rule left in an advisory guideline) written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. Review fixes 4 Nov 2026 (standards audit and concept review): distractor A (discipline the teams) replaced with stronger guideline wording, so the item no longer mirrors CISA d5_205; wrong explanation A and the Eliminate tip rewritten.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Business processes and resilience. Workaround short of capacity
questions.question: A council's continuity plan for losing its offices has all 900 staff work from home at the same time, but its remote access supports 250 users at once. What is the risk practitioner's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Most staff could not connect when the plan is used
options.B: Home working under the plan is untested with 900 staff
options.C: Home networks are less secure than the office network
options.D: Services will run more slowly from home than in offices

questions.key_concept: A continuity workaround counts only if it can deliver the service level the business needs at the scale the plan assumes.
questions.pre_read: Work out what would happen on the first morning the plan is used.
questions.correct_explanation: A continuity workaround counts only if it can carry the minimum service the council needs while its offices are lost. Remote access for 250 users means most of the 900 staff could not work when the plan is used, so the plan fails at the moment it is needed. The lack of a full-scale test is the runner-up: testing matters, but the capacity figures already show the gap that a test would confirm.

wrong_explanations.B: A full-scale test would confirm the problem, but the capacity figures already show that most staff could not connect; that known gap matters more.
wrong_explanations.C: Home network security is a separate risk to manage. It does not decide whether the council can keep working while its offices are lost.
wrong_explanations.D: Workarounds can be slower than normal working. What matters is whether they carry the service level needed, and this one cannot reach most staff.

tips: Eliminate: C raises a security risk, not a continuity gap, and D treats slower working as the problem when workarounds are expected to be slower.
Final two: A beats B because the capacity figures already show the workaround failing; a test would confirm what the numbers show.
Exam cue: judge a continuity workaround by whether it can carry the needed service level at the scale the plan assumes.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (service delivery objective); NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 2.2 (Types of Plans: Business Continuity Plan and Disaster Recovery Plan)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A5.2 (Continuity and Recovery Plans as Risk Responses: a workaround counts only if it can carry the minimum service level the owner needs). Round 4, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario (a council's work-from-home plan with remote access for a quarter of its staff) written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. Review fixes 4 Nov 2026 (standards audit and concept review): stem now says all 900 staff work from home at the same time, so the capacity gap cannot be read as staggered shifts.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. Decisions left to the custodian
questions.question: At a clinic group, IT runs the patient records database that the clinical director owns. Which of the following should the risk practitioner consider MOST appropriate for IT to decide on its own?

options.A: How long patient records are kept before they are deleted
options.B: When patient record backups run within the agreed recovery point
options.C: Which classification level the patient records should carry
options.D: Which outside partners may receive copies of patient records

questions.key_concept: Owners set an asset's requirements, such as class, retention and sharing; custodians decide how to meet them day to day.
questions.pre_read: For each option, ask whose need or decision the action serves.
questions.correct_explanation: A custodian looks after an asset day to day and decides how to meet the requirements its owner sets. Scheduling backups to meet the agreed recovery point is that kind of decision: the clinical director set the need, and IT chooses how to deliver it. Retention is the runner-up because IT runs the deletion jobs, but how long records are kept is a business and legal decision for the owner; IT carries it out.

wrong_explanations.A: IT carries out deletion, but how long patient records are kept is the owner's decision, based on business and legal needs.
wrong_explanations.C: Classification reflects how sensitive and critical the records are to the business, which the owner judges; IT applies the protection the class requires.
wrong_explanations.D: Sharing records outside the group is a decision about the data's use, which belongs to the owner, not the custodian holding it.

tips: Eliminate: C and D are classic owner decisions, the data's class and who outside may receive it, which a custodian applies but does not set.
Final two: B beats A because IT chooses how to meet a recovery need the owner agreed; retention, though IT runs the deletions, is set by the owner.
Exam cue: owners decide what is needed and who may use the data; custodians decide how to deliver it day to day.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (data custodian); ISACA Glossary (data owner)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A6.1 (Asset Inventory and Ownership: owners answer for use and protection; custodians such as IT look after the asset and decide how to meet the owner's requirements). Round 4, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario (a clinic group's patient records database run by IT) written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). Investments approved without risk input
questions.question: A logistics firm's investment approvals do not ask for risk input, and the risks of a new $3,000,000 warehouse platform surfaced only after signing. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Assess the platform's risk now for the enterprise register
options.B: Move the enterprise risk review from yearly to quarterly
options.C: Add a risk review step to investment approvals
options.D: Propose CFO approval for investments over $1,000,000

questions.key_concept: ERM works when risk input is built into decisions such as investment approvals, not run as a separate, after-the-fact review.
questions.pre_read: Note what the approval process asks for today.
questions.correct_explanation: The platform's risks surfaced late because investment decisions are made without risk input, so the same will happen with the next purchase. Building a risk review into investment approvals puts risk in front of decision makers while options are still open, as ERM integration intends. Assessing this platform's risk now is the runner-up: the register needs it, but it treats one late discovery and leaves the approval process unchanged.

wrong_explanations.A: The platform's risk does need assessing, but that treats one case; the next investment would again be approved without risk input.
wrong_explanations.B: A more frequent enterprise review still runs apart from decisions. Integration means risk input at the point each investment is approved.
wrong_explanations.D: A higher approval level changes who signs, not what they know; the CFO would still approve without risk input.

tips: Eliminate: B speeds up a review that sits apart from decisions, and D raises the approval level without adding any risk input.
Final two: C beats A because the gap is in how investments are approved; assessing one platform fixes this case but not the next.
Exam cue: when risk keeps arriving after decisions are made, build risk input into the decision process itself.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-03 (cybersecurity risk management activities and outcomes are included in enterprise risk management processes); COBIT 2019 APO05 (Managed Portfolio)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B1.3 (The Risk Management Framework and Its Approval: the framework is built into strategy, planning and investment decisions, not run as a side process). Round 4, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario (a logistics firm's platform bought through an approval process with no risk step) written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. Review fixes 4 Nov 2026 (standards audit and concept review): pre_read no longer frames the one-off versus root-cause choice. Cue pass 2, 5 Nov 2026: D reworded (was 'Ask the CFO to approve'): a wrong option now opens 'Propose', so that opening no longer points to the key.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. Assurance over the risk process
questions.question: A bank's board risk committee wants an independent view of whether the IT risk management process, run by the risk team, works. Which of the following should the risk practitioner suggest as the BEST provider?

options.A: The risk team, through a documented self-assessment
options.B: Internal audit, as part of its assurance plan
options.C: The CIO's office, which runs the IT systems
options.D: The compliance team, as a separate function

questions.key_concept: Internal audit, the third line, gives the board independent assurance that governance and the risk management process work.
questions.pre_read: Note who runs the process today.
questions.correct_explanation: Independent assurance comes from the third line: internal audit reports to the board's audit committee and does not run the process it reviews, so it can give the board an objective view of whether the risk team's process works. The compliance team is the runner-up: it is separate from the risk team, but it is a second-line function within management, so its view is not independent assurance.

wrong_explanations.A: A self-assessment can help the risk team improve, but a team reviewing its own process cannot give the committee an independent view.
wrong_explanations.C: The CIO's office is first line: it owns systems the process covers, so it is neither independent of the process nor placed to judge it.
wrong_explanations.D: Compliance is separate from the risk team but is still a second-line function within management; independent assurance is the third line's role.

tips: Eliminate: A has the risk team review its own process, and C asks the first line, whose systems the process covers, to judge it.
Final two: B beats D because independent assurance over the risk process is internal audit's role; compliance is a separate team but still in the second line.
Exam cue: when the board wants independent assurance that risk management itself works, look to internal audit, the third line.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Journal 2018 Volume 4 (Roles of Three Lines of Defense for Information Security and Governance); COBIT 2019 MEA04 (Managed Assurance)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B2.1 (The Three Lines and Their Jobs: the third line, internal audit, gives independent assurance, including on whether the risk management process itself works) and 1B1.3 (framework effectiveness is assessed, including by internal audit). Round 4, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario (a bank's board risk committee seeking an independent view of the risk team's process) written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. Ratings older than a major change
questions.question: Preparing a hospital's quarterly risk profile, due in three weeks, the risk analyst finds 40% of its clinical-system ratings predate last year's move of those systems to the cloud. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Update those ratings with their owners before reporting
options.B: Send the profile with a note on the ratings' age
options.C: Lower those ratings for the cloud's stronger controls
options.D: Drop those risks from the profile and tell their owners

questions.key_concept: A risk profile is only as current as the ratings behind it; refresh ratings that predate a major change before reporting.
questions.pre_read: Notice what changed after the ratings were set.
questions.correct_explanation: The profile is the leaders' decision view, so its ratings must describe the enterprise as it is. Ratings set before the cloud move may now be wrong in either direction, and with three weeks until the profile is due there is time to refresh them with their owners. Reporting with a note on their age is the runner-up: honest, but leaders would still decide on figures that may not describe today's risk.

wrong_explanations.B: A caveat suits a gap that cannot be closed before reporting; with three weeks left, these ratings can be refreshed, while a note leaves leaders deciding on stale figures.
wrong_explanations.C: The cloud move may have changed risk either way; lowering ratings without evidence credits controls no one has assessed.
wrong_explanations.D: Dropping the risks hides 40% of the exposure from leaders; telling the owners does not put it back in the profile.

tips: Eliminate: C credits the cloud with lower risk before anyone has assessed it, and D removes a large share of exposure from the leaders' view.
Final two: A beats B because there is time to refresh the ratings before the profile is due; a caveat suits gaps that cannot be closed in time.
Exam cue: before reporting a profile, check that the ratings behind it are current, especially after a major change.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO12.03 (Maintain a Risk Profile); NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 3.4 (Maintaining the Risk Assessment)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B3.1 (Risk Register Versus Risk Profile: the profile shows current risk; ratings that predate a major change are refreshed with their owners before reporting). Round 4, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario (a hospital profile built on ratings older than a cloud migration) written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. Cross-domain fixes 4 Nov 2026 (round 4): the stem now says the profile is due in three weeks, the fact that separates this item from crisc_d3_041 (report on time with the limitation stated when the deadline is tomorrow); explanation, wrong explanation B and Final two tip now use it. 'were set before' became 'predate' to keep the stem within 35 words, and the gate's explanation and wrong explanation B were shortened to the 75- and 30-word limits. Key A and options unchanged.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. One appetite for every risk type
questions.question: A drug maker's board set one low appetite for every risk type, and its research unit says this blocks AI drug-discovery experiments with no patient risk. What should the risk practitioner propose as BEST?

options.A: Exceptions to the low appetite for each experiment
options.B: One moderate appetite for risk across the company
options.C: An appetite set by the research unit for its own work
options.D: Separate appetite statements for each risk category

questions.key_concept: Appetite can differ by risk type, so an enterprise can accept innovation risk while keeping a low appetite for safety risk.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the experiments put at risk and what they do not.
questions.correct_explanation: Appetite can and should differ by risk type: an enterprise can welcome innovation risk while keeping a low appetite for patient safety. Proposing separate statements for the board to approve lets AI research go ahead within limits while patient-safety risk stays tightly bounded. Exceptions for each experiment are the runner-up: they free individual experiments, but they leave one appetite that misstates the board's intent and make exceptions the normal route.

wrong_explanations.A: Exceptions are meant for rare departures. Needing one for each experiment shows the appetite itself does not express the board's intent.
wrong_explanations.B: A single moderate level would loosen patient-safety risk as well, which the board wants kept low.
wrong_explanations.C: Units work within appetite; they do not set it. The board, with senior management, sets appetite for each risk type.

tips: Eliminate: B loosens patient-safety risk along with research risk, and C lets a unit set its own appetite, which belongs to the board.
Final two: D beats A because appetite can differ by risk type; routine exceptions would show that one blanket level misstates the board's intent.
Exam cue: when one appetite level fits some risks and blocks others, propose appetite by risk type for the board to approve.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (risk appetite); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-02 (risk appetite and risk tolerance statements are established, communicated and maintained)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B4.1 (Appetite, Tolerance and Capacity: appetite can differ by risk type) and 1B4.2 (the practitioner proposes; the board and senior management set appetite). Round 4, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario (a drug maker's single low appetite blocking AI research trials) written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. Review fixes 4 Nov 2026 (standards audit and concept review): 'trials' replaced by 'experiments' in the stem, option A, explanations and pre_read, since at a drug maker trials read as clinical trials, which involve patients.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. Supplier liability cap
questions.question: A hospital's imaging supplier kept a $50,000 liability cap, though a breach of patient data it holds could cost $2,000,000, and procurement marked the risk transferred. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep it marked transferred, with the cap noted
options.B: Record the loss the cap leaves as residual risk
options.C: Have the owner close the risk on contract signing
options.D: Ask the supplier to name an owner for the risk

questions.key_concept: A liability cap limits what a supplier repays; what the cap leaves stays with the enterprise as residual risk for its owner to weigh.
questions.pre_read: Compare the cap with the size of the possible loss.
questions.correct_explanation: A liability cap limits what the supplier repays, not what a breach would cost. With $50,000 recoverable against a possible $2,000,000 loss, most of the exposure, and every non-financial harm, stays with the hospital. Recorded as residual risk, the risk left after a response, it goes to its owner to weigh against appetite. Noting the cap beside a 'transferred' label is the runner-up: the label still tells leaders the risk has gone.

wrong_explanations.A: Noting the cap records the fact, but the 'transferred' label still tells leaders the hospital no longer carries a risk it mostly keeps.
wrong_explanations.C: Signing sets the terms; it does not remove the hospital's exposure to a breach of the patient data the supplier holds, so the owner has nothing to close.
wrong_explanations.D: The supplier can own its own controls, but the risk to the hospital's patients and objectives stays with a hospital owner.

tips: Eliminate: C has the owner treat signing as closing the risk, and D hands ownership of the hospital's risk to the supplier.
Final two: B beats A because the cap leaves most of the loss with the hospital; a 'transferred' label with a footnote still misstates who carries it.
Exam cue: contracts and caps shift some cost, not the accountability; record what stays with the enterprise as residual risk for its owner.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (risk transfer); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.SC-05 (requirements to address cybersecurity risks in supply chains are established, prioritized and integrated into contracts and other types of agreements with suppliers and other relevant third parties); ISACA Glossary (residual risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B5.3 (Contractual Requirements and Service Level Agreements: a liability cap limits what a supplier repays, not the loss; outsourcing moves the work, never the accountability). Round 4, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario (a hospital imaging supplier's liability cap against a much larger breach loss) written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. Review fixes 4 Nov 2026 (standards audit and concept review): 'retained risk' (not an ISACA Glossary term, and read as an acceptance only the owner can make) replaced by residual risk, the risk that remains after a response, in the key, explanation, key concept, Exam cue tip and related concepts; the explanation adds that non-financial harm stays in full; ISACA Glossary (residual risk) cited. Cue pass 5 Nov 2026: C now has the owner close the risk at signing, a second owner-naming distractor, so owner options no longer point to the key.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Organizational structure, roles and responsibilities. Second line informed after AI updates
questions.question: A retailer's RACI chart for monthly updates to its AI pricing model lists the second-line risk team as Informed after each update goes live. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: List the risk team as Accountable for each update
options.B: List the risk team as Responsible for retraining
options.C: List the risk team as Consulted before each update
options.D: List the risk team as Informed, with a periodic review

questions.key_concept: In RACI, consulted parties give input before a decision; the second line is consulted on AI model changes, not made accountable for them.
questions.pre_read: Note when the risk team hears about each update.
questions.correct_explanation: In a RACI chart, consulted parties give input before a decision and informed parties hear the result after it. Listing the second-line risk team as Consulted lets it challenge each pricing model update before release, while the business owner of pricing stays accountable. Making the risk team Accountable is the runner-up: it gives the team the involvement it lacks, but accountability for the model's outcomes belongs to the business owner, and one party is accountable.

wrong_explanations.A: Accountability for the pricing model's outcomes sits with its business owner. A second-line team made accountable would own what it should challenge.
wrong_explanations.B: Retraining is first-line work. A risk team that does it cannot challenge it objectively, and the gap before release remains.
wrong_explanations.D: A periodic look back still comes after updates are live, so the risk team never challenges a change before customers see its prices.

tips: Eliminate: B gives the second line first-line work it should challenge, and D keeps its input after release, adding only a periodic look back.
Final two: C beats A because the second line should challenge changes before release; accountability for the model stays with the pricing owner.
Exam cue: in RACI, consulted means input before the decision and informed means told after; put the second line where its challenge can still count.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 2.1 (roles, responsibilities and lines of communication for AI risks are documented and clear); ISACA Journal 2018 Volume 4 (Roles of Three Lines of Defense for Information Security and Governance)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A2.3 (RACI and Accountability, Including AI: consulted parties give input before a decision, informed parties hear after it; the business owner of an AI use case is accountable). questions.subtopic: 1A1 Strategy, goals and objectives. Timing of risk input to an AI strategy
questions.question: Which of the following is the MOST valuable point for the risk practitioner's input into a retailer's first AI strategy?

options.A: While leaders compare the strategic options
options.B: After the board approves the chosen strategy
options.C: When the first AI projects begin their design
options.D: At the strategy's first progress review

questions.key_concept: Risk input is most valuable while strategic options are compared, so leaders can choose a strategy whose risks fit appetite.
questions.pre_read: Picture the strategy's life from the choices leaders weigh to later progress reviews, then place each answer on it.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk input is worth most while it can still shape the choice: weighing each option's risks and opportunities against appetite helps leaders pick a strategy they can carry. After approval, the practitioner still identifies the risks to the chosen strategy's objectives, which makes that the runner-up, but by then the main choices are fixed and risk work can only adjust how the strategy is delivered.

wrong_explanations.B: After approval, identifying risks to the strategy's objectives is needed, but the choice it could have informed has already been made.
wrong_explanations.C: Project risk reviews are needed, but by design time the strategic choices that shape most AI risk have been settled.
wrong_explanations.D: A progress review checks delivery after the strategy is set; risk input arrives long after the options it could have shaped.

tips: Eliminate: C and D bring risk in during delivery or at a progress review, after the strategic choices that shape most of the risk are fixed.
Final two: A beats B because risk informs strategy best while options are still open; after approval it can only adjust how the strategy is delivered.
Exam cue: risk management supports setting strategy, not only delivering it; bring risk in while the options are compared.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO02 (Managed Strategy); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 2.3 (executive leadership takes responsibility for decisions about risks of AI system development and deployment)

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. One channel for raising concerns
questions.question: Control-room staff at a water utility tell the risk practitioner they can raise safety-system concerns only with their shift manager, who has dismissed two concerns this year. What should the practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Speak-up training for the utility's shift managers
options.B: A central review of the concerns shift managers log
options.C: Disciplinary action against the shift manager
options.D: A reporting route that bypasses line managers

questions.key_concept: Speaking up needs several channels, including one that bypasses line managers, so one person cannot stop a concern.
questions.pre_read: Count the routes a concern can take today.
questions.correct_explanation: Staff have one channel, and the person on it has twice dismissed their concerns, so safety issues can stop there. A route that bypasses line managers, such as an anonymous line to the safety function, lets concerns reach someone who will assess them, and protects those who use it. Training the shift managers is the runner-up: it may improve how they respond, but staff would still depend on the same single channel.

wrong_explanations.A: Training may improve how managers respond, but concerns would still pass only through them, so a dismissed safety concern still goes no further.
wrong_explanations.B: Reviewing what managers log covers only the concerns they chose to record; a concern a manager dismisses never reaches the review.
wrong_explanations.C: Disciplining one manager treats one person, not the design: staff would still have a single channel that one person can close.

tips: Eliminate: B reviews only what managers choose to log, and C acts on one manager while staff still have only one route.
Final two: D beats A because concerns need a route that does not depend on one manager; training may help, but the single channel remains.
Exam cue: speaking up needs more than one channel, including one that bypasses line managers, with protection for those who use it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-01 (organizational leadership is responsible and accountable for cybersecurity risk and fosters a culture that is risk-aware, ethical and continually improving); ISACA Glossary (risk culture)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A3.2 (Incentives, Speaking Up and Escalation: several reporting channels, including a route that bypasses line managers; protect those who report). questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. Acquired firm on a weaker policy
questions.question: After buying a smaller insurer, a group finds the insurer's staff still work to their old access policy, which is weaker than the group's in two areas. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Let the insurer keep its own policy as a separate business
options.B: Bring the insurer under the group policy on a dated plan
options.C: Rewrite the group policy to fit both firms' practices
options.D: Compare both policies at the next group policy review

questions.key_concept: Enterprise policy applies to acquired units too; gaps are closed on a dated plan, with owned, time-limited exceptions in between.
questions.pre_read: Note how the two policies differ and who now owns the insurer.
questions.correct_explanation: A group policy states management's intent for the whole enterprise, and the acquired insurer is now part of it, so staff working to weaker rules leave the group exposed beyond what its policy intends. Bringing the insurer under the group policy on a dated plan, with interim gaps handled as owned, time-limited exceptions, closes the difference. Keeping it separate is the runner-up: a subsidiary can keep local procedures, but not weaker protection.

wrong_explanations.A: A subsidiary can keep local procedures, but group policy sets the minimum for the whole enterprise; a weaker separate policy leaves the gap open.
wrong_explanations.C: Rewriting the group policy around the weaker practices lowers protection across the whole group to fit one acquisition.
wrong_explanations.D: Waiting for that review leaves staff working to weaker rules for months, and comparing policies does not decide which one applies.

tips: Eliminate: C lowers the whole group's policy to the weaker one, and D leaves the gaps open while waiting for a scheduled review.
Final two: B beats A because group policy sets the minimum across the enterprise; a separate, weaker policy keeps the gap the acquisition created.
Exam cue: after an acquisition, bring the new unit under enterprise policy on a dated plan, with owned, time-limited exceptions for the gaps.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.PO-01 (policy for managing cybersecurity risks is established based on organizational context, cybersecurity strategy and priorities and is communicated and enforced); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.PO-02 (policy for managing cybersecurity risks is reviewed, updated, communicated and enforced to reflect changes)

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Business processes and resilience. What a continuity plan reduces
questions.question: When the risk practitioner rates a warehouse fire scenario, which of the following does the distributor's tested business continuity plan MOST directly reduce?

options.A: The likelihood that a fire breaks out
options.B: The vulnerability of the warehouse systems
options.C: The impact of the fire on order fulfillment
options.D: The cost of insuring the warehouse building

questions.key_concept: A business continuity plan reduces the impact of a disruption on critical processes, not the likelihood that the disruption occurs.
questions.pre_read: Ask which part of the scenario each option describes.
questions.correct_explanation: A continuity plan does nothing to stop a fire starting; it limits what the fire does to the business by keeping or restoring order fulfillment through alternate sites, staff and suppliers. So when the scenario is rated, the plan lowers its impact, not its likelihood. Likelihood is the runner-up: preventive controls such as removing ignition sources lower it, but a continuity plan responds after the event.

wrong_explanations.A: Preventive controls such as safe storage and removing ignition sources lower the chance of a fire. A continuity plan acts after it starts.
wrong_explanations.B: Vulnerability is a weakness in the site or its systems, lowered by controls on them; a continuity plan does not fix those weaknesses but works around their loss.
wrong_explanations.D: Premiums may reflect good planning, but the plan's purpose is keeping fulfillment going, not lowering the cost of insurance.

tips: Eliminate: B is reduced by controls on the site and systems, and D confuses a possible side benefit with what the plan treats.
Final two: C beats A because a continuity plan acts after the event, limiting its effect on critical processes; preventive controls lower likelihood.
Exam cue: continuity and recovery plans reduce impact; preventive controls reduce likelihood. Match each control to the part of the risk it changes.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (business continuity plan); NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 2.2 (Types of Plans: Business Continuity Plan and Disaster Recovery Plan)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A5.2 (Continuity and Recovery Plans as Risk Responses: as a risk response, a continuity plan mainly reduces a disruption's impact, not its likelihood).
