questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. Customer data held by a supplier
questions.question: A retailer's asset inventory lists only systems it runs, yet a marketing agency holds 200,000 of its customer records for campaigns. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add the agency-held records to the asset inventory
options.B: Rely on the agency's own asset inventory for those records
options.C: Ask the agency for its latest security certification
options.D: Have the agency delete the records after each campaign

questions.key_concept: Data held by suppliers stays the enterprise's asset and risk, so it belongs in the enterprise's own inventory.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose customers the records belong to.
questions.correct_explanation: The records are the retailer's assets and its customers' data wherever they sit, so the retailer still owns the risk to them. Recording them in its asset inventory, with their owner, holder and classification, brings them into risk assessment and supplier oversight. Relying on the agency's inventory is the runner-up: it may list the records, but it serves the agency's purposes, and the retailer could not see or rate its own exposure.

wrong_explanations.B: The agency's inventory serves the agency. The retailer stays accountable for its customers' data and needs it in its own inventory to assess and oversee it.
wrong_explanations.C: A certificate is assurance about the agency, useful later, but it does not put the records into the retailer's view of what it must protect.
wrong_explanations.D: Deleting data after use may be a sound control, but choosing it before the records are inventoried and assessed skips the analysis.

tips: Eliminate: C gathers assurance before the retailer has recorded what the agency holds, and D picks a control before the data is inventoried and assessed.
Final two: A beats B because the retailer stays accountable for its customers' data; the agency's own list does not give the retailer that view.
Exam cue: if the enterprise relies on an asset or its data sits with a supplier, it belongs in the enterprise's own inventory.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM-07 (inventories of data and corresponding metadata for designated data types are maintained); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.SC-07 (the risks posed by a supplier, their products and services and other third parties are understood, recorded, prioritized, assessed, responded to and monitored)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A6.3 (Cloud, SaaS and AI Assets in the Inventory: modern inventories include data held by suppliers; if the enterprise relies on it, it belongs in the inventory). Round 4, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario (a retailer's customer records held by a marketing agency) written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. Review fixes 4 Nov 2026 (standards audit and concept review): key now says asset inventory, the inventory the stem names, not a separate data inventory; distractor B also says asset inventory, so the stem word is not echoed only in the key.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). Which local risks reach the enterprise register
questions.question: A university's 14 departments keep local risk registers. Which of the following should the risk practitioner propose as the BEST rule for deciding which risks reach the enterprise register?

options.A: The five highest-rated risks from each department
options.B: Risks that each department head chooses to escalate
options.C: Risks rated high on each department's own scale
options.D: Risks above set thresholds on one common scale

questions.key_concept: Unit risks reach the enterprise register when they cross thresholds on the common enterprise scale, not by quota or local rating.
questions.pre_read: Picture a large and a small department under each rule.
questions.correct_explanation: Risks can be compared across departments only when they are judged on one scale, so the escalation rule should be a threshold on the enterprise scale: any risk above it reaches the enterprise register, whichever department holds it. Taking each department's top five is the runner-up: it is simple and looks fair, but a small department's fifth risk may be trivial while a large one's sixth is critical.

wrong_explanations.A: A fixed number per department ignores size: trivial risks rise from one department while serious ones in another stay local.
wrong_explanations.B: Individual judgment gives 14 different rules, so similar risks are escalated in one department and kept local in another.
wrong_explanations.C: Local scales are not comparable: high in one department may be moderate in another, so the enterprise register would mix unlike ratings.

tips: Eliminate: B gives 14 different judgments, and C relies on local scales that cannot be compared across departments.
Final two: D beats A because escalation should follow the size of the risk on one scale; a fixed quota per department ignores how large each risk is.
Exam cue: roll risks up to enterprise level by thresholds on the common enterprise scale, not by quotas or local ratings.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286 Rev. 1 Section 3.8 (Creating and Maintaining an Enterprise-Level Cybersecurity Risk Register); NIST IR 8286C Rev. 1 Section 2.2 (Normalization of Cybersecurity Risk Registers: the same rating criteria enable comparison and tracking)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B1.2 (Common Taxonomy and Rating Scales: local risks rise to the enterprise register by impact thresholds on the enterprise scale). Round 4, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario (a university's 14 departmental registers feeding an enterprise register) written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. Review fixes 4 Nov 2026 (standards audit and concept review): 'impact thresholds' became 'thresholds' in the key, explanation and key concept, since escalation uses the whole rating on the common scale, not impact alone; the shorter key is no longer the longest option.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. Second-line pay tied to the first line
questions.question: A trading firm's second-line risk analysts sit with its trading desk and challenge the desk's risk ratings, and their bonuses are paid from the desk's profits. What should concern the risk practitioner MOST?

options.A: Their challenge is less independent than internal audit's
options.B: The analysts sit with the desk instead of the risk team
options.C: Their pay rewards weak challenge of the desk's ratings
options.D: The desk, not the analysts, owns the risks behind the ratings

questions.key_concept: The second line needs objectivity: pay or reporting tied to the results of the unit it challenges weakens that challenge.
questions.pre_read: Separate what is normal in the lines model from what is not.
questions.correct_explanation: The second line needs objectivity, not audit-style separation, and pay drawn from the desk's profits rewards the analysts for rating the desk's risks low. That weakens the challenge the firm relies on. Lacking internal audit's independence is the runner-up: it sounds like the same problem, but the second line sits within management by design; what is wrong here is an incentive that pulls against its judgment.

wrong_explanations.A: The second line sits within management by design and need not match audit's independence; its need is objectivity, which the pay link undermines.
wrong_explanations.B: Embedding analysts with a desk is a common model that improves their insight; the pay link, not where they sit, threatens objectivity.
wrong_explanations.D: The first line owning the risks it runs is how the lines model works; the second line challenges those ratings and does not own them.

tips: Eliminate: B objects to embedding, a normal model, and D objects to the first line owning its risks, which is how the lines model works.
Final two: C beats A because the second line needs objectivity, not audit's independence; pay tied to the desk's profits undermines exactly that.
Exam cue: for the second line, look for conflicts that weaken challenge, such as pay or reporting tied to the unit it oversees.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Journal 2018 Volume 4 (Roles of Three Lines of Defense for Information Security and Governance); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B2.2 (Independence, Challenge and Coordination Across Lines: the second line needs objectivity, not audit-style independence; its pay and reporting do not depend on the units it challenges). Round 4, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario (embedded risk analysts paid from a trading desk's profits) written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. Review fixes 4 Nov 2026 (standards audit and concept review): stem now says the analysts are second line, the fact the explanation relies on; embedded analysts could otherwise be first-line staff.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. Counting high-rated risks
questions.question: A retailer's quarterly profile reports how many risks in each category are rated high, and executives read a fall in technology from 12 to 8 as lower exposure. What is the risk practitioner's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The four risks no longer rated high are not shown
options.B: A count does not show how large the remaining risks are
options.C: Each category mixes risks owned by different units
options.D: The profile is reported quarterly instead of monthly

questions.key_concept: Counting high-rated risks does not measure exposure; the profile shows aggregated exposure against appetite.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a fall from 12 to 8 does and does not tell you.
questions.correct_explanation: A count treats every high-rated risk as equal, so a drop from 12 to 8 says nothing about the exposure left: the eight that remain could carry more than all twelve did, and related risks may compound. The profile should show aggregated exposure against appetite. Not showing the four that left the high band is the runner-up: traceability matters, but listing them would leave the count just as misleading about the risks that remain.

wrong_explanations.A: Tracing the four that moved is useful, but the larger problem remains: a count cannot show how much exposure the remaining eight carry.
wrong_explanations.C: Categories normally hold risks owned by different units; that does not distort the picture the way a simple count does.
wrong_explanations.D: Reporting more often would repeat the same weak measure; the problem is what is counted, not how often.

tips: Eliminate: C treats the normal mixing of owners as the issue, and D changes how often a weak measure is reported.
Final two: B beats A because the count itself misleads about exposure; tracing the four risks that left the band would not fix that.
Exam cue: to show how much risk is carried, report aggregated exposure against appetite; counts of high-rated risks do not measure it.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (risk aggregation); NIST IR 8286 Rev. 1 Section 4.1 (Applying the Enterprise Risk Register and Developing the Enterprise Risk Profile)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B3.2 (Aggregation and Keeping the Profile Current: do not just add or count scores; a count hides how large each risk is). Round 4, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario (a retailer's profile that counts high-rated risks per category) written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. Review fixes 4 Nov 2026 (standards audit and concept review): explanation wording clarified (the eight that remain could carry more exposure than all twelve did). Cross-domain gate 12 Nov 2026 (round 26): Exam cue narrowed to its own trigger, showing how much risk is carried; read bare, it pulled toward crisc_d1_232's runner-up A (total exposure beside the previous total), where the board asks why exposure rose.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Capacity falls below appetite
questions.question: A fine has cut a payments firm's capital, and the risk practitioner finds the board's appetite for fraud loss now exceeds the firm's risk capacity. What should the practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Report the gap to the board for an appetite review
options.B: Raise the gap at the board's next appetite review
options.C: Lower the fraud tolerances to fit within the new capacity
options.D: Record the shortfall as a new risk in the register

questions.key_concept: Appetite must sit within risk capacity; when capacity falls below it, the board that set appetite reviews it without waiting for the cycle.
questions.pre_read: Recall how appetite and capacity must relate, then check whether they still do.
questions.correct_explanation: Capacity is the outer bound: an appetite above it means the board is willing to accept fraud losses the firm could no longer survive. A fall in capacity triggers a review of appetite, so the gap goes now to the board, which set the appetite. Raising it at the next appetite review is the runner-up: it reaches the right body, but it leaves an appetite beyond capacity guiding decisions for months.

wrong_explanations.B: The board is the right body, but a change in capacity triggers review between cycles; waiting leaves an unsurvivable appetite guiding decisions.
wrong_explanations.C: Tolerances are the variation leaders allow around appetite, approved by senior management or the board, not set by the practitioner; tightening them leaves the board's appetite itself beyond capacity.
wrong_explanations.D: Recording the gap is useful, but a register entry does not bring it to the board, which alone can reset its appetite.

tips: Eliminate: C has the practitioner change limits that leaders approve, and D records the gap without bringing it to the board that set the appetite.
Final two: A beats B because a fall in capacity triggers an appetite review now; the review cycle would leave an unsurvivable limit in force.
Exam cue: appetite must sit inside capacity; when capacity falls, escalate to the level that set appetite without waiting for the cycle.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (risk capacity); ISACA Glossary (risk appetite)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B4.1 (Appetite, Tolerance and Capacity: capacity is the outer bound and appetite sits inside it) and 1B4.2 (appetite is reviewed when capacity changes). Round 4, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario (a payments firm whose capital, cut by a fine, no longer covers its fraud appetite) written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. Review fixes 4 Nov 2026 (standards audit and concept review): wrong explanation C and the Eliminate tip now say tolerances are the variation leaders allow, approved by senior management or the board (ISACA Glossary; consistent with crisc_d1_042), not set by the practitioner; 'beneath appetite' dropped, since tolerance can sit either side of the appetite point. Cue pass 12 Nov 2026 (fixed periods): option B dropped an incidental period word.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. Two frameworks or one
questions.question: A bank governs IT with COBIT 2019 and wants NIST CSF 2.0 for cybersecurity outcomes, but its CIO says it must choose one. Which of the following is the risk practitioner's BEST advice?

options.A: Replace COBIT 2019 with CSF 2.0 for IT governance
options.B: Keep COBIT 2019 and drop the plan for CSF 2.0
options.C: Use both, mapped to each other and to ERM
options.D: Run both separately with their own risk registers

questions.key_concept: Frameworks such as COBIT 2019 and NIST CSF 2.0 can be combined, mapped to each other and integrated with ERM.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each framework is designed to cover.
questions.correct_explanation: Frameworks are starting points that can be combined: COBIT 2019 covers governance and management of enterprise IT, while CSF 2.0 describes cybersecurity outcomes and is meant to be used with other frameworks. Mapping the two to each other and to ERM lets each do its job without duplicated work. Running both separately is the runner-up: it keeps both, but separate registers split the bank's view of risk and rate the same risks twice.

wrong_explanations.A: CSF 2.0 focuses on cybersecurity outcomes; it does not replace COBIT 2019's wider governance and management of enterprise IT.
wrong_explanations.B: Dropping CSF 2.0 gives up its cybersecurity outcomes; the frameworks complement each other, so there is no need to choose.
wrong_explanations.D: Separate registers split one set of risks into two views, so leaders cannot compare or aggregate them in enterprise terms.

tips: Eliminate: A and B both assume the bank must choose, when COBIT 2019 and CSF 2.0 cover different ground and can be combined.
Final two: C beats D because combined frameworks still feed one view of risk; separate registers split and duplicate it.
Exam cue: frameworks are combined and tailored, then integrated with ERM; no single framework has to cover everything.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 Section 1 (CSF Overview: the CSF is used in conjunction with other resources such as frameworks, standards and guidelines to manage cybersecurity risks); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-03 (cybersecurity risk management activities and outcomes are included in enterprise risk management processes)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B5.1 (Choosing and Tailoring a Framework: frameworks can be combined, such as COBIT 2019 for governance with NIST CSF 2.0 for cybersecurity outcomes, and mapped to ERM). Round 4, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario (a bank told by its CIO to choose between COBIT 2019 and NIST CSF 2.0) written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Organizational structure, roles and responsibilities. Evidence that ownership is in place
questions.question: Which of the following BEST shows the risk practitioner that ownership of a newly recorded risk, with no response yet decided, has been established?

options.A: The owner's name in the risk register entry
options.B: The risk team's proposal naming the owner
options.C: The owner's seat on the IT risk committee
options.D: The owner's signed acknowledgment of the entry

questions.key_concept: Ownership is established when the named owner acknowledges the risk, for example by signing off its register entry.
questions.pre_read: For each option, ask who produced that evidence.
questions.correct_explanation: Ownership is established when the named person knows the risk is theirs and takes it on. The owner's signed acknowledgment of the entry shows that, letting the practitioner validate the ownership they proposed; once responses are due, the owner's recorded decisions show the role in action. A name in the register is the runner-up: it records who should own the risk, but a name entered by others does not show acceptance.

wrong_explanations.A: A name entered by someone else records who should own the risk, not that the person knows it is theirs.
wrong_explanations.B: The risk team proposes owners, but a proposal is only the start: senior management confirms it, and the owner then takes the risk on.
wrong_explanations.C: A committee seat shows a part in oversight, not that the person has taken on this particular risk.

tips: Eliminate: B is only the risk team's proposal, before anyone has confirmed it, and C shows a committee role, not ownership of this risk.
Final two: D beats A because ownership is validated when the owner acknowledges the entry in writing; a name entered by others does not show acceptance.
Exam cue: the practitioner proposes and validates owners; look for evidence that the named owner has acknowledged the risk.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (risk owner); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A2.2 (Risk Owner, Control Owner and Risk Practitioner: the practitioner proposes and validates owners; ownership holds once senior management confirms it and the owner acknowledges the risk). Round 4, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario (evidence that a newly recorded risk has an owner) written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. Review fixes 4 Nov 2026 (standards audit and concept review): key is now the owner's signed acknowledgment of the entry, since ownership does not require agreeing with the rating (owners can dispute a rating, as in crisc_d1_094); explanation, wrong explanation A, key concept and Final two tip aligned; 'it proposed' became 'they proposed'. Cross-domain fixes 4 Nov 2026 (round 4): stem now says no response has yet been decided, and the explanation adds that recorded response decisions show the role in action once responses are due (the gate's wording shortened to the 75-word limit), so the item agrees with crisc_d3_022 (ownership validated by recorded decisions). Key D, options, wrong explanations and tips unchanged.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. Owner and second line disagree on a rating
questions.question: After reviewing the evidence together, an insurer's risk team still rates a policyholder-portal risk high, while the portal's owner, the customer services director, insists it is low. What is the risk practitioner's BEST next step?

options.A: Take both ratings to the risk committee to resolve
options.B: Enter the director's rating in the insurer's register
options.C: Record the risk team's rating over the director's
options.D: Record the average of the two ratings for now

questions.key_concept: When the owner and the second line still disagree on a rating after weighing the evidence, both views go to the risk committee.
questions.pre_read: Note what has already been tried to settle the disagreement.
questions.correct_explanation: The owner decides the response, but the rating is a judgment the second line exists to challenge. When owner and risk team still disagree after weighing the evidence together, both views go to the risk committee, which oversees ratings and can settle the matter. Recording the director's rating is the runner-up: owners are accountable for their risks, but deferring to them whenever they disagree would empty the second line's challenge.

wrong_explanations.B: Owners decide the response, not the facts; recording their rating whenever they disagree removes the challenge the second line provides.
wrong_explanations.C: Overriding the owner has the risk team decide alone; a disputed rating is escalated, not settled by one side.
wrong_explanations.D: An average belongs to neither view and hides the disagreement from those who oversee ratings.

tips: Eliminate: C lets the second line override the owner on its own, and D blends two views into a rating no one holds.
Final two: A beats B because the second line's challenge needs a path to escalate; deferring to the owner on every dispute empties it.
Exam cue: when the first and second lines still disagree on a rating after reviewing the evidence, escalate both views to the body that oversees ratings; access disputes go to senior management.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286B-upd1 Section 2.4.3 (Risk Owner: risk escalation and elevation); ISACA Journal 2018 Volume 4 (Roles of Three Lines of Defense for Information Security and Governance)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B2.2 (Independence, Challenge and Coordination Across Lines: the second line challenges and needs a path to escalate; disputed ratings go to the risk committee with both views). Round 4, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario (a hospital patient-portal rating disputed between the owner and the risk team) written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. Review fixes 4 Nov 2026 (standards audit and concept review): re-set from a hospital patient portal to an insurer's policyholder portal, to cut the batch's healthcare share; key and explanations unchanged. Cross-domain gate 12 Nov 2026 (round 17): Exam cue narrowed to rating disputes ('on a rating', 'the body that oversees ratings'), with access disputes going to senior management: the old cue ('when the first and second lines still disagree, escalate both views to the oversight body') keyed the wrong option C of crisc_d1_173 (round 17: a director still withholds incident logs from the second line), against notes 1B2.2. Neighbour added: crisc_d1_173; keep apart in practice sets.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. New rules found too late
questions.question: A payments firm has twice learned of new IT rules from its regulator only after they took effect, each time rushing costly fixes. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Assess the gaps left once the two new rules took effect
options.B: Monitor the regulator's draft and upcoming rules
options.C: Ask the regulator to give the firm earlier notice
options.D: Fund a reserve for future rushed compliance fixes

questions.key_concept: Repeated late compliance is a process gap: monitor draft and upcoming rules so each one is assessed and planned before it takes effect.
questions.pre_read: Note when the firm learned of each rule.
questions.correct_explanation: Both rushed fixes have the same cause: the firm has no watch on rules before they apply. Monitoring the regulator's draft and upcoming rules, with someone named to do it, lets each new rule be assessed and planned in time to fund the work. Assessing the gaps the two rules left is the runner-up: it is needed now, but it treats the last two cases and leaves the next rule unseen.

wrong_explanations.A: Assessing the remaining gaps is needed, but it treats the last two rules; the next one would again arrive unnoticed.
wrong_explanations.C: Regulators publish drafts and effective dates ahead of time; tracking them is the firm's responsibility, not the regulator's.
wrong_explanations.D: A reserve pays for rushed fixes; it does not prevent them, and late compliance still risks breaching the rules.

tips: Eliminate: C hands the firm's own monitoring duty to the regulator, and D funds the rushed fixes instead of preventing them.
Final two: B beats A because the cause is having no watch on upcoming rules; assessing two rules' gaps treats the symptoms and leaves the next rule unseen.
Exam cue: when compliance surprises repeat, fix the watch: monitor draft and upcoming rules so each is assessed before it takes effect.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-03 (legal, regulatory and contractual requirements, including privacy obligations, are understood and managed); COBIT 2019 MEA03 (Managed Compliance With External Requirements)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B5.2 (Compliance Obligations as a Source of Risk: regulatory change is monitored, and new rules trigger an impact assessment before their effective date). Round 4, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario (a payments firm that twice found new rules only after they applied) written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. The gate's explanation was shortened to the 75-word limit. Key letter B unchanged; the key is not the longest option. Neighbours checked: crisc_d1_045, CISA d2_165 (same rule, fix the regulatory watch, from the IS auditor's side, with different distractors; no contradiction).

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Strategy, goals and objectives. Delay asked for an AI launch
questions.question: An airline's customer director owns a strategic AI rebooking assistant whose tested risk is within appetite, but the security lead wants six more months of repeat tests. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Ask the director to delay launch for the extra tests
options.B: Insure the airline against losses from the assistant
options.C: Have the director accept the rated risk for launch
options.D: Log the security lead's objection in the risk register

questions.key_concept: Within appetite, the owner accepts and monitors a strategic risk; delaying the objective for extra treatment has a cost of its own.
questions.pre_read: Note what the assistant is for and what the testing showed.
questions.correct_explanation: The assistant serves a strategic objective, and its tested risk already sits within appetite, so its owner, the customer director, can accept the risk and launch, with the acceptance recorded and monitored. A six-month delay is the runner-up: it gives up half a year of the objective's benefit to reduce a risk that needs no further treatment. A delayed opportunity is also an effect on objectives.

wrong_explanations.A: Delay feels like the cautious choice, but the risk is already within appetite; six months of extra tests would cost the strategic objective more than they reduce.
wrong_explanations.B: Insurance shifts part of a loss when a risk needs treatment; this one is already within appetite, so the premium buys nothing the owner needs.
wrong_explanations.D: Logging the objection records a view but decides nothing; the owner still has to accept the risk before the assistant can launch.

tips: Eliminate: B transfers a risk that is already within appetite, and D records the security lead's view without anyone deciding.
Final two: C beats A because a risk within appetite is accepted by its owner and monitored; delaying a strategic launch for more tests gives up the objective for no needed reduction.
Exam cue: within appetite, the owner accepts and monitors; a delay or extra treatment has a cost to the objective too.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (risk acceptance); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MANAGE 1.1 (a determination is made as to whether the AI system achieves its intended purposes and whether its development or deployment should proceed); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-07 (strategic opportunities or positive risks are characterized and are included in organizational cybersecurity risk discussions)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A1.1 (Risk in Service of Business Objectives: upside risk counts, so a missed or delayed opportunity also affects objectives), with the acceptance rule in 1B4.3 and 1A1.2 (AI initiatives need a risk owner and appetite fit). Round 6, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario (an airline's AI rebooking assistant, tested within appetite, with a security lead asking for a six-month delay) written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. Acceptance keyed under the round 6 plan: the owner accepts within appetite, recorded and monitored; the practitioner recommends. Neighbours checked: crisc_d3_002 (within appetite, an extra monitoring tool; same rule, but here the proposal is a delay that costs a strategic objective, and no wrong-owner acceptance distractor is reused), CISA d1_194 (controls until residual risk reaches zero), crisc_d3_003 and crisc_d3_087 (avoid or mitigate when above appetite), crisc_d1_039 (exposure well below appetite), crisc_d1_083 (timing of input to an AI strategy), crisc_d4_005 (launch-date pressure on acceptance testing). questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. Reports that seem to go nowhere
questions.question: Staff concern reports at a hotel chain have halved in a year; each is investigated, but a survey finds staff think reports go nowhere. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Tell reporters what came of the concern they raised
options.B: Run a campaign reminding staff how to report concerns
options.C: Add an anonymous option to the reporting route
options.D: Make raising a concern a duty in the code of conduct

questions.key_concept: People keep raising concerns when they see what comes of them; feedback to each reporter closes the loop.
questions.pre_read: Note what happens to each report and what staff believe happens.
questions.correct_explanation: Every report is investigated, yet staff think reports go nowhere, so the fall comes from reporters never hearing back. Telling each reporter what came of their concern closes the loop and shows that speaking up is worth the effort. A campaign on how to report is the runner-up: reports are still arriving, so staff know the route, and a reminder does not answer their belief that nothing happens.

wrong_explanations.B: A campaign is tempting, but reports are still arriving, so staff know how to report; it leaves their belief that nothing happens untouched.
wrong_explanations.C: Anonymity helps when people fear reprisal; here staff doubt that anything happens, and an anonymous report makes feedback to the reporter harder.
wrong_explanations.D: A duty to report changes the rules, not what staff see; reporters would still hear nothing back, so the fall would continue.

tips: Eliminate: C answers a fear of reprisal the survey does not show, and D adds a duty without changing what staff see happen.
Final two: A beats B because the cause is missing feedback, not an unknown route; telling reporters what came of their concern rebuilds the habit.
Exam cue: when reporting falls, ask what reporters experience next; closing the loop with feedback keeps people speaking up.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (risk culture); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-01 (organizational leadership is responsible and accountable for cybersecurity risk and fosters a culture that is risk-aware, ethical and continually improving)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A3.2 (Incentives, Speaking Up and Escalation: reported concerns are logged, assessed and closed with feedback to the reporter; without feedback, people decide reporting is pointless). Round 6, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario (a hotel chain whose concern reports halved although each is investigated) written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. Neighbours checked: crisc_d1_024 (near-miss reports fell once they counted against the reporter: the cause there is a penalty, here missing feedback), crisc_d1_084 (one channel through a dismissive shift manager: a channel fix, offered here as a wrong option only for fear the stem does not show), crisc_d1_046 (gauging culture), CISA d1_028 (fear of retaliation as the culture finding). No CC or AAIA item on feedback to reporters.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. Stricter local rule
questions.question: A retailer's standard requires deleting customer records within five years; one country unit's standard sets three, as local law requires, and the CIO wants one five-year rule. What should the risk practitioner advise as BEST?

options.A: Apply the five-year rule in the country unit as well
options.B: Report the unit as breaching the group's standard
options.C: Request a group exception for the unit's local rule
options.D: Keep the unit's stricter standard alongside the group's

questions.key_concept: A lower layer may tighten a higher one but not relax it; a stricter local rule that meets the group rule needs no exception.
questions.pre_read: Read the group rule's limit closely, then compare the unit's rule with it.
questions.correct_explanation: Deleting after three years still meets a group rule that says within five, so the unit's standard tightens the group's without relaxing it, and it meets local law. A lower layer may be stricter than a higher one, so it can stand alongside the group standard. An exception is the runner-up: exceptions record an owner's acceptance of not meeting a requirement, and here the requirement is met.

wrong_explanations.A: Replacing the unit's rule with the group's would let records stay up to five years, past the three years local law allows; the group rule sets an outer limit.
wrong_explanations.B: Deleting at three years is inside the group's five-year limit, so the unit meets the standard; a stricter rule is not a breach.
wrong_explanations.C: An exception covers a requirement that is not met and the risk an owner accepts; the unit meets the group rule, so there is nothing to except.

tips: Eliminate: A would push the unit past its local law, and B calls a stricter rule a breach when it meets the group limit.
Final two: D beats C because a lower layer may tighten a higher one; an exception is only for a requirement that is not met.
Exam cue: a local rule can be stricter than the group's, never looser; check whether the higher rule is actually broken before raising an exception.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Business processes and resilience. Recovery slower than the target
questions.question: An exercise restored a distributor's invoicing in three days, against the process owner's one-day target; meeting it would cost $400,000 a year, and three days is within appetite. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Fund an upgrade to meet the owner's one-day target
options.B: Have the owner accept the three-day recovery on record
options.C: Have IT reset the recovery target to three days
options.D: Log the gap for the owner's next plan review

questions.key_concept: A tested recovery slower than the target but within appetite may be accepted by the process owner on record, instead of funding a costly fix.
questions.pre_read: Compare the tested recovery with the target, then with appetite.
questions.correct_explanation: The exercise shows recovery takes three days, not one, but three days is within appetite, so no further treatment is needed. The recovery target is the process owner's, so the owner accepts three days on record, and the RTO and plan are updated to match. Having IT reset the target is the runner-up: it brings the plan in line with the test, but changing a business recovery target is the owner's decision, not IT's.

wrong_explanations.A: The upgrade meets the owner's one-day target, but three days is already within appetite, so $400,000 a year buys a reduction the business does not need.
wrong_explanations.C: IT can report the tested recovery time, but the target comes from the business; resetting it without the owner's acceptance moves a decision that is the owner's.
wrong_explanations.D: Waiting for that review leaves the plan promising one day while recovery takes three; the owner can decide now, while the exercise result is fresh.

tips: Eliminate: A spends $400,000 a year on a risk already within appetite, and D leaves the plan promising a recovery the exercise showed it cannot deliver.
Final two: B beats C because the recovery target belongs to the process owner; IT can report the tested time, but only the owner can accept three days and have the RTO changed.
Exam cue: a gap found in testing is not always treated; within appetite, the owner can accept it on record and the RTO and plan are updated to match.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (recovery time objective); ISACA Glossary (risk acceptance); COBIT 2019 DSS04 (Managed Continuity)

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). Sign a framework is not working
questions.question: Which of the following would BEST show the risk practitioner that an insurer's risk management framework is not working as intended?

options.A: Major losses from risks that no assessment had identified
options.B: A rise in the number of risks recorded in the register
options.C: Units taking longer than planned to finish their assessments
options.D: Several units reporting risks above appetite this year

questions.key_concept: A risk management framework is judged by its outcomes: major losses from risks it never identified show it is not working.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a framework is for, then which option tests that.
questions.correct_explanation: A framework exists to help the enterprise find and manage the risks to its objectives, so major losses from risks no assessment identified show it failing at its purpose and needing review. Units reporting risks above appetite is the runner-up: it can look like failure, but finding exposure and sending it for decisions is what a working framework does; the failure sign is loss from risks it never found.

wrong_explanations.B: More recorded risks can mean better identification, not failure; a count alone does not show whether the framework protects objectives.
wrong_explanations.C: Slow assessments point to effort or resourcing; the framework can still find and manage the right risks when units finish late.
wrong_explanations.D: Risks reported above appetite show the framework finding exposure and sending it for decisions; that is the framework working, not failing.

tips: Eliminate: B counts recorded risks, which can rise as identification improves, and C measures how fast units work, not whether the right risks are found.
Final two: A beats D because a framework is judged by its outcomes; risks reported above appetite show it finding exposure, while losses from unidentified risks show it missing them.
Exam cue: use of a framework shows it is embedded; outcomes show whether it works. Exposure it surfaces is success; losses it never saw are failure.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OV-02 (the cybersecurity risk management strategy is reviewed and adjusted to ensure coverage of organizational requirements and risks); COBIT 2019 EDM03 (Ensured Risk Optimization)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1B1.3 (The Risk Management Framework and Its Approval: effectiveness is judged by outcomes, such as major losses from risks it never identified). Round 6, 4 Nov 2026: original item (signs that an insurer's framework is not working) written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. Neighbours checked: crisc_d1_034 (BEST evidence a framework is embedded is units using its methods: use, not effectiveness; the Exam cue names the difference), crisc_d1_061 (review after major change checks scope and roles), crisc_d1_078 (internal audit's independent assurance over the process), CISA d2_091 (a true program versus periodic exercises). No CC or AAIA item on framework effectiveness signals. Review fixes 4 Nov 2026 (round 6 audit, concept review and blind test): runner-up D replaced (a newer framework edition was a strawman) with units reporting risks above appetite, a real misreading of success as failure; explanation and tips follow (audit and concept review, one reconciled version). Keep apart from crisc_d1_034.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. Appetite lowered under current ratings
questions.question: After a bank's board lowered its appetite for customer data risk, the risk analyst finds that four risks rated last month, once within appetite, now exceed it. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Have the owners re-rate the four risks for the new appetite
options.B: Keep showing the four as within appetite until the profile refresh
options.C: Ask the board to phase in its new appetite over a year
options.D: Tell the four risks' owners they are now above appetite

questions.key_concept: A changed appetite moves the comparison, not the ratings; risks newly above it go first to their owners for a response.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the board changed and what it did not change.
questions.correct_explanation: Appetite is the line ratings are compared with, not part of the rating: the four risks were rated last month, and lowering the line changed only how they compare with it. They now exceed appetite, so their owners must learn of it first and choose a response. Having owners re-rate them is the runner-up: it repeats an analysis that is current and delays the decision the new appetite requires.

wrong_explanations.A: The ratings are a month old and still current; appetite is the line they are compared with, so re-rating them only delays the owners' response.
wrong_explanations.B: The profile compares current risk with today's appetite; showing these risks as within a limit the board has lowered would mislead leaders until the refresh.
wrong_explanations.C: The board sets appetite; the analyst can explain what the change means, but asking to phase it in second-guesses a decision that is the board's.

tips: Eliminate: B measures the profile against an appetite the board has replaced, and C asks the board to soften a limit only it sets.
Final two: D beats A because a new appetite moves the comparison, not the ratings; owners of risks now above it need to know first so they can respond.
Exam cue: when appetite or tolerance changes, compare the current ratings with the new line and take any new breaches to their owners.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (risk appetite); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-02 (risk appetite and risk tolerance statements are established, communicated and maintained); NIST IR 8286 Rev. 1 Section 4.1 (Applying the Enterprise Risk Register and Developing the Enterprise Risk Profile)

A FIRST item whose key is not an assessment; the reassess option is the trap. Neighbours checked: crisc_d1_067 (lowered appetite with old KRI thresholds: propose new thresholds; here the comparison of current ratings), crisc_d1_079 (ratings older than a major change are refreshed with owners first: there the ratings are stale, here they are a month old), crisc_d1_037 (a credited control that failed: re-rate without it), crisc_d1_091 (capacity falls below appetite), crisc_d1_018 (KRI breach escalated to the owner). Review fixes 4 Nov 2026 (round 6 audit, concept review and blind test): no content change; keep apart from crisc_d1_067 in practice sets (both a lowered appetite meeting existing settings). Cue pass 12 Nov 2026 (fixed periods): option B dropped an incidental period word.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. Evidence that challenge works
questions.question: Which of the following BEST shows the risk practitioner that a telecom's second-line challenge of business units' risk ratings is effective?

options.A: Minutes of the team's regular meetings with each unit
options.B: The team's sign-off on each unit's ratings before reporting
options.C: Ratings units revised after the team questioned them
options.D: Business units' high satisfaction with the team's reviews

questions.key_concept: Second-line challenge is shown to work by the outcomes it changes, such as ratings units revised after questioning, not by meetings or sign-offs.
questions.pre_read: Ask which record would look different if the challenge were weak.
questions.correct_explanation: Challenge works when it changes outcomes: ratings that units revised after the team questioned them show the second line tested the units' views and moved them where the basis was weak. A sign-off before reporting is the runner-up: it shows the team saw each rating, but a signature looks the same whether the team probed the basis or passed it unread.

wrong_explanations.A: Meeting minutes show contact, not challenge; the team can meet each unit and still pass ratings on unquestioned.
wrong_explanations.B: A sign-off shows the team saw each rating, but approval looks the same whether the basis was tested or not.
wrong_explanations.D: Satisfied units may simply mean the team rarely pushes back; comfort with the second line is not evidence that its challenge works.

tips: Eliminate: A shows that meetings took place, not what they changed, and D measures how comfortable units are, which weak challenge can raise.
Final two: C beats B because effective challenge shows in ratings that moved; a sign-off proves review happened, not that it tested anything.
Exam cue: evidence that oversight works is a changed outcome traceable to it; meetings, signatures and satisfaction show activity only.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Journal 2018 Volume 4 (Roles of Three Lines of Defense for Information Security and Governance); COBIT 2019 APO12 (Managed Risk)

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. Insurance condition not met
questions.question: A freight firm's ransomware risk is rated within appetite, relying on a cyber policy that pays only if remote access uses MFA, which 15% of remote accounts lack. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Have the control owner add MFA to accounts lacking it
options.B: Reassess the risk as if the policy would not pay
options.C: Ask the insurer to reassess the policy condition at renewal
options.D: Have the owner accept the risk as rated within appetite

questions.key_concept: An insurance condition the firm does not meet can void the cover, so the risk is reassessed without the transfer before a response is chosen.
questions.pre_read: Note what the rating depends on and whether that still holds.
questions.correct_explanation: The rating counts on insurance, but the policy pays only if remote access uses MFA, and 15% of accounts lack it, so the insurer may refuse a ransomware claim while the condition is unmet. The risk is first reassessed as if the policy would not pay, then taken to its owner if it now exceeds appetite. Adding MFA is the runner-up: it may be the right fix, but the owner chooses it after the analysis.

wrong_explanations.A: Closing the MFA gap may well follow, but having the control owner act before the risk is reassessed skips the analysis the risk owner needs to choose a response.
wrong_explanations.C: Asking the insurer to revisit the policy condition at renewal may fail, and it leaves today's rating resting on cover that may not pay.
wrong_explanations.D: Acceptance is the owner's call only on a sound rating; this one counts on cover the insurer may refuse while the condition is unmet.

tips: Eliminate: C hopes the insurer changes its terms later, and D accepts a within-appetite rating that rests on cover that may not pay.
Final two: B beats A because the rating rested on a transfer that may fail; reassess first, then the risk owner picks the fix.
Exam cue: a contract or policy condition the firm does not meet can void a transfer; rate the risk without the cover before choosing a response.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (risk transfer); ISACA Glossary (current risk); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-03 (legal, regulatory and contractual requirements, including privacy obligations, are understood and managed)

No CC or AAIA item on an unmet insurance condition. questions.subtopic: 1A1 Strategy, goals and objectives. Assumption behind a strategy
questions.question: A bank's small-business strategy assumes an instant-payment scheme opens next spring; the scheme is delayed 18 months, and the risk practitioner finds the first-year client target will be missed. What should the practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Revise the first-year client target to match
options.B: Assess the scheme's platform risk after launch
options.C: Tell the strategy's owner of the expected shortfall
options.D: Hold it for the owner's planned strategy review

questions.key_concept: When a key assumption behind a strategy fails, the practitioner takes its effect on the objective to the strategy's owner, who decides what changes.
questions.pre_read: Note what the strategy depended on and who answers for its targets.
questions.correct_explanation: The strategy rested on an assumption that no longer holds, and the practitioner has already found the effect: the first-year target will be missed. The owner needs that now, while there is time to choose a response, such as another payment route, a later target or a changed plan. Revising the target is the runner-up: it matches the plan to the facts, but targets belong to the owner, whose decision the practitioner informs.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the target no longer fits the facts. But a strategic target is the owner's to set; changing it takes a business decision away from the owner.
wrong_explanations.B: The scheme's own outage or security risk matters once it launches; the risk to the objective today comes from the delay, not the platform.
wrong_explanations.D: A failed assumption is a trigger to look again now; holding it for the planned review leaves the owner months behind a shortfall already in view.

tips: Eliminate: B assesses a platform that has not launched, and D waits for the planned review after a key assumption has already failed.
Final two: C beats A because targets belong to the strategy's owner; the practitioner brings the finding, and the owner decides what changes.
Exam cue: when evidence breaks an assumption a strategy relies on, take its effect on the objective to the objective's owner without waiting for the next cycle.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO02 (Managed Strategy); COBIT 2019 EDM03 (Ensured Risk Optimization); ISACA Glossary (risk owner)

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. Exception request for AI decline reviews
questions.question: A lender's standard, following its country's lending law, requires officer review of every AI-declined loan; the risk owner seeks an exception below $2,000, with wrong declines there rated within appetite. What is the BEST advice?

options.A: Keep the review of each small-loan decline
options.B: Have the risk owner accept the risk on record
options.C: Have the owner approve reviewing 10% of small declines
options.D: Ask the vendor to confirm the model's accuracy

questions.key_concept: An exception can relax a rule the enterprise set for itself, not a legal requirement the rule carries; a within-appetite rating does not change that.
questions.pre_read: Note where the rule comes from as well as how the risk is rated.
questions.correct_explanation: Within appetite, the owner would normally accept. But the lending law requires this review, and the standard carries that duty. An exception can relax a rule the lender set, not one the law sets, and the rating covers wrong declines, not the breach that skipping reviews would be. Accepting on record is the runner-up: it is the usual answer within appetite, but here it would have the lender knowingly break the law.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the owner decides within appetite, but acceptance covers risk the lender may choose to carry; the law makes this review a duty no rating can waive.
wrong_explanations.C: Sampling suits a rule the lender sets for itself, but the law requires review of each decline; a one-in-ten sample still leaves nine in ten unreviewed.
wrong_explanations.D: Vendor evidence on accuracy speaks to how often declines are wrong, which the rating already covers; it does not change the legal duty to review each one.

tips: Eliminate: C has the owner approve reviewing a tenth of the declines the law requires reviewed one by one, and D checks accuracy when the issue is a legal duty.
Final two: A beats B because acceptance works on risk within appetite, but a legal requirement is not the owner's to waive, whatever the rating.
Exam cue: when a standard carries a legal requirement, a within-appetite rating does not open the way to an exception or acceptance; the requirement is still met.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). Categories of IT risk
questions.question: A risk analyst is checking that an airline's enterprise risk register covers the three Risk IT categories. Which of the following entries BEST illustrates IT benefit or value enablement risk?

options.A: Check-in system outages that delay flights
options.B: Revenue missed by not adopting dynamic pricing
options.C: A crew-scheduling rollout a year behind plan
options.D: A breach of passenger data at a booking agent

questions.key_concept: Risk IT has three IT risk categories: benefit or value enablement (missed chances to use technology), program and project delivery, and operations and service delivery.
questions.pre_read: Recall the three Risk IT categories and what sets each apart.
questions.correct_explanation: Value enablement risk is the risk of missing chances to use technology to make processes more efficient or to enable new business, so revenue missed by not adopting dynamic pricing is the example. A register of failures alone misses this upside, which ERM exists to weigh. The late crew-scheduling rollout is the runner-up: it also concerns value not yet delivered, but a project that slips is program and project delivery risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Outages of a live system are operations and service delivery risk, the most familiar category, not value enablement.
wrong_explanations.C: A rollout a year late is program and project delivery risk: IT's contribution to a new solution is at risk, not a chance left unused.
wrong_explanations.D: A breach at a partner is operations and service delivery risk reached through a third party, not a missed opportunity.

tips: Eliminate: A and D are failures of live systems and services, which is operations and service delivery risk.
Final two: B beats C because value enablement is about chances not taken; a late rollout is a project that is not delivering.
Exam cue: IT risk is wider than failure; on CRISC items, an opportunity the enterprise misses through technology is IT risk too and belongs in the register.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Business processes and resilience. Paper payments in a continuity exercise
questions.question: In an exercise simulating a three-day finance system outage, a university's payments clerks issued paper checks with no second approval to keep suppliers paid. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Assess how fast the finance system can recover
options.B: Add a second approver to paper payments
options.C: Drop paper checks from the continuity plan
options.D: Assess the payment risk the workaround adds

questions.key_concept: A continuity workaround can add risk of its own, such as a dropped approval; assess it with the process owner before relying on the plan.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what the exercise proved against what the workaround changed.
questions.correct_explanation: The exercise proved the process can continue, but the workaround drops the second approval, so for three days payments could go out wrong or to a fraudster unchecked. A response can bring new risk, so the practitioner first assesses it with the process owner, who then chooses a check, a cap or acceptance. Adding a second approver is the runner-up: it may be the fix, but choosing it before analysis skips the owner's decision.

wrong_explanations.A: Recovery speed is the disaster recovery plan's question; the exercise showed the business could carry on, and the new exposure lies in unchecked payments.
wrong_explanations.B: A second approver may well be the fix, but choosing it before the risk is analyzed decides the response for the process owner.
wrong_explanations.C: Dropping the workaround removes the risk only by leaving suppliers unpaid in an outage, which defeats the plan the exercise has just shown works.

tips: Eliminate: A goes back to system recovery when the process already kept running, and C removes the workaround that kept suppliers paid.
Final two: D beats B because the workaround's risk is not yet analyzed; assess it with the process owner, who then chooses the fix.
Exam cue: a continuity workaround is a risk response too; check which control it drops and assess that risk before the plan relies on it.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. Reporting by risk category
questions.question: A retailer's board sets appetite per risk category, and the risk analyst's draft profile shows supplier risk 30% over its category appetite but total exposure within appetite. How should the analyst BEST report this?

options.A: As a total within the board's overall appetite
options.B: As a supplier variance within tolerance
options.C: As supplier excess above its category appetite
options.D: As one score averaged across the categories

questions.key_concept: Where the board sets appetite per category, each is reported against its own limit; headroom in one category does not offset an excess in another.
questions.pre_read: Note the level at which the board set its limits.
questions.correct_explanation: The board set an appetite per category, so each is a limit in its own right. Supplier risk is 30% over its limit whatever the others show: headroom elsewhere cannot absorb risk with its own causes and owners. The profile reports the excess for the board to decide on. Reporting the total as within appetite is the runner-up: the sum is accurate, but netting hides the excess the category limit exists to catch.

wrong_explanations.A: The total is accurate, which makes it tempting, but the board set limits per category; netting them presents one limit's excess as a position within appetite.
wrong_explanations.B: Tolerance is a deviation leaders set in advance; the stem sets none for supplier risk, so calling a 30% excess a variance within tolerance relabels it as allowed.
wrong_explanations.D: Averaging blends the supplier excess into the other categories, so what the board's category limit should catch drops out of view.

tips: Eliminate: B renames an excess as a tolerance no one set, and D averages the categories so it drops out of view.
Final two: C beats A because the board's limit is per category; a total within appetite does not cancel one category's excess over its own limit.
Exam cue: report each risk against the level where its limit was set; headroom in one category does not pay for an excess in another.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (risk appetite); ISACA Glossary (risk aggregation); NIST IR 8286 Rev. 1 Section 4.1 (Applying the Enterprise Risk Register and Developing the Enterprise Risk Profile)

Neighbours checked: crisc_d1_068 (the mirror case: each risk within tolerance, together over the board's appetite; keep apart), crisc_d1_090 (counting high-rated risks does not measure exposure), crisc_d1_101 (a lowered appetite moves the comparison, not the ratings), crisc_d1_080 (separate appetite statements per category), crisc_d3_079 (averaging heat-map scores misleads). No CISA, CC or AAIA item on netting one category's breach against another's headroom. Also a counter-pattern to the within-appetite cue: the stem says the total is within appetite, yet the key reports a breach. Review fixes 4 Nov 2026 (round 7 audit and concept review): key and explanations say 'excess over its category appetite' instead of 'breach', since the bank keeps 'breach' for tolerance and option B names tolerance (audit). The audit's key wording 'As supplier risk above its category appetite' was adjusted to 'As supplier excess above its category appetite' so that 'risk', a stem word, is not echoed only by the key.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. Consequences for limit breaches
questions.question: At a brokerage, junior traders who breach dealing limits lose their bonus; the top earner has breached them four times with verbal warnings only. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST for risk culture?

options.A: Apply the same consequences at every level
options.B: Block limit breaches in the trading system
options.C: Retrain the top trader on the dealing limits
options.D: Raise the top trader's limits to fit results

questions.key_concept: Culture follows the consequences people see: when a top performer's breaches go unpunished, staff learn the rule is optional, so consequences apply at every level.
questions.pre_read: Ask what staff learn from how each breach was handled.
questions.correct_explanation: Staff watch what happens after a breach. Juniors lose their bonus while the top earner gets warnings, so everyone learns that the limits bind only those who earn less. The fix is for leaders to apply the same consequences at every level. Blocking breaches in the trading system is the runner-up: it stops these breaches, but the lesson that rules bend for top earners stays and spreads to controls no system can enforce.

wrong_explanations.B: A hard block is a useful control for dealing limits, but it treats the symptom; staff still see that a top earner's breaches went unpunished.
wrong_explanations.C: The trader knows the limits and has breached them four times; training answers a gap in knowledge, not consequences applied unevenly.
wrong_explanations.D: Dealing limits come from the firm's appetite, not a trader's results; raising them rewards the breaches and confirms the double standard.

tips: Eliminate: C trains a trader who already knows the limits, and D raises limits set from appetite to reward the breaches.
Final two: A beats B because the culture problem is the lesson staff draw from uneven consequences; a system block stops one breach type but leaves that lesson.
Exam cue: when a culture question shows rules enforced by rank, look for the answer that makes consequences consistent, not a new control or more training.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (risk culture); NIST SP 800-39 Section 2.7 (Organizational Culture)

No CC or AAIA item on consequences enforced by rank. Key form: a leadership action on the cause.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. What the inventory records
questions.question: A clinic group learned from a supplier, not its inventory, that 40 imaging workstations lose updates in six months. Which of the following should the risk analyst propose as the BEST addition to the inventory?

options.A: Each asset's purchase price and age
options.B: Each asset's vendor support end date
options.C: Each asset's last security update date
options.D: Each asset's room and serial number

questions.key_concept: An inventory that records when vendor support ends lets owners plan replacement or treatment before assets fall out of support.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the inventory is meant to help the owners do.
questions.correct_explanation: The group heard from a supplier, so its inventory could not show that 40 workstations were about to lose updates. Recording each asset's vendor support end date lets the practitioner see the date coming, raise the risk with the asset's owner and leave time to replace, isolate or accept it. The last security update date is the runner-up: it shows how current an asset is today, but not when its updates will stop.

wrong_explanations.A: Price and age describe what an asset cost and how old it is; a recent model can lose support early, so neither shows when updates end.
wrong_explanations.C: The last update date looks back; an asset patched last week can still lose support next month, which this field would not show.
wrong_explanations.D: Room and serial number help find and count devices, but say nothing about when they stop being supported.

tips: Eliminate: A uses price and age, which do not set when support ends, and D records where a device sits, not its risk.
Final two: B beats C because the support end date looks forward; the last update date shows only where the asset stands today.
Exam cue: when an inventory cannot show a risk coming, such as lost vendor support, add the field that shows it before it arrives, not one that describes the asset.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM-08 (systems, hardware, software, services and data are managed throughout their life cycles); COBIT 2019 BAI09 (Managed Assets)

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Strategy, goals and objectives. Treatment outlasting its objective
questions.question: A telecom's board will close its fixed-line business in 18 months, but the fixed-line director's risk response plan still funds a two-year, $1,200,000 billing platform rebuild. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Report the rebuild to the board that decided the closure
options.B: Move the rebuild budget to the mobile business's risks
options.C: Ask the director to weigh the rebuild against the closure
options.D: Keep the rebuild going as the plan the director approved

questions.key_concept: When strategy ends or shortens an objective, the treatments planned for it go back to their owner to weigh against the new horizon.
questions.pre_read: Note what the plan was approved for and what has changed since.
questions.correct_explanation: The rebuild was planned to protect fixed-line billing, but that business closes in 18 months, before a two-year rebuild could finish. A treatment is worth its cost only while the objective it protects lasts, so the director, as owner, should weigh it again, perhaps against cheaper cover for the months left. Reporting to the board is the runner-up: the board set the strategy, but this treatment sits in the director's own plan.

wrong_explanations.A: The board decided the closure; revisiting a treatment inside the director's plan is the director's call, and the board sees the result in the profile.
wrong_explanations.B: Moving budget between businesses is a management decision; the practitioner brings options, and billing outages still need cover until the closure.
wrong_explanations.D: The plan was approved before the closure was decided; a rebuild finishing six months after the business closes may cost more than the risk it removes.

tips: Eliminate: B has the practitioner move a budget that management controls, and D keeps a plan whose objective ends before the rebuild is done.
Final two: C beats A because the rebuild sits in the director's plan; when strategy changes, the owner re-decides the treatment without the board deciding it.
Exam cue: when strategy shortens or ends an objective, the treatments planned for it go back to their owner to weigh against the new horizon.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. Obligations as risk sources
questions.question: An energy retailer's legal team keeps a list of its 40 regulatory obligations. Which of the following BEST lets the risk practitioner manage those obligations as sources of risk?

options.A: A signed risk attestation from each unit head
options.B: Register entries for the risk of missing each obligation
options.C: A map from each obligation to the control that meets it
options.D: The legal team's own register of the obligations

questions.key_concept: Each compliance obligation is a source of risk: the risk of failing it is rated and owned in the risk register like any other.
questions.pre_read: Note exactly what the stem wants the obligations treated as.
questions.correct_explanation: Treating an obligation as a source of risk means asking what happens if it is missed, such as fines, license conditions or harm to customers. A register entry for that risk gives it a rating against appetite and a business owner, so it is weighed beside every other risk. A control map is the runner-up: it shows how each obligation is met, but not the impact of failing it or who decides on that risk.

wrong_explanations.A: An attestation records that unit heads believe they comply; it neither rates the effect of a failure nor gives the risk an owner.
wrong_explanations.C: Mapping obligations to controls is sound compliance practice, but it shows how each duty is met, not what missing it would cost or who owns that risk.
wrong_explanations.D: A list kept by legal is where tracking starts, but kept apart from the risk register, its entries get no rating against appetite and are not weighed beside other risks.

tips: Eliminate: A records belief in compliance, not a rated risk, and D keeps the obligations in a legal list outside the risk process.
Final two: B beats C because a register entry rates the impact of failing an obligation and names its owner; a control map shows only how it is met.
Exam cue: on CRISC items, a law, rule or contract term enters risk management as the risk of failing it, rated and owned in the register.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-03 (legal, regulatory and contractual requirements, including privacy obligations, are understood and managed); COBIT 2019 MEA03 (Managed Compliance With External Requirements); ISACA Glossary (risk register)

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. Fairness concern closed on accuracy
questions.question: A lender's AI loan-triage model sends older applicants to slow review at twice the usual rate; its owner, the lending director, dismissed staff concerns since accuracy meets target. What is the risk analyst's BEST advice?

options.A: Have the disparity rated as a risk for the director
options.B: Ask the data scientists to rebalance the model's training data
options.C: Accept the director's closure as the owner's risk decision
options.D: Refer the staff's concern to internal audit to review

questions.key_concept: A fairness concern about an AI model is a risk to rate and take to its owner, even when the model meets its accuracy target.
questions.pre_read: Separate what staff raised from what the owner checked.
questions.correct_explanation: An accuracy target shows whether the model predicts well overall; it does not show whether slowing older applicants is acceptable, which can mean unfair treatment, complaints and legal exposure. Staff raised the concern in good faith, so it is rated as a risk and taken to the director, who then decides. Accepting the closure is the runner-up: the owner decides, but on an analyzed risk, not on a measure that tests something else.

wrong_explanations.B: Rebalancing the training data is a treatment chosen before anyone knows whether the gap is unfair or justified, and choosing the response is the director's call.
wrong_explanations.C: The director owns the model's risks but closed the concern on accuracy, a measure that does not test how older applicants are treated, so the risk is still unanalyzed.
wrong_explanations.D: Internal audit gives independent assurance later; analyzing a newly raised risk and taking it to the owner is the second line's job now.

tips: Eliminate: B changes the model's data before the gap is analyzed, and D hands a new risk to internal audit, whose role is independent assurance.
Final two: A beats C because the owner decides on an analyzed risk; an accuracy target does not test fairness, so the closure rests on the wrong measure.
Exam cue: a concern raised in good faith is analyzed like any risk; meeting one target does not close a risk the target never measured.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Owner's request inside the limits
questions.question: A cinema chain's ticketing director owns the risk of two-hour ticketing outages, assessed last week within appetite and tolerance, and wants to accept it; nothing has changed since. What should the risk practitioner recommend FIRST?

options.A: Reassess the outage risk before the director can accept it
options.B: Ask the board's risk committee to approve the acceptance
options.C: Fund a standby system to remove the outage risk
options.D: Have the director accept the risk with a date to review it

questions.key_concept: When a current assessment puts a risk within appetite and tolerance and nothing has changed, the owner's acceptance on record comes first.
questions.pre_read: Note who owns the risk and how it compares with the limits.
questions.correct_explanation: The assessment is a week old, nothing has changed, and the risk sits within both appetite and tolerance, so the limits leaders set already allow it. The first step is the director's decision as owner: accept on record, then monitor. Reassessing is the runner-up: after a change in the risk or its setting it would come first, but here it repeats current analysis and delays the owner's decision.

wrong_explanations.A: Reassessment comes first after a change; with a week-old assessment and nothing changed, it repeats work the owner can decide on now.
wrong_explanations.B: The committee approves carrying risk above a limit it set; inside appetite and tolerance, the owner decides without escalation.
wrong_explanations.C: A standby system treats a risk already inside the limits, spending money the rating says the business need not spend.

tips: Eliminate: B escalates a risk that sits inside the limits leaders set, and C buys treatment for a risk already within appetite.
Final two: D beats A because the assessment is current and nothing has changed; reassessing comes first only after a change.
Exam cue: check what has changed since the rating; with no change and the risk inside both limits, the owner's decision is the first step, not another assessment.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. Two policies in conflict
questions.question: A consultancy's top-level travel policy allows client work over hotel Wi-Fi on VPN, but its top-level security policy bans it on public networks; neither says which prevails. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Apply the security policy as the stricter of the two
options.B: Ask senior management to reconcile the two policies
options.C: Ask each department head to choose the policy that applies
options.D: Propose an IT standard that bridges both policies

questions.key_concept: When peer policies conflict and neither takes precedence, the senior management that approved both reconciles them; applying the stricter one is at most a stopgap.
questions.pre_read: Note which layer each rule sits in before deciding which applies.
questions.correct_explanation: Both are top-level policies, which senior management approves, so neither outranks the other and staff cannot follow both. The conflict goes back to that level to reconcile, for example by setting when a VPN makes hotel Wi-Fi acceptable. Applying the stricter policy is the runner-up: it may serve as a stopgap, but between peer policies it sets aside a choice senior management made and leaves the conflict in place.

wrong_explanations.A: Following the stricter policy can serve as a stopgap, but it leaves the conflict in place and overrides a choice senior management made; only that level can reconcile peers.
wrong_explanations.C: Having each department choose splits one enterprise rule into many, so client data is protected differently across the consultancy.
wrong_explanations.D: A standard sits below both policies and must meet each; it cannot permit what one policy forbids, so the conflict is settled above it.

tips: Eliminate: C splits an enterprise rule by department, and D asks a lower layer to settle a conflict between the policies above it.
Final two: B beats A because the two policies are peers and neither takes precedence; following the stricter one leaves the conflict standing, so it goes to the level that approved both.
Exam cue: when rules conflict, check each one's layer; a lower layer may tighten a higher one, but a conflict between peers goes back to the level that approved both.
