questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. Risks left out while in treatment
questions.question: A bank's board risk profile omits risks with an approved, unfinished treatment plan: six of its nine risks above appetite. Which of the following should concern the risk practitioner MOST?

options.A: Plans for risks above appetite approved without the board
options.B: Whether the six plans will reach their target risk
options.C: Exposure above appetite today that the board cannot see
options.D: A profile listing fewer risks than the register holds

questions.key_concept: The profile reports current risk, which counts only responses already in place, so risks with approved but unfinished plans stay in it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the board uses the profile to decide.
questions.correct_explanation: Current risk counts only responses already in place, so an approved plan does not lower it. Leaving those risks out hides two-thirds of the exposure above appetite from the board, which set that appetite and oversees it. Whether the plans will reach their target risk is the runner-up: it matters, but it is tracked for risks the board can see, and here the board cannot see what the plans are for.

wrong_explanations.A: Owners choose responses within the framework; the board oversees exposure against its appetite rather than approving each treatment plan.
wrong_explanations.B: Plans can miss their target, but that is monitored once the risks are reported; first the board needs the current exposure the plans address.
wrong_explanations.D: A profile selects and combines register entries, so holding fewer lines than the register is normal, not a gap.

tips: Eliminate: A gives the board approval of plans that owners decide, and D treats a profile shorter than the register as a fault.
Final two: C beats B because an approved plan is not yet a response in place; the board must see current exposure before plan progress matters.
Exam cue: current risk counts only what is already in place; a risk in treatment stays in the profile at today's rating until its response is working.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Organizational structure, roles and responsibilities. Owner who does not decide
questions.question: A retailer's logistics director has owned a risk rated above appetite for five months without choosing a response, despite three reminders from the risk analyst. What is the analyst's BEST action?

options.A: Escalate the undecided risk to senior management
options.B: Send the director a fourth reminder with a deadline
options.C: Record the director's silence as acceptance of the risk
options.D: Have IT begin the treatment the analyst recommended

questions.key_concept: An owner's silence is not acceptance: a risk above appetite left undecided after repeated reminders is escalated above the owner.
questions.pre_read: Weigh how long the risk has waited and what has been tried.
questions.correct_explanation: Five months and three reminders show the director is not deciding, while a risk above appetite stays neither treated nor accepted. Escalating to senior management, who assign owners and expect them to act, puts the decision back on track; they may press the director or reassign the risk. Another reminder is the runner-up: it keeps the matter with the owner, but three have failed and the exposure continues.

wrong_explanations.B: A deadline suits a first delay, but after three reminders over five months the pattern is clear and the exposure above appetite continues.
wrong_explanations.C: Acceptance is a decision the owner makes and records; reading silence as acceptance invents a decision no one took on a risk above appetite.
wrong_explanations.D: Starting a treatment the owner never chose has the analyst and IT decide the response, which is the owner's decision to make.

tips: Eliminate: C turns silence into an acceptance no one made, and D has IT start a treatment the owner never chose.
Final two: A beats B because three reminders over five months have failed; a risk above appetite left undecided goes above the owner, not round again.
Exam cue: an owner's inaction is not acceptance; when an owner will not decide on a risk above appetite, escalate to the level that assigns owners.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Business processes and resilience. Recovery test reporting
questions.question: For three years, a grain cooperative's recovery test results went only to IT, so process owners learned of missed recovery targets they set only during real outages. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Escalate the past missed targets to the board's risk committee
options.B: Have IT retest each system until it meets its owner's target
options.C: Record this year's missed targets for their process owners
options.D: Report each recovery test's results to the process owners

questions.key_concept: Recovery test results go to the process owners who set the targets, so they can decide on any gap.
questions.pre_read: Notice who receives the results and for how long.
questions.correct_explanation: Recovery targets belong to the process owners, so test results are evidence they need to decide whether to fund a fix, accept a gap or revisit a target. Sent only to IT, misses stay hidden until a real outage. Reporting every test's results to the process owners fixes that route. Recording this year's misses is the runner-up: it helps now, but next year's results would still reach IT alone.

wrong_explanations.A: The board oversees appetite and major exposures, not individual test results; the process owners who set the targets are the ones who need them.
wrong_explanations.B: Retesting may follow, but IT would be choosing the response to gaps it does not own, and owners would still not see the results.
wrong_explanations.C: Recording this year's misses helps once, but results would keep going only to IT, so next year's gaps would again stay hidden.

tips: Eliminate: A sends test results past the owners to the board, and B has IT choose responses to gaps the process owners own.
Final two: D beats C because the cause is the reporting route; recording this year's misses helps once, but future results would still reach IT alone.
Exam cue: recovery test results go to the process owners who set the targets; when results keep missing them, fix the reporting route, not one year's gaps.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. Acceptance request for an AI model
questions.question: A construction firm rated the tampering risk of its AI bid-pricing model within appetite, using the model's $60,000 build cost as impact, and its owner wants to accept. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Ask the owner to accept the risk on record as rated
options.B: Ask the owner to revalue the model by its effect on bids
options.C: Escalate the owner's acceptance decision to the risk committee
options.D: Have IT add integrity checks to the model before acceptance

questions.key_concept: An asset's value for risk rating is the business harm its loss or misuse would cause, not what it cost to build or buy.
questions.pre_read: Check what each input to the rating rests on before judging the request.
questions.correct_explanation: An asset's value for risk analysis is what its loss or misuse would cost the business, not what it cost to build. A tampered pricing model could misprice bids worth far more than $60,000, so the within-appetite rating rests on the wrong figure. Accepting as rated is the runner-up: the owner may accept risk within appetite, but only on a rating that reflects the model's real value.

wrong_explanations.A: Owners may accept risk within appetite, but this rating takes the model's build cost as its impact, so the acceptance would rest on an understated figure.
wrong_explanations.C: The owner has authority for risk within appetite; the problem is the rating's basis, which a committee would inherit just as it stands.
wrong_explanations.D: Adding controls before the risk is properly valued puts treatment ahead of analysis; the corrected rating may or may not call for them.

tips: Eliminate: C sends to a committee a decision the owner can make within appetite, and D adds controls before the risk is properly rated.
Final two: B beats A because the rating values the model at its build cost; acceptance within appetite is the owner's call, but only on a rating that reflects business value.
Exam cue: when a within-appetite rating values an asset by its cost, fix the valuation before anyone accepts; value comes from what the business stands to lose.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). Impact scale and a safety scenario
questions.question: A rail operator's enterprise impact scale measures only money, so a signaling-data scenario that could endanger passengers rates low on its $90,000 direct cost. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Rate the scenario high by judgment, outside the scale
options.B: Raise the scenario's dollar impact to reflect the danger
options.C: Keep a separate safety scale beside the enterprise scale
options.D: Propose adding safety to the enterprise impact scale

questions.key_concept: Enterprise impact scales measure what matters to objectives, such as safety and customers as well as money, so every risk is rated on them.
questions.pre_read: Read what the scale measures before judging the rating.
questions.correct_explanation: Impact scales should measure what matters to the enterprise's objectives, and for a rail operator that includes passenger safety. A money-only scale under-rates every safety scenario, not just this one, so the fix is to propose safety measures for the enterprise scale, which senior management approves. Rating this scenario high by judgment is the runner-up: it corrects one rating but leaves the others low and cannot be compared with the rest.

wrong_explanations.A: An override fixes one rating, but other safety scenarios still rate low, and a rating set outside the scale cannot be compared or combined with the rest.
wrong_explanations.B: Inflating the dollar figure misstates the financial estimate and buries the real reason for the rating; safety needs its own measure on the scale.
wrong_explanations.C: A second scale gives ratings that cannot be compared with the enterprise register; one scale with business-based measures lets every risk be ranked together.

tips: Eliminate: B makes the dollar estimate carry a harm money does not measure, and C creates a second scale whose ratings cannot be compared with the enterprise's.
Final two: D beats A because the scale itself under-rates every safety scenario; an override fixes one rating and leaves the gap in place.
Exam cue: when a scale cannot express a harm that matters to objectives, fix the shared scale through its approvers rather than overriding single ratings.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. Control team inside IT
questions.question: A postal service's CIO formed an IT control team to test IT's own controls, and the CFO proposes disbanding the second-line IT risk team as a duplicate. What is the risk practitioner's BEST advice?

options.A: Move the control team under the CRO as the second line
options.B: Disband the IT risk team, relying on the control team
options.C: Keep the IT risk team challenging the control team's work
options.D: Ask internal audit to take over the IT risk team's challenge

questions.key_concept: A control team set up by, and reporting to, the function it checks is first-line self-testing; the second line still oversees and challenges it.
questions.pre_read: Place each team in a line by whom it reports to and what it does.
questions.correct_explanation: The control team reports to the CIO and tests IT's own controls, so it is a first-line function: useful self-checking, but not objective about the risks it checks. The second-line IT risk team oversees and challenges that work. Moving the control team under the CRO is the runner-up: it would create a second line, but IT would lose its own checks and the first line would stop testing the controls it runs.

wrong_explanations.A: Under the CRO the team would become second line, but IT would be left with no checks of its own, moving first-line monitoring onto the second line.
wrong_explanations.B: The control team reports to the CIO whose controls it tests; that is first-line self-checking, which cannot replace objective second-line challenge.
wrong_explanations.D: Internal audit gives periodic independent assurance; taking on ongoing challenge would make it part of management's oversight and weaken that independence.

tips: Eliminate: B counts a team reporting to the CIO as challenge of the CIO's own controls, and D moves ongoing second-line challenge onto internal audit.
Final two: C beats A because the control team's self-testing belongs in the first line; moving it would strip IT of its own checks rather than add challenge.
Exam cue: a control team inside the function it checks is first line; keep it, and keep an objective second line to challenge its results.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. Sales terms the platform cannot meet
questions.question: A SaaS provider pays sales staff at signing; they knowingly promised security terms the platform cannot meet to win deals, and $1,500,000 in penalties followed months later. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the platform team build the features sales promised
options.B: Have the risk team approve each contract's security terms
options.C: Add a security review of contract terms before signing
options.D: Defer part of sales pay, reducing it if losses follow

questions.key_concept: Deferring part of the pay of risk-taking roles, and reducing it if losses emerge, aligns rewards with risk that surfaces after the deal.
questions.pre_read: Ask why staff acted as they did before weighing the fixes.
questions.correct_explanation: Staff broke the terms knowingly because pay rewards the signature and ignores losses that surface months later. Deferring part of sales pay, reduced if a contract later causes loss, ties the reward to the risk taken. A pre-signing security review is the runner-up: it would catch some terms, but while pay rewards signing alone, the pressure to win deals moves onto the reviewer, so the cause remains.

wrong_explanations.A: Building each promised feature lets sales promises set the platform's roadmap, and pay would still reward the next term the platform cannot meet.
wrong_explanations.B: Having the risk team approve deals makes the second line take a first-line decision, and leaves the pay that drove the behavior in place.
wrong_explanations.C: A review adds a check, but staff paid at signing still gain from pushing risky terms through; the incentive behind the breaches remains.

tips: Eliminate: A lets sales promises set the platform's roadmap, and B has the second-line risk team approve deals the first line owns.
Final two: D beats C because pay rewards signing and ignores losses that surface later; a review adds a gate but leaves the reason to push past it.
Exam cue: when people knowingly take risks their pay rewards, fix the incentive; deferred pay that later losses can reduce links reward to the risk taken.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Organizational structure, roles and responsibilities. Change between committee meetings
questions.question: A ferry operator's booking-system risk rose to moderate, within appetite, tolerance and escalation thresholds, and the IT director wants the risk committee alerted before its meeting next month. What is the risk analyst's BEST response?

options.A: Report the change at the committee's scheduled meeting
options.B: Tell the committee about the change before its meeting
options.C: Hold the report until the change crosses a threshold
options.D: Propose treatment to bring the risk back down to low

questions.key_concept: Escalation thresholds decide what leaves the reporting cycle; a change that stays within them is reported at the committee's scheduled review.
questions.pre_read: Compare the change with each limit the stem names.
questions.correct_explanation: The framework sets escalation thresholds so that only changes crossing them go to decision makers out of cycle; this rise stays within appetite, tolerance and those thresholds. The committee reviews the profile at its scheduled meeting, where the change and its trend are reported. Telling the committee early is the runner-up: it looks prudent, but treating in-limit changes as escalations dilutes the signal the thresholds exist to give.

wrong_explanations.B: Out-of-cycle escalation is for changes that cross a threshold; this one does not, and early alerts for in-limit moves blur what escalation means.
wrong_explanations.C: Exception-only reporting hides the trend; in-limit changes still belong in the committee's scheduled report so it can see where exposure is heading.
wrong_explanations.D: Risk within appetite and tolerance needs no treatment to return it to low; its owner may accept and monitor it.

tips: Eliminate: C waits for a breach, so the committee that reviews the profile misses the rising trend, and D treats a risk within appetite and tolerance as if it needed reducing.
Final two: A beats B because no escalation threshold is crossed; the scheduled review is the route for in-limit changes, and out-of-cycle escalation is kept for breaches.
Exam cue: escalate out of cycle only when a threshold is crossed; a change within limits, and its trend, goes in the next scheduled report.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. Sector Community Profile
questions.question: Which of the following should the risk practitioner recommend as the BEST use of a sector Community Profile by a water utility adopting NIST CSF 2.0?

options.A: A replacement for the utility's risk framework
options.B: A record of the outcomes the utility achieves today
options.C: A regulator's checklist the utility is audited against
options.D: A starting point for the utility's Target Profile

questions.key_concept: A CSF 2.0 Community Profile is a sector baseline that an organization can use as the basis for its Target Profile, then tailor.
questions.pre_read: Recall what each kind of CSF profile describes.
questions.correct_explanation: A Community Profile is a baseline of CSF outcomes shared by organizations in a sector, and NIST CSF 2.0 says an organization can use one as the basis for its Target Profile, then tailor it to its own mission, threats and requirements. A record of today's outcomes is the runner-up: both are CSF profiles, but what the utility achieves now is its Current Profile, drawn from its own practices.

wrong_explanations.A: CSF 2.0 is used alongside an enterprise's risk management framework and ERM; a set of sector outcomes cannot replace the utility's own risk framework.
wrong_explanations.B: The outcomes the utility achieves today form its Current Profile, drawn from its own practices; a sector baseline describes shared targets, not today's state.
wrong_explanations.C: A Community Profile is voluntary, sector-shared guidance, not a regulator's checklist; the utility tailors it rather than being audited against it.

tips: Eliminate: A swaps the utility's own risk framework for a set of sector outcomes, and C treats voluntary sector guidance as a regulator's audit checklist.
Final two: D beats B because a Community Profile describes shared target outcomes; what the utility achieves today is its own Current Profile.
Exam cue: outside baselines and frameworks are starting points to tailor, not finished answers to adopt as published.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Strategy, goals and objectives. Cloud move turned down
questions.question: A sports club's IT committee rejected a cloud ticketing move on data risk alone; the current platform hit full load, and the club plans 30% more members. What is the risk analyst's BEST advice?

options.A: Rate the current platform's risk to the membership goal
options.B: Reassess the cloud move's data risk in greater depth
options.C: Ask IT to add capacity to the current platform
options.D: Propose lowering the membership target to fit the platform

questions.key_concept: Keeping the current state carries risk too; it is rated against the objective so leaders can compare it with the risk of change.
questions.pre_read: Note what the committee's decision was based on.
questions.correct_explanation: The committee weighed only the risk of moving; staying on a platform already at full load is also a risk, here to the club's plan for 30% more members. Rating that risk gives decision makers both sides against the objective. Reassessing the move's data risk is the runner-up: it refines the half the committee already saw and still leaves the risk of standing still unmeasured.

wrong_explanations.B: This refines the half of the picture the committee already weighed; the risk that the current platform poses to the membership plan stays unrated.
wrong_explanations.C: Adding capacity is a response chosen before the risk is rated, and whether it beats the cloud move is not yet known.
wrong_explanations.D: Cutting the objective to fit a one-sided risk view reverses the order; objectives come first and risk is judged against them.

tips: Eliminate: C picks a fix before the platform's risk is rated, and D bends the club's objective to fit a decision made on half the picture.
Final two: A beats B because the missing view is the risk of standing still; reassessing the move refines only what the committee already saw.
Exam cue: not changing is a choice with its own risk; rate the status quo against the objective as well as the proposed change.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. Flag for skipping a template
questions.question: A compliance check flagged a map publisher's cartographers for skipping the AI prompt guideline's template, which does not fit map labels; they meet the AI use standard. What is the risk analyst's BEST advice?

options.A: Escalate the skipped template to the AI governance committee
options.B: Log an exception to the guideline for the cartographers
options.C: Close the finding raised against the cartographers
options.D: Propose making the guideline's template mandatory

questions.key_concept: Guidelines are advisory; compliance is judged against the mandatory layers, so a reasoned departure from a guideline is not a finding.
questions.pre_read: Identify which layer of the policy hierarchy the check applied.
questions.correct_explanation: A guideline recommends good practice and allows departures for a sound reason; compliance is judged against the mandatory layers, and the cartographers meet the AI use standard. With a template that does not fit map labels, the finding should be closed. Making the template mandatory is the runner-up: it would turn advice into a rule, but nothing in the case shows a risk that the rule would reduce.

wrong_explanations.A: A reasoned departure from an advisory guideline is not a finding, so there is nothing for a committee to decide; the mandatory standard is met.
wrong_explanations.B: Exceptions are for mandatory rules people cannot meet; departing from an advisory guideline needs no exception, owner or expiry.
wrong_explanations.D: A guideline becomes a rule only when a risk calls for it; here the standard is met and the template does not fit map work.

tips: Eliminate: A escalates a departure that is not a finding, and B raises an exception, which is meant for a mandatory rule, against advice.
Final two: C beats D because nothing shows a risk that a mandatory template would reduce; the cartographers already meet the standard that is mandatory.
Exam cue: judge compliance against policies, standards and procedures; a guideline departure with a sound reason is not a finding.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). Unit declines the rating method
questions.question: A law firm's litigation group, its largest unit, still refuses the approved framework's rating method after the risk analyst's walk-through, saying its partners know their risks. What is the analyst's BEST next step?

options.A: Allow the group to rate its risks by partners' own judgment
options.B: Raise the refusal with the framework's executive sponsor
options.C: Rate the group's risks for it on the firm's own scale
options.D: Have the group's partners retrain on the rating method

questions.key_concept: An approved framework binds every unit; a unit that refuses its methods goes to the senior leaders behind it, through the executive sponsor.
questions.pre_read: Read what the analyst has already done before choosing a next step.
questions.correct_explanation: Senior management approved the framework, and the leaders behind it decide how much freedom any unit has over its methods; a unit that still refuses after explanation is a governance issue for them, raised through the framework's executive sponsor. Rating the group's risks on its behalf is the runner-up: it fills the enterprise view, but it takes the assessment from the first line and leaves the refusal unresolved.

wrong_explanations.A: Only the leaders who approved the framework can let a unit depart from its method; the analyst cannot grant that freedom to the group.
wrong_explanations.C: Second-line staff rating a unit's risks for it take the assessment from the people who own them and leave the unit outside the method.
wrong_explanations.D: The group has had the method explained and still refuses; more training builds skill but does not change a decision not to follow an approved framework.

tips: Eliminate: A has the analyst grant a departure that only the approving leaders can allow, and D answers a refusal, not a skill gap, with more training.
Final two: B beats C because rating the group's risks for it moves the assessment to the second line; the refusal itself needs the framework's sponsor.
Exam cue: when a unit will not follow an approved framework, take it to the authority behind the framework rather than working around it.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. Audit relying on second-line tests
questions.question: Internal audit at a national charity plans to rely on the risk team's yearly tests of 20 donation-processing controls. What should the risk analyst provide as the BEST basis for that reliance?

options.A: A summary of the test conclusions signed by the CRO
options.B: Control owners' written statements that each control works
options.C: Records of each test's samples, steps and results
options.D: Risk owners' approval of the ratings that followed the tests

questions.key_concept: Internal audit can rely on second-line testing only after judging its quality, so the second line supplies documented samples, steps and results.
questions.pre_read: Ask what internal audit must be able to do before it relies on someone else's work.
questions.correct_explanation: To rely on another line's work, internal audit must judge its quality for itself: the testers' competence and objectivity, and what was tested, how and with what results. Records of samples, steps and outcomes for each control let it do that. A CRO-signed summary is the runner-up: it carries authority, but it gives only conclusions, which audit would have to take on trust instead of evaluating.

wrong_explanations.A: A signed summary gives conclusions without the work behind them; audit cannot judge the quality of tests it cannot see, whoever signs.
wrong_explanations.B: Owners' statements are first-line assertions about their own controls; they are not evidence of the second-line testing that audit plans to rely on.
wrong_explanations.D: Risk owners approve ratings and responses; their approval says nothing about how well the controls were tested.

tips: Eliminate: B offers first-line assertions in place of test evidence, and D gives risk owners' rating approvals, which say nothing about how the tests were done.
Final two: C beats A because audit relies only on work it can evaluate; a signed summary of conclusions still has to be taken on trust.
Exam cue: when one line relies on another's work, the basis is the work itself, documented well enough to be reviewed or re-performed.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. Board question on a security program
questions.question: A packaging maker's board asks whether last year's $800,000 security program lowered its risk exposure. Which of the following should the risk analyst use as the BEST basis for the answer?

options.A: The program's report of spending against budget
options.B: The program owner's count of controls delivered on time
options.C: Risk owners' views on whether their own risks have fallen
options.D: Current ratings of the targeted risks beside last year's

questions.key_concept: A program's effect on exposure is shown by comparing the targeted risks' ratings over time, not by its spending or output.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the program did from what the board asked about.
questions.correct_explanation: Whether exposure fell is answered by the risk profile over time: the current ratings of the risks the program targeted, set beside last year's, show the change the board asked about. The count of controls delivered on time is the runner-up: it shows the program did its work, but output is not outcome, and new controls may not have moved the ratings.

wrong_explanations.A: Spending against budget shows financial control of the program, not whether the risks it targeted are any lower.
wrong_explanations.B: Controls delivered on time measure the program's output; exposure falls only if those controls work against the risks they were meant to reduce.
wrong_explanations.C: Owners' impressions are opinions without the rating method behind them; the board's question needs ratings compared over time, not views.

tips: Eliminate: A reports the program's spending, not its effect on risk, and C collects owners' opinions in place of ratings made by the agreed method.
Final two: D beats B because the board asked about exposure; delivered controls are output, and only the ratings over time show the outcome.
Exam cue: to show whether risk changed, compare the same risks' ratings across periods; activity, spend and opinions describe effort, not exposure.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. Inventory behind a planned assessment
questions.question: A museum's risk analyst will rate risks to its collection systems from an asset inventory last updated 14 months ago, before a year of digitization projects. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Reconcile the inventory with purchase records and a discovery scan
options.B: Ask each asset owner to rate risks to their listed assets
options.C: Check each asset owner's classification against policy
options.D: Have project owners add their new systems to the inventory

questions.key_concept: Before rating risks from an asset inventory, the practitioner checks it is complete and current, not just for the changes already known.
questions.pre_read: Look at the dates in the stem before choosing a first step.
questions.correct_explanation: Ratings are only as complete as the asset list behind them, and this inventory is 14 months old. Reconciling it with purchase records and a discovery scan finds the projects' systems and any other services bought, moved or retired since, before rating starts. Adding the projects' systems is the runner-up: it fixes the change the analyst knows about but leaves the rest of those 14 months unchecked.

wrong_explanations.B: Rating from an inventory known to be 14 months out of date leaves out whatever it misses; completeness comes before owners rate.
wrong_explanations.C: Checking classifications tests entries already listed; it cannot reveal services or other assets the inventory misses.
wrong_explanations.D: This fixes the one known change, but 14 months of other purchases, moves and retirements may also be missing from the list.

tips: Eliminate: B rates from a list known to be out of date, and C checks the classes of listed entries but cannot find assets that are missing.
Final two: A beats D because the projects are only the change the analyst knows about; reconciling finds every gap from the last 14 months.
Exam cue: before rating from an inventory, register or dataset, check it is complete and current; ratings inherit every gap in it.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Business processes and resilience. Supplier outage the plan never listed
questions.question: A one-day outage at a recycling firm's only fuel supplier grounded its trucks; the collections continuity plan, written around the routing software, never listed fuel. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the routing software's owner shorten its recovery time
options.B: Have the collections owner map the process's dependencies
options.C: Have IT add fuel supply to the disaster recovery plan
options.D: Have the collections owner add a second fuel supplier

questions.key_concept: A continuity plan built around one system misses the process's other dependencies; the process owner maps people, suppliers, data and systems end to end.
questions.pre_read: Look at how the plan was scoped before choosing a fix for the gap the outage showed.
questions.correct_explanation: Continuity planning starts from the business process and everything it depends on: people, suppliers, data and systems. A plan written around the routing software found its fuel dependency only when it failed, and it may be missing others. Mapping them end to end with the collections owner fixes how the plan was scoped. A second fuel supplier is the runner-up: it closes the one gap already exposed and leaves the rest unexamined.

wrong_explanations.A: The routing software did not fail; a faster restore leaves the trucks grounded the next time a supplier or other non-system dependency fails.
wrong_explanations.C: Fuel supply is a business dependency, not a system to restore; the IT disaster recovery plan covers technology, while the continuity plan covers the process.
wrong_explanations.D: A second supplier treats the one gap the outage exposed, but a plan scoped to software may still miss other people, supplier and data dependencies.

tips: Eliminate: A speeds the restore of a system that never failed, and C puts a business supplier into the IT recovery plan, which covers technology, not the process.
Final two: B beats D because the plan's software-only scope caused the miss; a second supplier fixes the gap already found, while mapping finds the rest.
Exam cue: when a plan misses a dependency because of how it was scoped, fix the scope, not only the one gap; continuity starts from the whole process.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Breaches that keep returning
questions.question: A cement maker's AI kiln-control model breached the error tolerance senior management set in five of six months; each escalated breach was cleared by retraining within days. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Ask the model owner to seek a review of the tolerance
options.B: Have the model owner retrain the model once a week
options.C: Have the model owner accept the breaches until year end
options.D: Analyze why the model's error keeps exceeding tolerance

questions.key_concept: Repeated tolerance breaches point to a cause the quick fixes miss; analyze it before changing the treatment or asking to move the limit.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what five breaches in six months say that a single breach would not.
questions.correct_explanation: One breach calls for escalation and a fix; five in six months show the fix treats the symptom. Analyzing why the error keeps returning shows whether the cause lies in the model, its input data or the process, or whether the limit needs review. Having the model owner seek a tolerance review is the runner-up: the limit may need to change, but asking before the cause is known risks fitting the line to the results.

wrong_explanations.A: A limit review may follow, but seeking one before the cause is known risks fitting the tolerance to the results.
wrong_explanations.B: Retraining each week is a treatment picked before the cause is known; if the model's inputs are the problem, retraining more often can keep failing.
wrong_explanations.C: Running above a tolerance needs approval from the level that set it, and accepting repeated breaches leaves their cause in place.

tips: Eliminate: B picks a treatment before anyone knows why the error returns, and C has the owner accept breaches of a limit that only senior management can relax.
Final two: D beats A because a limit is reviewed once the cause is known; asking to move it first can hide a failing model behind a wider line.
Exam cue: a breach that keeps coming back is a pattern; analyze its cause before changing the treatment or the threshold.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. Outcomes left out of a profile
questions.question: Senior management approved a court service's NIST CSF 2.0 Target Profile with no supply chain outcomes, yet its top risk is an outage of its hosted e-filing service. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Assess the hosting provider's controls under its contract
options.B: Replace the tailored profile with the complete CSF 2.0 Core
options.C: Ask senior management to reopen the profile's tailoring
options.D: Record the hosting outage as outside the framework's scope

questions.key_concept: A tailored framework must reach the enterprise's top risks; when it omits one, the tailoring goes back to the leaders who approved it.
questions.pre_read: Check how the framework's scope lines up with the register before choosing a step.
questions.correct_explanation: Tailoring keeps the outcomes that address the enterprise's risks, so a Target Profile without supply chain outcomes no longer fits a service whose top risk sits with a provider. Tailoring is a senior management decision, so the analyst takes the gap back to it. Assessing the provider's controls is the runner-up: it is useful work on one supplier, but the profile would still leave every supplier risk outside the outcomes the court service plans for.

wrong_explanations.A: Reviewing this provider helps with one risk, but the approved profile would still plan no supply chain outcomes for the court service.
wrong_explanations.B: Taking the whole Core unchanged discards tailoring; the fix is to restore the outcomes the court service's risks need, not to adopt everything.
wrong_explanations.D: Framework scope does not decide which risks the court service faces; a top risk falling outside scope shows the scope is wrong.

tips: Eliminate: B drops tailoring in favor of the whole Core, and D treats the framework's scope as if it removed the risk it leaves out.
Final two: C beats A because the gap is in the approved tailoring; assessing one provider helps, but the profile would still omit supply chain outcomes.
Exam cue: when a framework's tailoring misses a top register risk, take the tailoring back to its approvers instead of patching around one case.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). Impact bands after growth
questions.question: A textiles maker has quadrupled its revenue since setting its impact scale, and 70% of its risks now rate in the top band. What is the risk analyst's BEST basis for new bands?

options.A: The firm's current financial size and risk capacity
options.B: An even spread of today's risks across the five bands
options.C: The bands that a larger firm in the same sector uses
options.D: Each unit head's view of the rating their risks deserve

questions.key_concept: Impact bands show what a loss means to the enterprise now, so they follow its current size and capacity, not the spread of ratings.
questions.pre_read: Ask what an impact band is meant to tell a decision maker.
questions.correct_explanation: An impact band tells leaders how much a loss would hurt this enterprise, so its break points follow the firm's current size and the losses it can absorb. Bands set at a quarter of today's revenue overstate each loss's significance. An even spread of today's risks is the runner-up: it would separate them on a chart, but each band would then show a risk's rank, not what a loss would mean to the business.

wrong_explanations.B: Fitting bands to spread ratings evenly turns each band into a ranking, so a band no longer says how much a loss would hurt the firm.
wrong_explanations.C: A larger firm can absorb bigger losses, so its bands would understate what a given loss means to this textiles maker.
wrong_explanations.D: Bands set from each head's view of what their risks deserve vary by unit, so ratings could not be compared on one enterprise scale.

tips: Eliminate: C borrows a larger firm's bands, sized to its own losses, and D lets each unit head's opinion shape a scale that must be common to all.
Final two: A beats B because a band must say what a loss means to this firm; an even spread makes the bands a ranking instead.
Exam cue: scales measure business significance; when the business changes size, recalibrate the break points to it, never to the ratings.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. Exceptions kept outside the register
questions.question: An accounting firm's 35 approved exceptions to its encryption standard sit in an IT spreadsheet that the risk register never references. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the security team track the exceptions' expiry dates
options.B: Add the count of open exceptions to the register report
options.C: Have risk owners re-sign the 35 exceptions this year
options.D: Link each exception to its risk owner's register entry

questions.key_concept: An approved exception is accepted risk, so it is linked to a register entry with its owner, where it is aggregated, reported and reviewed.
questions.pre_read: Recall what an approved exception means for risk before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: An approved exception is risk its owner has accepted for a time, so it belongs with the enterprise's other risks: linked to a register entry under its owner, where it is aggregated, reported in the profile and reviewed. Having the security team track expiry dates is the runner-up: expiry discipline matters, but the accepted risk would still be invisible to the register and the profile.

wrong_explanations.A: Expiry checks keep exceptions from lapsing unnoticed, but the accepted risk they carry would still sit outside the register and the profile.
wrong_explanations.B: A count shows volume, not exposure; 35 exceptions on low-value systems and 35 on client data would look the same.
wrong_explanations.C: Re-signing all 35 renews them without fresh analysis and still leaves the risk they carry outside the register.

tips: Eliminate: B reports a count that says nothing about how much risk the exceptions carry, and C renews them without new analysis or a place in the register.
Final two: D beats A because an exception is accepted risk that belongs in the register under its owner; expiry checks alone leave it out of sight.
Exam cue: exceptions, waivers and acceptances are risks; link them to the register and their owner so they are aggregated and reported.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Organizational structure, roles and responsibilities. Decisions above the executive committee
questions.question: Which of the following should the risk analyst MOST appropriately take to a newspaper's board for decision, not to its executive committee?

options.A: Approval of updated risk assessment procedures
options.B: A change to the overall enterprise risk appetite
options.C: A risk owner's choice of response within appetite
options.D: The choice of owner for a newly recorded risk

questions.key_concept: The board, with senior management, sets risk appetite; senior management approves the framework and assigns owners, and risk owners choose responses.
questions.pre_read: Sort each decision by the level that holds the authority for it.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk appetite is the broad amount of risk the enterprise will take in pursuit of its objectives, and setting or changing it is the board's decision, made with senior management. Approving updated risk assessment procedures is the runner-up: they carry out the board-approved approach, so senior management, here the executive committee, approves them under board oversight. Risk owners choose responses within appetite, and senior management assigns owners.

wrong_explanations.A: Procedures under the framework are a management matter; senior management, here the executive committee, approves their updates under board oversight.
wrong_explanations.C: Choosing a response within appetite is the risk owner's decision; the board oversees appetite and the profile, not single responses.
wrong_explanations.D: Senior management assigns risk owners; the board does not pick owners for individual risks.

tips: Eliminate: C hands the board a risk owner's response within appetite, and D gives it the naming of owners, which senior management does.
Final two: B beats A because appetite is the board's call; procedures that carry out the framework are approved by senior management under board oversight.
Exam cue: the board sets appetite and oversees; senior management runs the framework's procedures and assigns owners; risk owners choose responses.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. A unit with no near misses
questions.question: Over two years, a toy maker's design unit has logged no security near misses, while three similar units each log about 20 a year. What should the risk analyst consider the MOST likely explanation?

options.A: The design unit's controls keep near misses from occurring
options.B: The design unit faces fewer threats than the other units
options.C: Near misses in the design unit are going unreported
options.D: The design unit's staff took more awareness training

questions.key_concept: Near misses are part of normal operations, so a unit that reports none while similar units report many most likely has issues going unreported.
questions.pre_read: Recall what a near miss is and when it gets recorded.
questions.correct_explanation: A near miss is an event caught before it causes harm, such as a blocked phishing click, so units with working controls still record them. None in two years, beside similar units' 20 a year, most likely means near misses go unreported, a risk culture concern to explore with the unit. Stronger controls are the runner-up, but controls that stop threats create near misses to log rather than removing them.

wrong_explanations.A: Controls that stop threats generate near misses, such as blocked clicks; strong controls would show up as reports, not as none.
wrong_explanations.B: The units are similar, so their exposure should be comparable; a gap from about 20 a year to none is not explained by threat levels.
wrong_explanations.D: Training should raise reporting, since staff learn to spot and report near misses; it cannot explain a unit that reports nothing.

tips: Eliminate: B assumes a similar unit faces almost no threats, and D credits training, which should raise reporting, for a unit that reports nothing.
Final two: C beats A because a near miss is a threat caught in time; strong controls create reports to log, so silence points to under-reporting.
Exam cue: in culture questions, a lasting silence in reporting is a warning sign; healthy cultures report near misses early and often.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Strategy, goals and objectives. Patching goal and lab experiments
questions.question: An engineering college's IT department holds a goal of patching every server within seven days, and twice this term forced reboots ended week-long, grant-funded lab experiments. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Review the patching goal against research objectives with lab owners
options.B: Exempt lab servers from the patching goal with each lab owner's sign-off
options.C: Add network isolation for the lab servers before the next cycle
options.D: Report patch compliance against IT's objectives to senior management

questions.key_concept: IT goals serve enterprise goals; when an IT goal starts harming the objective it supports, revisit the goal with the business owners.
questions.pre_read: Separate the cause of the clash from its symptoms before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: IT goals exist to serve enterprise goals. A seven-day goal applied to every server is now harming the research it should protect, so the goal itself is revisited with the lab owners, weighing slower patching against lost experiments. Exempting lab servers with sign-off is the runner-up: it stops the reboots, but it drops patching on those servers without analysis and leaves the misaligned goal in place.

wrong_explanations.B: An exemption stops the reboots but removes patching from the lab servers without analyzing that risk, and the goal that caused the clash stays unchanged.
wrong_explanations.C: Isolation is a control chosen before anyone has weighed the research objective against the patching risk, and it does not stop forced reboots.
wrong_explanations.D: A compliance rate shows IT meeting its own goal, not the harm that goal is doing to the research it is meant to support.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Business processes and resilience. Two new responders before the exercise
questions.question: A port authority replaced 2 of its 14 berth-allocation continuity responders, neither a team lead; both were trained, and the plan's yearly exercise is two months away. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Review the business impact analysis before the yearly exercise
options.B: Ask the process owner to run an extra exercise this month
options.C: Have the process owner mark the plan untested until the exercise
options.D: Have the process owner include both in the yearly exercise

questions.key_concept: Plans are exercised on a regular cycle and after major change; a small staff change, already trained, is tested at the next scheduled exercise.
questions.pre_read: Judge the size of the change before choosing how to test for it.
questions.correct_explanation: Plans are exercised on a regular cycle and after major change, and newly appointed responders are trained soon after joining. Two trained responders replacing two others, neither a lead, is routine maintenance with no trigger for testing out of cycle; the yearly exercise two months away tests them in role. An extra exercise this month is the runner-up: it tests the newcomers sooner, but spends exercise effort on a change too small to need one.

wrong_explanations.A: A business impact analysis ranks processes by the harm their disruption causes; swapping two responders changes neither the process nor that harm.
wrong_explanations.B: Testing after major change is sound, but two trained, non-lead responders are a routine change, and the yearly exercise is only two months away.
wrong_explanations.C: Two trained, non-lead responders do not undo the plan's last test; marking it untested overstates a routine change and misreports the plan's readiness to leaders.

tips: Eliminate: A revisits the impact analysis, which a staff change does not alter, and C calls a tested plan untested over a routine, trained change.
Final two: D beats B because a small, trained staff change is no trigger for out-of-cycle testing; the yearly exercise two months away covers it.
Exam cue: exercise plans on schedule and after major change; routine changes are handled by plan upkeep and the next scheduled exercise.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. Controllers missing from the inventory
questions.question: A shipyard's asset inventory, built from IT network scans, omits the 60 controllers that run its dry-dock pumps and cranes on a separate plant network. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Name IT as the controllers' owner in the asset inventory
options.B: Add the controllers and owners to the enterprise inventory
options.C: Have the dock operations owner keep a separate controller list
options.D: Have each plant controller's owner rate its risk before listing it

questions.key_concept: Every asset the enterprise relies on, plant controllers included, belongs in the one inventory that feeds risk assessment.
questions.pre_read: Recall what the asset inventory is used for in risk management.
questions.correct_explanation: If the enterprise relies on an asset, it belongs in the one inventory that feeds risk assessment, wherever it runs, recorded with its business owner and the process it supports. The controllers are missing only because the scans never reached the plant network. A separate list kept by the dock operations owner is the runner-up: it gives the controllers an owner, but keeps them out of the inventory that enterprise risk assessments draw on.

wrong_explanations.A: IT is at most a custodian here; the controllers serve dock operations, so a business owner answers for them, not the team that ran the scans.
wrong_explanations.C: A separate list gives the controllers an owner but leaves them outside the inventory that enterprise risk assessments use, so the gap remains.
wrong_explanations.D: Risk assessment draws on the inventory; rating each controller before it is listed reverses that order and leaves the inventory gap open.

tips: Eliminate: A names a custodian as owner, and D rates risks before the assets are in the inventory that assessments draw on.
Final two: B beats C because one enterprise inventory feeds risk assessment; an owner's side list leaves the controllers outside it.
Exam cue: plant, cloud and AI assets belong in the inventory that risk assessments draw on; a side list no assessment uses is still a gap.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. Validating team asked to own a model's risk
questions.question: An insurance broker's claims director wants the second-line risk team, which validates the unit's AI claims-triage model, to own the model's risk. What is the risk analyst's BEST advice?

options.A: Confirm the claims director as owner of the model's risk
options.B: Have the claims director and the risk team hold the risk jointly
options.C: Move the model's risk to the risk team that validates it
options.D: Give internal audit the model's risk for independent assurance

questions.key_concept: The business unit that uses an AI model owns its risk; the second line validates and challenges the model without taking ownership.
questions.pre_read: Recall what each line of defense does with a risk.
questions.correct_explanation: The first line owns its risks, and the claims unit uses the model to make its decisions, so the claims director stays the risk owner. The second-line team validates and challenges the model, and it keeps its objectivity only if it does not own what it reviews. Holding the risk jointly is the runner-up: it keeps the director involved, but each risk needs one accountable owner, and sharing blurs who decides.

wrong_explanations.B: Each risk needs one accountable owner; joint holding blurs who decides and puts the reviewing team partly in charge of what it reviews.
wrong_explanations.C: Validation is second-line oversight; owning the risk would have the team judge its own position and take the decision away from the unit using the model.
wrong_explanations.D: Internal audit gives independent assurance and does not take on management's risks; owning this one would compromise its independence.

tips: Eliminate: C hands a first-line risk to the second line that reviews it, and D asks internal audit to own a risk it must assure.
Final two: A beats B because one accountable owner holds each risk; joint holding with the reviewing team blurs accountability and objectivity.
Exam cue: the unit that uses an AI model owns its risk; validators and auditors check it, they never own it.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. Ratings that fell when the bands changed
questions.question: After an architecture practice doubled in size, its partners approved wider impact bands; this quarter's profile rates three risks lower, though controls and threats are unchanged. What is the risk analyst's BEST action?

options.A: Check whether exposure on the three risks has fallen
options.B: Confirm the three lower ratings with their risk owners
options.C: Report both quarters' ratings on the new impact bands
options.D: Have the risk owners re-rate the three risks on the old bands

questions.key_concept: When a rating method changes, restate the prior period on the new method so the profile compares like with like.
questions.pre_read: Ask what actually changed between the two quarters.
questions.correct_explanation: The three ratings fell when the bands moved, while controls and threats stayed the same, so the fall reflects the method, not lower exposure. Restating last quarter on the new bands gives partners a like-for-like comparison in which any real change still shows. Checking whether exposure has fallen is the runner-up: it looks like careful validation, but the cause of the fall is already known, and the report would still compare two different scales.

wrong_explanations.A: Validation is sound practice, but the cause is already known, new bands with controls and threats unchanged, and the report would still mix two scales.
wrong_explanations.B: The ratings are right on the new bands; owners confirming them does not make this quarter comparable with the last.
wrong_explanations.D: The partners approved the new bands for current reporting; rating on retired bands misstates what a loss now means to the larger firm.

tips: Eliminate: B confirms ratings that are not in doubt, and D rates on a scale the partners have retired.
Final two: C beats A because the cause of the fall is already known, a method change; restating the prior quarter shows partners the true comparison.
Exam cue: when a rating method changes, restate the earlier period on the new method so trends compare like with like.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Monthly limit and yearly report
questions.question: A freight forwarder's board set a tolerance of four hours of tracking-system downtime a month, while IT reports only yearly availability, with a 99.5% target. Which of the following is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: The board's tolerance restated as 99.5% yearly availability
options.B: A monthly downtime measure against the four-hour tolerance
options.C: A tighter yearly availability target of 99.9% for IT
options.D: A KPI for how fast IT restores the tracking system

questions.key_concept: A tolerance is monitored in its own unit and period; a yearly average can hide a monthly breach.
questions.pre_read: Check what each measure could hide before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: A tolerance is a measurable limit on how far a risk may vary, so it is monitored in its own terms. A 99.5% yearly target allows about 44 hours of downtime a year, enough for a month far above four hours to pass unseen. A tighter 99.9% yearly target is the runner-up: it cuts the yearly allowance to under nine hours, but one bad month could still double the tolerance unnoticed.

wrong_explanations.A: The tolerance is the board's limit; restating it to fit IT's report changes the limit instead of measuring against it.
wrong_explanations.C: At 99.9% a year, IT may still have one month with over eight hours down, double the tolerance, and the yearly figure would not show it.
wrong_explanations.D: Restore speed is a KPI of IT's recovery process; it does not show total downtime in a month against the board's limit.

tips: Eliminate: A rewrites the board's limit to suit IT's report, and D tracks restore speed, a process KPI, not monthly downtime.
Final two: B beats C because a yearly target, however tight, can hide a month above four hours; the limit is monitored in its own period.
Exam cue: monitor a tolerance in the unit and period it is set in; a yearly average can hide a monthly breach.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Organizational structure, roles and responsibilities. Named owner with a small approval limit
questions.question: A ferry builder names its CAD team lead as owner of a hull-design ransomware risk above appetite; each response option costs more than the lead's $10,000 approval limit. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Have the CIO fund the response from the IT budget
options.B: Ask senior management to reassign the risk to a budget holder
options.C: Escalate each spending request to the engineering director
options.D: Split the response into steps within the $10,000 limit

questions.key_concept: A risk owner needs the authority and resources to decide the response; when the named owner lacks them, senior management names another.
questions.pre_read: Notice what each option does to who decides the response.
questions.correct_explanation: A risk owner is the person with the authority and accountability to make risk-based decisions. The lead cannot fund any response, so the risk would sit above appetite with no one able to decide; senior management assigns owners, so it names one who can, such as the engineering director. Escalating each spending request is the runner-up: it gets money approved, but the lead stays accountable for choices someone else makes.

wrong_explanations.A: IT can fund and run controls, but the risk sits with the business whose designs are at stake; paying for a fix does not make IT the decider.
wrong_explanations.C: Escalation gets each request approved, but the lead stays accountable for decisions the director makes; ownership belongs with whoever holds the authority.
wrong_explanations.D: Splitting a response to fit under an approval limit defeats the limit and still leaves the overall choice with someone who cannot make it.

tips: Eliminate: A hands a business risk's decisions to IT because IT holds a budget, and D carves the response up to slip under an approval limit.
Final two: B beats C because a risk owner holds both accountability and authority; escalating each request leaves the lead answerable for decisions someone else makes.
Exam cue: when the named owner cannot decide or fund any response, have senior management name an owner who can; do not work around the limit.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Indicator after a tolerance change
questions.question: A credit bureau's board approved a faster-release strategy and raised its failed-change tolerance from 2% to 5%; failures run at 3%, but the KRI turns red above 2%. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Report each red result to the risk owner as a breach

options.C: Ask the risk owner to bring failures back under 2%
options.D: Draft new KRI thresholds for the risk owner to agree

questions.key_concept: When leaders change a tolerance, KRI thresholds are re-aligned to the new limit, with an early-warning level set below it.
questions.pre_read: Compare the indicator's red level with the limit now in force.
questions.correct_explanation: KRI thresholds carry the tolerance into day-to-day monitoring, so they follow the limit the board now sets. The board raised it to 5% to support an approved strategy, so the analyst drafts thresholds, with an amber level below 5%, for the risk owner to agree. Keeping the 2% red level is the runner-up: it feels cautious, but red would flag results the board has accepted, and staff soon learn to ignore it.

wrong_explanations.A: Failures at 3% sit inside the 5% tolerance, so there is no breach; reporting one misstates the risk position to the owner.
wrong_explanations.B: An early warning belongs below the new 5% limit, set on purpose; red at the old limit flags accepted results and teaches staff to ignore red.
wrong_explanations.C: The board accepted up to 5% to pursue its strategy; forcing failures back under the old limit overrides that decision and slows the releases it approved.

tips: Eliminate: C holds failures to a limit the board has replaced, and A reports results inside the new tolerance as breaches.
Final two: D beats B because thresholds track the tolerance in force; an early-warning level is set on purpose below 5%, not left at the old limit.
Exam cue: when leaders move a tolerance, up or down, re-align the KRI thresholds with the risk owner; old thresholds signal a limit that no longer applies.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. Overrides of an AI tool after a sign-off rule
questions.question: Once a title insurer required manager sign-off to override its AI title-search tool, but none to accept it, overrides fell from 9% to 1% and missed defects rose. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Replace the override approval with sampled review of all findings
options.B: Have the process owner set a minimum override rate per examiner
options.C: Have the model owner tune the tool to catch the missed defects
options.D: Ask the process owner to brief examiners on challenging acceptances

questions.key_concept: Human oversight of AI works only if challenging the tool is as easy as agreeing with it; extra friction on overrides teaches staff to agree.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the new rule made easier and what it made harder.
questions.correct_explanation: Overrides fell after the sign-off rule, not after any change to the tool: challenging the AI now costs examiners effort and scrutiny while agreeing costs nothing, so they agree. Replacing the sign-off with sampled review of all findings removes that pull and still checks quality. Tuning the tool is the runner-up: fewer misses would help, but examiners would keep passing whatever errors the model still makes.

wrong_explanations.B: An override quota pushes examiners to override for the number, not on the merits, swapping one distortion for another.
wrong_explanations.C: Tuning helps the tool, but missed defects rose when the sign-off rule began; examiners would still pass the errors any model makes.
wrong_explanations.D: A briefing leaves the sign-off rule in place, so challenging the tool still costs examiners more than agreeing with it.

tips: Eliminate: B sets an override quota that rewards the count over judgment, and D briefs examiners while keeping the rule that discourages overrides.
Final two: A beats C because misses rose when the rule made challenge costly; removing that pull fixes the cause, while tuning leaves examiners passing future errors.
Exam cue: when behavior shifts right after a rule or incentive changes, fix the rule; training and tooling leave the pull in place.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. Policy issued under the CIO's signature
questions.question: A fund administrator's CIO issued an enterprise data-handling policy under their own signature, and two business heads say it does not bind their units. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Log the two units as exceptions to the policy
options.B: Enforce the policy through IT's technical controls
options.C: Have each unit's process owner adopt it for their unit
options.D: Have the policy's owner seek senior management approval

questions.key_concept: An enterprise policy states management's intent, so senior management approves it; a policy one executive issues alone lacks authority over other units.
questions.pre_read: Recall who approves each layer of the policy hierarchy.
questions.correct_explanation: A policy states management's overall intent and binds the enterprise once senior management approves it. The CIO can draft and own a data-handling policy but cannot impose it on other units alone, so the owner takes it to senior management for approval. Having each unit adopt it is the runner-up: it wins local buy-in, but units could decline or vary it, leaving several rules where the enterprise needs one approved intent.

wrong_explanations.A: Exceptions are owned, time-limited departures from an approved policy; this one lacks approval, and refusing it wholesale is not an exception.
wrong_explanations.B: Technical enforcement without approval imposes IT's rule on the business; controls should carry out a policy that leaders have approved.
wrong_explanations.C: Unit-by-unit adoption lets each head decline or vary the policy, leaving several rules where the enterprise needs one approved intent.

tips: Eliminate: A treats refusal of an unapproved policy as exceptions, and B uses IT controls to enforce a rule that has no enterprise authority.
Final two: D beats C because enterprise policy takes its authority from senior management approval; unit-by-unit adoption splits one intent into several rules.
Exam cue: enterprise-wide policy is approved by senior management; IT may draft and own it, but cannot make it binding on the business alone.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). IT treatment order and enterprise priorities
questions.question: A mortgage servicer's executive committee ranks escrow payment errors its top enterprise risk, but IT funds treatments by its own ratings, placing the escrow system 14th of 30. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Have the escrow system's owner fund its treatments first
options.B: Have IT's system owners re-rank their risks with fresh tests
options.C: Rank IT treatments by the enterprise risks they reduce
options.D: Ask the enterprise risk's owner to rate it on IT's scale

questions.key_concept: IT risk treatments are prioritized by their effect on enterprise risks and objectives, so local spending follows enterprise priorities.
questions.pre_read: Look for why one risk ranks so differently at two levels.
questions.correct_explanation: In ERM, IT risk matters through its effect on enterprise objectives, and enterprise priorities flow down to guide local spending. IT ranks the escrow system 14th because its own scale misses the enterprise impact, so any of its 30 treatments may be funded in the wrong order. Funding the escrow treatments first is the runner-up: it closes today's gap, but the other 29 treatments stay ranked on IT's own scale.

wrong_explanations.A: This fixes the one visible mismatch, but IT would still fund its other treatments on a scale that misses enterprise impact.
wrong_explanations.B: Fresh tests update the ratings, but on the same IT-only scale, so the ranking would still miss the enterprise impact.
wrong_explanations.D: This moves the enterprise view onto a local scale, the wrong way round; local ratings should map up to enterprise priorities.

tips: Eliminate: B refreshes ratings on the same IT-only scale, and D pulls an enterprise risk down onto IT's local scale.
Final two: C beats A because the ranking method causes the mismatch; funding one system first fixes today's case and leaves 29 treatments in IT's order.
Exam cue: when local priorities clash with enterprise ones, fix how local risks are ranked against enterprise objectives, not just the one case that surfaced.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. Unlimited liability in a renewal
questions.question: A debt collector's bank client wants renewal terms making the collector liable without limit for any breach of the bank's debtor data, signed this week. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Have the account's owner seek a liability cap before signing
options.B: Estimate the exposure the term adds for the account's owner
options.C: Ask the account's owner to buy cyber cover for the new liability
options.D: Advise declining the renewal as beyond risk capacity

questions.key_concept: A new contract term is a source of risk: estimate the exposure it adds before anyone negotiates, insures or declines.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the owner needs to know before choosing any response.
questions.correct_explanation: Contract terms are a source of risk, and unlimited liability for the bank's debtor data could exceed what the collector can absorb. Before anyone negotiates, insures or declines, the analyst estimates the exposure the term adds, so the account's owner decides with figures. Seeking a liability cap is the runner-up: it may well be the right response, but without the exposure the owner cannot judge what cap would be acceptable.

wrong_explanations.A: A cap may be the right response, but without the exposure figure the owner cannot judge what cap is acceptable or whether to sign.
wrong_explanations.C: Insurance is chosen before the exposure is known, and cyber cover can exclude liability a firm takes on by contract.
wrong_explanations.D: Whether the term exceeds capacity is unknown until the exposure is estimated; declining now gives up the client before the facts are in.

tips: Eliminate: C buys insurance before the exposure is sized, and D declares the term beyond capacity before anyone has estimated it.
Final two: B beats A because the owner needs the exposure figure to judge any cap; negotiating first means bargaining without knowing what is at stake.
Exam cue: a new contract term, law or obligation is a risk source; estimate what it adds before choosing to negotiate, transfer or decline.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. Request to write the response to an audit finding
questions.question: Internal audit found a glassworks' furnace-control backups had never been restore-tested; the plant director asks the risk team to write management's response and action plan. What is the risk analyst's BEST advice?

options.A: Help the plant director draft the response and action plan
options.B: Write the response and action plan for the plant director to sign
options.C: Ask internal audit, as the finding's owner, to set the plan
options.D: Make the risk team the owner of the backup restore tests

questions.key_concept: Management owns its response to an audit finding; the second line helps shape it but does not write management's commitments.
questions.pre_read: Sort the options by which line would end up doing the work.
questions.correct_explanation: A management response commits the first line to actions, owners and dates, so the plant director must own it. The risk team can advise on the risk and help shape a realistic plan, keeping its role of challenging progress later. Writing the response for the director to sign is the runner-up: it is quick, but the second line would author the first line's commitments and then monitor a plan it wrote.

wrong_explanations.B: Signing a plan someone else wrote weakens the director's ownership, and the risk team would later challenge commitments it drafted itself.
wrong_explanations.C: Internal audit reports findings and later checks the fix; setting management's plan would compromise its independence when it follows up.
wrong_explanations.D: Running the restore tests would put the second line in charge of a first-line control it must later challenge objectively.

tips: Eliminate: C asks internal audit to design the fix it must later verify, and D gives the second line a first-line control to run.
Final two: A beats B because management owns its response; the risk team helps shape it, but writing it would leave the team monitoring its own plan.
Exam cue: the second line advises, facilitates and challenges; asked to write or own first-line work, it helps the owner do it instead.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Strategy, goals and objectives. Project risk log scope
questions.question: A regional transit authority's $9,000,000 real-time arrivals project aims to lift ridership 8%, yet its risk log covers only schedule and budget. Which addition should the risk analyst recommend as MOST important?

options.A: Risks that rising ridership will overload the arrivals servers
options.B: Penalties the vendor owes for releases that run late
options.C: A business owner for each schedule and budget risk
options.D: Risks that the system will not deliver the ridership gain

questions.key_concept: A project's risk log should include the risk of missing the benefit it was approved for, not only schedule and budget risk.
questions.pre_read: Read the stem for the project's purpose and for what its log already covers.
questions.correct_explanation: The project exists to lift ridership, so the risk that matters most to the authority is that the system goes live on time and on budget yet riders do not come. Risk IT calls this benefit/value enablement risk, a category apart from project delivery. Naming a business owner for each schedule and budget risk is the runner-up: ownership helps, but the log would still say nothing about the goal the money is for.

wrong_explanations.A: Capacity under heavier use is a service delivery risk the team can test; it does not ask whether the system will bring the riders it was funded for.
wrong_explanations.B: Vendor penalties recover part of the cost of delay, so they belong with schedule risk; they add nothing on whether the ridership goal will be met.
wrong_explanations.C: Business owners for delivery risks strengthen accountability, but the log would still miss the largest risk: a finished system that does not lift ridership.

tips: Eliminate: A is a capacity risk for live service and B a contract remedy for delay; neither asks whether the system will bring the riders it was funded for.
Final two: D beats C because risk is judged against the objective the project serves; owners for delivery risks help, but the log would still miss whether ridership rises.
Exam cue: when a project's risk log tracks only time and cost, look for the option that adds the risk of missing the benefit it was approved for.
