questions.subtopic: 1A5 Business processes and resilience. Two directors want the first restore
questions.question: A city hospital trust's continuity plan, owned by its chief operating officer, sets no order for restoring clinical systems; the pharmacy and radiology directors each want theirs first. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Have IT restore first whichever system recovers faster
options.B: Set the two systems' order by patient impact for IT
options.C: Ask the plan's owner to set the order on patient impact
options.D: Have the process owners settle the plan's order themselves

questions.key_concept: When process owners conflict over recovery priority, the owner of the continuity plan who spans both sets the order on business impact.
questions.pre_read: List each role in the stem and what it is accountable for.
questions.correct_explanation: Recovery order is a business decision, and when two process owners each claim first place, it goes to the person accountable for the plan across both: here the chief operating officer, deciding on patient impact. Letting the two directors settle it is the runner-up: process owners do set recovery needs, but two owners already at odds have no shared authority to break the tie.

wrong_explanations.A: Restore speed is a technical measure; the faster system may matter less to patients, and IT would be setting a business priority it does not own.
wrong_explanations.B: Patient impact is the right basis, but the analyst would be making the decision; the analyst can supply the impact analysis for the plan's owner to decide on.
wrong_explanations.D: Process owners set recovery needs, but these two already disagree; leaving it to them risks having no agreed order when an outage starts.

tips: Eliminate: A lets IT set a business priority by a technical measure, and B has the analyst decide the order instead of informing the decision.
Final two: C beats D because the order is a business decision, and when two process owners clash it goes to the owner of the plan that spans both.
Exam cue: when owners at the same level conflict, take the decision to whoever is accountable across both, with the impact facts; don't decide it yourself.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. Board weighing an AI registration system
questions.question: A humanitarian NGO's risk profile shows its beneficiary-data risk just within appetite, and its board is weighing an AI face-matching system to register 200,000 refugees. What should the risk analyst BEST give the board?

options.A: How the system would change that risk's position against appetite
options.B: The system's own risk rating, compared with appetite
options.C: The program owner's estimate of registration time saved
options.D: The data owner's sign-off on sharing records with the vendor

questions.key_concept: A board weighing a new initiative needs its effect on the enterprise risk profile against appetite, not a rating of the initiative alone.
questions.pre_read: Check where the named risk already sits against appetite before judging what the board needs.
questions.correct_explanation: The profile is the board's view of total exposure, and this risk already sits at the edge of appetite. What the board needs is how adding the face-matching system would shift that enterprise position. Rating the system on its own against appetite is the runner-up: it may pass alone, yet its added exposure could push the combined beneficiary-data risk over the line.

wrong_explanations.B: A stand-alone rating can look acceptable while the enterprise's beneficiary-data risk, already near its limit, would cross appetite once the system is added.
wrong_explanations.C: Time saved is a benefit the board will weigh, but a benefit estimate from the program's owner says nothing about how the risk position changes.
wrong_explanations.D: Approval to share records comes later, if the board goes ahead; it is a control step, not the risk information the board's decision needs.

tips: Eliminate: C offers only the program's benefits and D a later control step; neither tells the board how the decision changes its risk position.
Final two: A beats B because the profile shows total exposure; a system rated alone can pass while the combined beneficiary-data risk crosses appetite.
Exam cue: when a board weighs a new initiative, give it the change to the enterprise risk profile against appetite, not a stand-alone rating.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. Most labs hold the same exception
questions.question: A state university's standard requires managed laptops, yet 45 of its 60 research labs hold approved exceptions, each renewed on its own as it expires. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have each lab's risk owner reassess its exception at renewal
options.B: Examine why most labs need an exception to the standard
options.C: Ask the standard's owner to end the labs' exceptions
options.D: Grant permanent exceptions with each lab head as owner

questions.key_concept: Many exceptions to one rule signal that the rule or the process needs review; examine the cause rather than renewing case by case.
questions.pre_read: Compare the number of exceptions with the number of labs the rule covers.
questions.correct_explanation: When three in four labs need an exception, the pattern itself is the finding: the rule may not fit research work, or labs may lack a workable way to comply. Examining that cause lets the standard's owner fix the rule or the process once. Having each owner reassess at renewal is the runner-up: it keeps every exception sound, but treats 45 symptoms and never asks why they recur.

wrong_explanations.A: Fresh analysis at each renewal keeps single exceptions sound, but it handles 45 cases one at a time and never tests whether the rule itself fits.
wrong_explanations.C: Ending exceptions before knowing why labs need them could halt research or push staff to unmanaged workarounds; the cause comes first.
wrong_explanations.D: Exceptions are time-limited by design so the risk is decided again; making them permanent hides the gap from future review.

tips: Eliminate: C ends exceptions before the cause is known, and D makes them permanent, removing the expiry that forces a fresh decision.
Final two: B beats A because many exceptions to one rule point to a cause in the rule or the process; case-by-case renewal treats symptoms.
Exam cue: a high or rising count of exceptions to one rule is a signal to examine the rule or the process, not just to renew each case.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. Wipe planned for a retired database
questions.question: Having migrated current records, a county tax office's IT team plans to wipe the old property-records database next week; records older than 2015 exist nowhere else. What should the risk analyst recommend FIRST?

options.A: Copy the older records to an archive before the wipe
options.B: Wipe the database under IT's media disposal standard
options.C: Ask senior management to decide the database's disposal date
options.D: Ask the records' owner which older records must be kept

questions.key_concept: The asset owner decides retention and disposal; a custodian such as IT carries out that decision, even when decommissioning a system.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the wipe would destroy before judging who should act first.
questions.correct_explanation: Deciding which records to keep, and for how long, belongs to the records' owner, who knows the legal and business needs; IT as custodian carries out the decision. Asking the owner first keeps the only copy of older records from being lost by default. Archiving everything is the runner-up: it avoids loss, but IT would be setting retention itself and could keep taxpayer data longer than it should.

wrong_explanations.A: With a week before the wipe there is time to ask; copying everything has IT set retention, and taxpayer data kept past its period is exposure.
wrong_explanations.B: A disposal standard says how to wipe media safely, not whether the records on it may be destroyed; that decision belongs to their owner.
wrong_explanations.C: Disposal of one database is an asset owner's decision within the retention rules; senior management sets policy, not the fate of single assets.

tips: Eliminate: B treats a wiping method as permission to destroy records, and C sends a single asset's disposal up to senior management.
Final two: D beats A because retention is the owner's call; archiving everything avoids loss, but IT would be deciding retention for the owner.
Exam cue: before a custodian disposes of, copies or shares an asset, check that the owner has decided; custodians carry out owners' decisions.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. Rating request beyond the analyst's expertise
questions.question: A bus manufacturer's engineering director, who owns brake-control software risk, asks the risk analyst to rate that risk; the analyst has never assessed embedded vehicle software. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Rate it from the office software owner's threat list
options.B: Rate it and state the expertise gap in the report
options.C: Have the risk owner add an expert in that software
options.D: Have the risk owner rate it in the analyst's place

questions.key_concept: Practitioners take on only work they can complete competently; when a rating needs expertise they lack, they bring qualified help in.
questions.pre_read: Note what the analyst lacks before judging which option gives a rating others can rely on.
questions.correct_explanation: The Code of Professional Ethics asks members to take on only work they can complete with the necessary skills. The gap here can be closed: an expert in the software, added through the owner, lets the analyst give a rating that can be relied on. Rating it while stating the gap is the runner-up: it is honest, but a caveated rating of a brake-safety risk still rests on judgment the analyst lacks.

wrong_explanations.A: An office-IT threat list misses how safety-critical embedded software fails, so the rating would look complete while resting on the wrong threats.
wrong_explanations.B: Stating the gap is honest, but the owner would still get a weak rating of a safety risk; the Code asks for the skills, not a caveat.
wrong_explanations.D: The owner asked for the analyst's rating; handing it back leaves the skill gap open and gives the owner nothing beyond their own view.

tips: Eliminate: A applies an office-IT threat list to safety-critical embedded software, and D hands the rating back to the owner who asked for it.
Final two: C beats B because the Code asks for the skills the work needs; stating the gap is honest but still leaves a weak rating of a safety risk.
Exam cue: when work needs expertise you lack, close the gap with qualified help before you deliver; a caveat alone does not make the result reliable.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Organizational structure, roles and responsibilities. Integrity check moved to samples
questions.question: At an aerospace parts maker, the IT operations manager owns a machining-program integrity check and wants to run it on samples; the quality director owns the defective-parts risk. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Have the risk owner decide whether sampling is acceptable
options.B: Have the control owner decide whether sampling is acceptable
options.C: Ask the quality director to take over the integrity check
options.D: Ask the IT steering committee to approve the sampling

questions.key_concept: A control change that cuts coverage raises residual risk, so the risk owner decides; the control owner proposes and runs it.
questions.pre_read: Note who owns the check and who owns the risk it protects before you weigh the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Checking only samples means an altered program could reach the machines unseen, so the residual risk of defective parts rises, and that risk belongs to the quality director. The risk owner decides whether that added exposure is acceptable. Having the control owner decide is the runner-up: the IT operations manager runs the check and can propose the change, but would be accepting extra risk on someone else's behalf.

wrong_explanations.B: The control owner answers for the check working and can propose the change, but cutting its coverage raises a risk the quality director owns.
wrong_explanations.C: The quality director owns the risk, not the systems the check runs on; one risk can have several control owners, and the sampling decision does not need a new one.
wrong_explanations.D: A steering committee sets IT priorities; it owns neither the defective-parts risk nor the check, and a committee decision leaves no single accountable person.

tips: Eliminate: C moves the control to a director without authority over its systems, and D gives the decision to a committee that owns neither the risk nor the check.
Final two: A beats B because cutting a control's coverage raises residual risk, which only the risk owner can accept; the control owner proposes and runs the change.
Exam cue: when a control owner wants to weaken a control, ask whose risk rises; that risk owner decides, and the control owner then carries out the change.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). Risk decisions IT learns of late
questions.question: A city government's IT team twice learned of executive committee risk decisions too late, most recently buying servers for a billing system the committee chose not to fund. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Have the billing risk owner tell IT to stop the purchases
options.B: Ask the committee to revisit its decision in light of IT's work
options.C: Keep the server purchases going for the billing system
options.D: Send each committee risk decision to the teams that act on it

questions.key_concept: In ERM, risk information flows up and decisions flow down; senior management's risk decisions must reach the teams that act on them, in time.
questions.pre_read: Note what IT knew when it acted, and how many times this has happened.
questions.correct_explanation: The committee's decision was made; it simply never reached the team spending money on that system, and this is the second time. ERM needs leaders' risk decisions to flow back down to the teams that manage each risk, so a standing route for them fixes the cause. Having the risk owner stop these purchases is the runner-up: it ends this waste, but the next decision would go missing the same way.

wrong_explanations.A: Stopping the purchases is right for this case, but after two misses the gap is the route decisions travel; the next decision would still go astray.
wrong_explanations.B: The committee set an enterprise priority; reopening it because IT spent without knowing lets lower-level spending drive enterprise decisions.
wrong_explanations.C: Funding a system the committee chose not to fund puts money where leaders decided not to, and leaves the communication gap in place.

tips: Eliminate: B lets IT's uninformed spending reopen an enterprise decision, and C keeps funding what the committee chose not to fund.
Final two: D beats A because two misses point to the route decisions travel; stopping these purchases fixes one case and leaves the next decision to go astray.
Exam cue: in ERM, risk information flows up and decisions flow back down; when lower levels keep acting on decisions they never heard, fix the downward route.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Owner's two-hour limit under a six-hour tolerance
questions.question: A rail freight operator's board set a six-hour tolerance for train-dispatch outages; the dispatch director, who owns that risk, wants the dispatch team held to a two-hour limit. What is the risk analyst's BEST response?

options.A: Ask the board to approve the two-hour limit first
options.B: Support the risk owner in applying the two-hour limit
options.C: Keep the dispatch team on the board's six-hour tolerance
options.D: Report the two-hour limit to the board as a conflict

questions.key_concept: Owners may set limits stricter than the board's tolerance within their authority and budget; a looser limit goes back to whoever set the tolerance.
questions.pre_read: Note who set each limit and what each one covers before choosing a response.
questions.correct_explanation: The board's tolerance is the outer limit: no dispatch outage may pass six hours without going to the board. A two-hour limit inside it is stricter, sits within the director's authority as risk owner and flags trouble earlier. Asking the board to approve it is the runner-up: the board must approve any limit looser than its own, but a tighter one leaves everything the board set unchanged.

wrong_explanations.A: Board approval is needed to loosen its tolerance; a stricter limit inside it leaves the board's limit untouched, so seeking approval only adds delay.
wrong_explanations.C: The board's figure is a ceiling, not a required setting; holding the team to it gives up a stricter limit the risk owner is entitled to set.
wrong_explanations.D: A stricter limit inside the tolerance cannot clash with it; reporting it as a conflict misreads how tolerance passes down to the units that apply it.

tips: Eliminate: C treats the board's tolerance as a required setting rather than a ceiling, and D reads a stricter limit as a clash with the board's.
Final two: B beats A because a tighter limit within the risk owner's authority leaves the board's tolerance untouched; a looser one would need the board's approval.
Exam cue: tolerances pass down as ceilings; owners may set stricter limits within their own authority and budget, but anything looser goes back to whoever set the original.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Business processes and resilience. Same responders in two plans
questions.question: A water utility's IT recovery plan and its plant cyberattack plan, each exercised on its own last spring, name the same four engineers as lead responders. What should concern the risk analyst MOST?

options.A: The four engineers being needed by both plans in one attack
options.B: The separate exercises held for each of the two plans
options.C: Two plans kept for incidents that one plan could cover
options.D: Refresher training the four engineers need on both plans

questions.key_concept: Plans that one event can set off together must not count on the same people; check what plans share, not just each plan alone.
questions.pre_read: Picture the plans being used, not just written, before you rank the concerns.
questions.correct_explanation: A cyberattack on a water utility can hit its IT systems and its plant controls together, setting off both plans at once. Each plan then counts on the same four engineers, so one or both would stall when needed most. Exercises run separately are the runner-up: they explain why nobody noticed the clash, but they are a testing gap, not the exposure itself.

wrong_explanations.B: Separate exercises are why the clash went unseen, and a joint exercise would show it, but what should concern the analyst most is the exposure the clash creates.
wrong_explanations.C: IT recovery and plant cyberattack response cover different systems and work; separate plans are normal as long as they are coordinated.
wrong_explanations.D: Both plans were exercised last spring, so nothing points to stale skills; training would not let the same engineers be in two places.

tips: Eliminate: C treats separate plans as the flaw, though different scopes justify them, and D assumes stale skills that recent exercises do not suggest.
Final two: A beats B because the MOST serious concern is the exposure; separate exercises explain why the clash went unseen, but the clash is what fails in an attack.
Exam cue: when one event can set off two plans, check what they share, such as people, sites or suppliers; a shared single point fails both at once.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. AI model ratings passed on unchallenged
questions.question: A mobile carrier's second-line risk team reports the AI model teams' own risk ratings to the board as given, saying it lacks the skills to question them. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Ask internal audit to review the AI ratings in its place
options.B: Borrow a data scientist from the model teams to challenge them
options.C: Add AI expertise to the risk team from outside the model teams
options.D: Have the AI models' risk owner approve the ratings as final

questions.key_concept: Second-line challenge needs the skills to question the first line, from people independent of that work; for AI, expertise outside the model teams.
questions.pre_read: Note which line produced the ratings and which line is meant to question them.
questions.correct_explanation: The model teams are the first line rating their own work, and the second line exists to challenge those ratings before the board relies on them. That takes AI skills from people who did not build the models. Borrowing a data scientist from the model teams is the runner-up: it adds the skills, but that person would be questioning colleagues and then returning to them, so the challenge would not be objective.

wrong_explanations.A: Internal audit gives periodic independent assurance; putting it in the second line's place leaves no ongoing challenge and draws audit into management's work.
wrong_explanations.B: A data scientist on loan brings the skills but not objectivity: they would be challenging colleagues' ratings and then going back to that team.
wrong_explanations.D: The risk owner needs challenged ratings to decide well; approving unchallenged self-ratings as final skips the review the second line owes the board.

tips: Eliminate: A puts internal audit, the third line, in the second line's place, and D has the risk owner approve ratings nobody has challenged.
Final two: C beats B because challenge needs objectivity as well as skill; a data scientist on loan from the model teams would be questioning their own colleagues.
Exam cue: when the second line cannot challenge a technical area, add the skills from outside the team being challenged rather than handing the job to audit or the first line.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. Event that calls for an early refresh
questions.question: Which of the following events MOST clearly calls for the risk analyst to refresh a grocery chain's whole risk profile before its next scheduled update?

options.A: A change of owner for the chain's payment-card risk
options.B: The chain's launch of a home-delivery service
options.C: A risk owner's confirmation that last cycle's ratings hold
options.D: The fine a rival chain received after a card breach

questions.key_concept: Refresh the risk profile when the business or its risks change materially, such as a new service or market, not only on the calendar.
questions.pre_read: For each event, ask whether the chain's exposure itself would change.
questions.correct_explanation: A new home-delivery service brings new processes, systems, suppliers and customer data, so the chain's exposure changes and the profile is out of date until it is refreshed. A rival's fine is the runner-up: it is a useful signal to review the chain's own card-data risk, which can be done on its own, but it does not change what the chain does or the set of risks it runs.

wrong_explanations.A: A new owner takes over the same risk at the same level; the register entry changes, but the chain's exposure does not.
wrong_explanations.C: An owner confirming that ratings still hold is evidence the profile remains accurate, not a reason to rebuild it.
wrong_explanations.D: A peer's fine can prompt a review of the chain's own card-data entry, but it adds no new activity and no change across the whole profile.

tips: Eliminate: A changes who manages a risk, not its size, and C confirms the current ratings; neither changes the chain's exposure.
Final two: B beats D because a new service changes what the chain does and the risks it runs; a rival's fine is a signal for one existing risk.
Exam cue: refresh the profile off-cycle when the business itself changes, such as an acquisition, new market or new service; outside events prompt a review of the affected risk.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. IT's view that a new law does not apply
questions.question: A state university's IT director has concluded that a new state cybersecurity law for public agencies does not apply to the university. What should the risk analyst recommend FIRST?

options.A: Assess the university's gaps against the law's requirements
options.B: Record the law as out of scope in the obligations register
options.C: Have each risk owner judge whether the law touches their area
options.D: Ask legal counsel to confirm whether the law applies

questions.key_concept: Whether a law applies is a legal judgment: confirm it with counsel before scoping gaps or recording the law as out of scope.
questions.pre_read: Note what has been decided about the law so far, and by whom.
questions.correct_explanation: Whether a law covers the university is a legal judgment, and an IT director's view is not a sound basis for scoping obligations. Counsel's answer decides whether the law becomes a compliance obligation with an owner and a gap assessment. Assessing gaps is the runner-up: it is the right next step if the law applies, but done first it may waste effort or rest on a misread scope.

wrong_explanations.A: A gap assessment follows once the law is confirmed to apply; started now, it may measure the university against a law that does not cover it.
wrong_explanations.B: Recording the law as out of scope turns an unverified IT opinion into the register's position, so the obligation could be missed with no one owning it.
wrong_explanations.C: Risk owners judge impacts in their own areas, not what a law means; separate readings could also leave the university with conflicting positions.

tips: Eliminate: B records an unverified IT opinion as the university's position, and C has each risk owner interpret the law, which risks conflicting readings.
Final two: D beats A because applicability comes first and is a legal call; a gap assessment is the next step once counsel confirms the law applies.
Exam cue: before scoping or dismissing a new law, confirm through legal counsel that it applies; then treat it as an obligation with an owner.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Strategy, goals and objectives. AI offer engine after a sales rise
questions.question: A regional savings bank aims to keep customers for life; its AI offer engine, judged by products sold, lifted sales 25% while complaints about unsuitable offers doubled. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Retrain the engine to weigh complaints alongside sales
options.B: Report the 25% sales rise as meeting the engine's objective
options.C: Rate the engine's risk to the bank's retention objective
options.D: Switch the engine off until its owner reviews it

questions.key_concept: An AI tool can meet its own measure while harming the objective it serves; rate its risk against that objective, not its own metric.
questions.pre_read: Note what the engine is measured on and what the bank's strategy is for.
questions.correct_explanation: The engine is doing what it is measured on, selling more, while the complaints suggest it works against the bank's aim of keeping customers for life. The analyst first rates that risk against the retention objective, so the engine's owner can weigh it beside the sales gain. Retraining is the runner-up: it may become the chosen treatment, but done now it skips both the analysis and the owner's decision.

wrong_explanations.A: Retraining is a treatment; chosen before the risk to retention is rated, it guesses at the fix and takes the decision away from the engine's owner.
wrong_explanations.B: Sales are the engine's own measure, not the bank's objective; reporting the rise as success hides the harm the complaints point to.
wrong_explanations.D: Switching off a tool that lifted sales, before any analysis, is a response the owner decides once the risk is rated, not a first step.

tips: Eliminate: B treats the engine's own sales measure as the bank's objective, and D switches the engine off before anyone has rated the risk or the owner has decided.
Final two: C beats A because the risk to the retention objective is rated first; retraining is a treatment the owner may choose once that rating is known.
Exam cue: when an AI tool hits its own metric while the business objective suffers, rate the risk against the objective it serves before changing the tool.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. Time for some of the inventory
questions.question: A seed company's risk analyst has time to assess 150 of 2,400 inventoried assets; the inventory records each asset's BIA criticality, open vulnerabilities and replacement cost. What is the analyst's BEST approach?

options.A: Rely on the BIA's impact ratings to choose the 150
options.B: Start with the 150 with the most open vulnerabilities
options.C: Rate the assets by what each would cost to replace
options.D: Choose a random sample of 150 from the inventory

questions.key_concept: With limited time, assess first the assets the business depends on most, judged by impact such as BIA criticality, not flaw counts or price.
questions.pre_read: Before ranking, ask what each option measures: impact, likelihood or something else.
questions.correct_explanation: With time for only some assets, the analyst assesses first those whose loss would most harm the business, and the inventory already holds that view: each asset's criticality, as rated in the business impact analysis. Open vulnerabilities are the runner-up: they raise likelihood, but a flaw-heavy asset that supports nothing critical can matter less than a well-patched one behind a critical process.

wrong_explanations.B: Open flaws raise likelihood, but ranking by them alone skips impact, so assets supporting nothing critical could be assessed before vital ones.
wrong_explanations.C: Replacement cost is a price, not business impact; a cheap server can support the company's most critical process and still rank last.
wrong_explanations.D: A random sample suits testing a population, not choosing where risk is greatest; it spreads scarce effort over assets that matter little.

tips: Eliminate: C values assets by price rather than business impact, and D samples at random, which suits audit testing, not choosing where risk work counts most.
Final two: A beats B because effort goes first to what the business most depends on; vulnerability counts speak to likelihood, not to what a loss would cost.
Exam cue: when time limits a risk assessment, start from business impact, such as the BIA's criticality and sensitivity ratings; flaw counts and price come in later, inside the analysis.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. Shifts cut after a report
questions.question: Two weeks after a hygienist reported shared logins on a dental clinic chain's X-ray software, the clinic manager cut the hygienist's shifts, and three colleagues withdrew similar reports. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Hold a staff briefing on the hotline's anonymous route
options.B: Assess the shared-login risk with the X-ray software's owner
options.C: Ask the clinic manager to restore the hygienist's shifts
options.D: Ask the speak-up policy's owner to look into the shift cut

questions.key_concept: Apparent retaliation silences other reporters, so it goes first to whoever owns reporter protection; the reported risk is still assessed, not dropped.
questions.pre_read: Separate what was reported from what has happened since, then weigh each option against both.
questions.correct_explanation: Three withdrawn reports show the shift cut is already silencing staff, so the first step is to take it to the owner of the speak-up policy, who can investigate and protect reporters. Assessing the shared-login risk is the runner-up: it must happen, but with reports withdrawn the analyst would rate it on a partial picture, and other concerns would keep going unreported.

wrong_explanations.A: Anonymity helps people report, but a briefing does nothing about a reporter whose shifts were cut; staff have seen what happens to named reporters.
wrong_explanations.B: The login risk needs rating, but done first it misses the withdrawn reports and leaves the cause of the silence in place.
wrong_explanations.C: The clinic manager made the cut under question; asking them to reverse it skips any investigation and leaves reporters unprotected.

tips: Eliminate: A only reminds staff of a channel they have stopped trusting, and C asks the manager who made the cut to undo it, with no investigation or protection.
Final two: D beats B because the apparent retaliation is silencing reports now; the login risk is rated once reporters are protected and withdrawn concerns can return.
Exam cue: when someone who spoke up appears to be punished, take it first to whoever protects reporters; risk reporting depends on people still speaking up.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. Procedure rewritten for a new tool
questions.question: Which of the following should the risk analyst name as the MOST appropriate approver of a cement maker's access-request procedure, rewritten for a new ticketing tool and still meeting every requirement of its access standard?

options.A: The owner of the access standard the procedure meets
options.B: Senior management, which approved the access policy
options.C: The manager whose team carries out the procedure
options.D: The risk analyst who reviewed the rewritten steps

questions.key_concept: A procedure belongs to the team that performs it; a rewrite that still meets the standard is approved there, not by the standard's owner.
questions.pre_read: Work out which layer of the policy hierarchy the change actually touches.
questions.correct_explanation: A procedure sets out the steps for meeting a standard and belongs to the team that performs it, so a rewrite that still meets every requirement is approved by that team's manager. The standard's owner is the runner-up: that owner decides changes to the standard itself, and would be asked only if the new steps relaxed a requirement, which these do not.

wrong_explanations.A: The standard's owner decides changes to the standard; a procedure that still meets every requirement leaves the standard untouched, so that approval is not needed.
wrong_explanations.B: Senior management approves policies, which state intent; sending procedure rewrites up to it slows routine changes and blurs who owns what.
wrong_explanations.D: The analyst can check the steps against the standard and advise, but approving management's procedures is not the practitioner's decision.

tips: Eliminate: B sends a routine procedure up to senior management, which approves policy, and D has the risk analyst approve a management document instead of advising on it.
Final two: C beats A because the rewrite leaves every requirement of the standard intact; the standard's owner decides only changes that would relax the standard.
Exam cue: approval sits at the layer a change touches: procedures with the team that runs them, standards with their owner, policy with senior management.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Business processes and resilience. Where the recovery runbooks are kept
questions.question: A pension fund keeps its cyberattack recovery runbooks and responder call list only on a file server inside the network the plan restores. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Rely on restoring the file server first in the plan
options.B: Hold copies of the plan that responders can reach offline
options.C: Have the plan owner re-approve the runbooks and the call list
options.D: Encrypt the runbooks and call list on the file server

questions.key_concept: A recovery plan must be reachable during the event it covers, so copies are held off the systems it restores.
questions.pre_read: Imagine the attack has happened, then test each option against that moment.
questions.correct_explanation: A recovery plan has to be usable during the event it covers, and an attack on this network would lock responders out of their runbooks and call list just when they need them. Copies held offline, with responders and at the alternate site, keep the plan available. Restoring the file server first is the runner-up: it still needs responders who can reach each other and know the steps, which is what they would lack.

wrong_explanations.A: Restoring the server first still depends on responders who can find the steps and reach each other, which the attack has already taken away.
wrong_explanations.C: Re-approval confirms the content but leaves the only copies on the network the attack would disable.
wrong_explanations.D: Encryption protects the plan's confidentiality; the gap here is availability, and encrypted copies on a disabled server are still out of reach.

tips: Eliminate: C re-approves the content without moving it, and D adds confidentiality when the gap is availability; both leave the only copies on the network that fails.
Final two: B beats A because responders need the plan to start recovery; putting the server first in the restore order assumes they can follow steps they cannot reach.
Exam cue: ask whether a plan survives the event it covers: copies, contacts and tools must stay reachable without the systems being recovered.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.6 (Plan Maintenance: copies of the plan are given to recovery personnel and a copy is stored at the alternate site and with the backup media, so the plan is available if local copies cannot be accessed); COBIT 2019 DSS04 (Managed Continuity)

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). Request for wider impact bands
questions.question: Citing 6% funding growth, a public broadcaster's director wants wider impact bands; the framework re-bases them at scheduled reviews, next in five months, or if funding moves 20%. What is the risk analyst's BEST advice?

options.A: Re-base the bands now on the broadcaster's current funding
options.B: Have the director approve wider bands as a risk owner
options.C: Grant the director's unit wider bands until the scheduled review
options.D: Re-base the bands at the next scheduled framework review

questions.key_concept: Rating scales change on the framework's own schedule or triggers; a change that meets no trigger waits for the next scheduled review.
questions.pre_read: Check the framework's own rule for changing bands before weighing the request.
questions.correct_explanation: The framework already says when bands change: at scheduled reviews, or sooner if funding moves 20%. A 6% rise trips neither, so the request waits for the review five months away, where current funding is weighed. Re-basing now is the runner-up: it would shift ratings mid-cycle for a change the approved trigger treats as minor, breaking comparison with the last period's profile.

wrong_explanations.A: Bands do follow the broadcaster's size, but a 6% rise is inside the approved trigger; re-basing now shifts ratings and breaks period-to-period comparison for little gain.
wrong_explanations.B: Impact bands belong to the enterprise framework senior management approved; a director, as one risk owner, cannot widen them.
wrong_explanations.C: Bands for one unit break the common scale, even until the scheduled review, so its risks could no longer be compared or rolled up; the analyst cannot grant them either.

tips: Eliminate: B lets one risk owner change the enterprise's scale, and C gives one unit its own bands, which breaks the common scale every unit's ratings rely on.
Final two: D beats A because the 6% rise is inside the approved 20% trigger; re-basing off-cycle would shift ratings without a material change, and the review is close.
Exam cue: when a framework names its own triggers, a change inside them waits for the scheduled review; act early only when a trigger is met.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Strategy, goals and objectives. Two directors split on a design
questions.question: A mining company's production and safety directors disagree on whether haul-truck sensor data should run through a cloud service, and the risk analyst rated both designs within appetite. Who should MOST appropriately decide?

options.A: The safety director, owner of haul-truck collision risk
options.B: The chief operating officer, owner of mining operations
options.C: The production director, owner of the throughput objective
options.D: The risk committee, owner of the enterprise risk profile

questions.key_concept: When two owners' objectives conflict and both options fit appetite, the executive over both decides; neither owner overrules the other.
questions.pre_read: Note whose objectives the choice touches and whether either design breaches a limit.
questions.correct_explanation: Both designs fit appetite, so no limit forces the answer; the choice trades the production director's objective against the safety director's. Neither peer can overrule the other, so the chief operating officer, who owns the operations both objectives serve, weighs the two using the analyst's ratings. The safety director is the runner-up: as owner of collision risk they decide responses to that risk, but not a trade-off with a peer's objective inside appetite.

wrong_explanations.A: Owning collision risk lets the safety director decide responses to it, but with both designs inside appetite, the choice weighs two directors' objectives, which neither can settle alone.
wrong_explanations.C: As one side of the dispute, the production director would settle a trade-off against a peer's objective in their own favor.
wrong_explanations.D: A risk committee oversees and challenges ratings; it owns neither the profile's risks nor a trade-off between two business objectives that sits inside appetite.

tips: Eliminate: C lets one side of the dispute decide against a peer's objective, and D makes a committee an owner; committees oversee and challenge but own neither risks nor business trade-offs.

Final two: B beats A because both designs are within appetite, so this is a choice between two objectives; the executive over both weighs them, while the safety director decides only responses to collision risk.
Exam cue: when two owners' objectives clash and every option fits appetite, the decision goes to the executive over both; the analyst supplies each option's risk.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Organizational structure, roles and responsibilities. Board asks to approve acceptances
questions.question: A dairy cooperative's board asks to approve every IT risk acceptance before it takes effect, including acceptances of risks within appetite. What is the risk practitioner's BEST advice?

options.A: Leave acceptances within appetite to their risk owners
options.B: Route acceptances to the board before they take effect
options.C: Delegate acceptance approvals to the board's risk committee
options.D: Delegate acceptances within appetite to the risk practitioner

questions.key_concept: The board sets appetite and oversees; risk owners accept risks within it, and the board oversees those decisions through reporting.
questions.pre_read: Sort the decisions in the stem by the level that should make each one.
questions.correct_explanation: The board sets appetite and oversees how it is applied; within appetite, accepting a risk is the risk owner's decision, and the board oversees them through regular risk reporting. The board's risk committee is the runner-up: it seems a lighter compromise, but approving acceptances inside appetite still moves owners' decisions up to board level and blurs who is accountable for each risk.

wrong_explanations.B: This is the board's request as made: approving each acceptance turns oversight into management and leaves owners waiting on the board for decisions within their authority.
wrong_explanations.C: A board committee acts for the board; approving acceptances inside appetite still pulls owners' decisions up and blurs accountability, which regular reporting avoids.
wrong_explanations.D: The practitioner analyzes, recommends and reports; accepting risk belongs to the business manager accountable for the affected objective, not to the risk function.

tips: Eliminate: B gives the board management's decisions, and D hands acceptance to the practitioner, who analyzes and reports risk but never accepts it.

Final two: A beats C because the acceptances in question sit within appetite, which risk owners decide; a board committee approving them still pulls management decisions up and blurs who is accountable.
Exam cue: the board sets appetite and oversees through reporting; inside appetite and their authority, risk owners accept, and anything beyond goes up.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. AI-use register limited to generative tools
questions.question: A translation agency's AI-use register covers only generative AI tools, so it omits older machine-learning systems, such as the model that assigns jobs to freelance translators. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Rate the job-assignment model's risk with its business owner
options.B: List the model under IT in the AI-use register
options.C: Ask the register's owner to widen the AI definition
options.D: Record the job-assignment model as standard software

questions.key_concept: An AI-use register must cover every kind of AI the business relies on; a narrow scope hides systems, so fix the scope first.
questions.pre_read: Ask why the model is missing, and what else might be missing for the same reason.
questions.correct_explanation: The register's scope, not one oversight, is why the job-assignment model is missing, and other older machine-learning systems are out of view too. Widening what counts as AI, through the register's owner, brings them all in for owners and risk ratings. Rating the job-assignment model with its owner is the runner-up: it is needed, but it closes one gap while the scope keeps hiding the rest.

wrong_explanations.A: Rating the model with its owner is needed, but it fixes one omission; the register's narrow scope keeps other older machine-learning systems out of view.
wrong_explanations.B: IT may run the model, but a business owner answers for how it assigns jobs; listing it under IT puts a custodian where that owner should be.
wrong_explanations.D: A plain software record lacks what an AI entry holds, such as purpose, training data and version, and leaves the model out of AI risk review.

tips: Eliminate: B records a business model under IT, a custodian, and D files it as plain software without the purpose, data and version details an AI record needs.
Final two: C beats A because the register's scope leaves out every older machine-learning system, not just this one; rating one model closes one gap while the scope keeps hiding the rest.
Exam cue: when an item is missing because of how a list is scoped, fix the scope with the list's owner; rating the found item follows.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. First line withholds incident logs
questions.question: After the risk practitioner explained the request, a wind-farm operator's operations director still refuses to give the second-line risk team turbine-control incident logs, calling them commercially sensitive. What is the practitioner's BEST next step?

options.A: Take the access dispute to senior management for a decision
options.B: Rate the risk from the incident summaries the director provides
options.C: Escalate the director's refusal to the board's risk committee
options.D: Record the logs in the register as withheld by their owner

questions.key_concept: Second-line challenge needs first-line evidence; when access is refused, senior management, accountable for both lines, settles it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the second line needs to challenge a rating, and who answers for both lines.
questions.correct_explanation: The second line challenges first-line ratings on evidence, and the director's refusal stands after explanation. Senior management, accountable for both the first and second lines, can secure the access, with the team bound to keep the logs confidential. Rating from the director's summaries is the runner-up: it keeps work moving, but the team would be checking the first line's account against itself, which is no challenge at all.

wrong_explanations.B: Summaries chosen by the director show only what the first line wants seen; the second line cannot challenge ratings it cannot test against the logs.
wrong_explanations.C: The board oversees, but senior management answers for both lines and can settle an access dispute; going to the board first skips that level.
wrong_explanations.D: Recording the refusal treats the director as able to block oversight; the second line's access is a governance matter, not the first line's choice.

tips: Eliminate: C skips the senior managers who answer for both lines and can settle the dispute, and D accepts the refusal as the owner's call, leaving the second line unable to challenge.

Final two: A beats B because ratings checked only against the director's own summaries are not challenged; the second line needs the underlying logs, and senior management, accountable for both lines, can grant access.
Exam cue: when the first line withholds what the second line needs to challenge, take it to the management level over both lines; never settle for the first line's own account.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. Division sold, systems still run for the buyer
questions.question: An elevator maintenance company sold its building-security division but will run the division's alarm-monitoring systems for the buyer for a year under contract. How should the risk analyst FIRST update the risk profile?

options.A: Remove the division's risks from the profile once the buyer takes over
options.B: Keep the division's risks with their owners while services continue
options.C: Name the CIO as owner of the division's risks
options.D: Rate the risks the company takes on by serving the buyer

questions.key_concept: A sale changes the profile both ways: the sold unit's risks leave, while services still run for the buyer bring new risks to rate.
questions.pre_read: List what the sale took away and what the company still does, then match the profile to that.
questions.correct_explanation: The division's objectives now belong to the buyer, but the company still runs its alarm-monitoring systems, now as a service provider holding the buyer's data with duties to the buyer. Those new risks are rated first; what to drop or keep follows. Keeping the old risks is the runner-up: the systems still run on the company's estate, but the old ratings measure harm to a business it no longer owns, not its new exposure.

wrong_explanations.A: The division's own risks do leave with the sale, but the company still runs its systems for the buyer; removing them alone shows that exposure as gone.
wrong_explanations.B: The systems still run on the company's estate, but the old ratings measure harm to a business it no longer owns, not its risks in serving the buyer.
wrong_explanations.C: The division's own risks now threaten the buyer's objectives, not the company's; naming any owner for them leaves the new service risks unrated.

tips: Eliminate: A treats the exposure as gone while the company still runs the systems, and C assigns an owner to risks that now threaten the buyer's objectives, while the new service risks stay unrated.
Final two: D beats B because the sale changed whose objectives the old risks threaten; the company's exposure is now serving the buyer, which the old ratings never measured.
Exam cue: after any change in the business, ask which risks left and which arrived; rate the new exposure first, then retire what left.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Basis for risk capacity
questions.question: Which of the following should the risk practitioner use as the BEST basis when helping a waste-management firm's board judge its risk capacity?

options.A: The payout limits on the firm's current insurance policies
options.B: The firm's capital, credit lines and permit conditions
options.C: The largest IT-related loss the firm has suffered
options.D: The loss levels its risk owners have already accepted

questions.key_concept: Risk capacity is the loss the enterprise could bear and survive, set by its own financial resources and binding constraints such as permits.
questions.pre_read: Recall what capacity measures, then pick the input that measures the same thing.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk capacity is the most loss the firm could absorb and still survive, so it rests on what holds the firm up: its capital, its access to credit and the permits it must keep to operate. Insurance limits are the runner-up: cover adds to what the firm can absorb, but only for insured events and up to each policy's limit, so it cannot be the whole basis.

wrong_explanations.A: Insurance adds to what the firm can absorb, but only for covered events and up to each limit; capacity rests on the firm's own resources.
wrong_explanations.C: The worst loss so far is history; capacity asks how much the firm could lose and survive, which a past loss neither sets nor caps.
wrong_explanations.D: Levels owners accepted are decisions made within appetite, itself set inside capacity; using them as capacity's basis turns the outer limit into a record of past choices.

tips: Eliminate: C takes the worst loss so far, which is history, not a survival limit, and D uses owners' accepted levels, which are choices made within appetite, itself set inside capacity.
Final two: B beats A because capacity rests on the firm's own resources and binding limits; insurance helps only for covered events, up to its limits, so it is one input at most.
Exam cue: capacity asks what the enterprise could lose and still survive; look to its finances and binding constraints, not appetite, history or one transfer tool.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. Undefined term in a reporting rule
questions.question: A new rule makes a law firm report significant cyber incidents to its regulator, but the incident procedure never defines significant, so handlers judge it differently. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Train incident handlers on the rule's exact wording
options.B: Name the IT director owner of reporting decisions
options.C: Have the obligation's owner set reporting criteria
options.D: Report incidents once client data is confirmed lost

questions.key_concept: A legal duty that leaves a test open needs criteria set by the obligation's owner, so the firm meets it the same way each time.
questions.pre_read: Ask why handlers reach different answers, and who decides how the firm meets the rule.
questions.correct_explanation: Handlers differ because the rule's test was never turned into the firm's own criteria, so whether an incident is reported depends on who handles it. The obligation's owner decides how the firm meets the rule and should set the criteria, which handlers then apply. Training on the rule's wording is the runner-up: it teaches the words, but those words are the part handlers already read differently.

wrong_explanations.A: Handlers already read the same wording and reach different answers; training on it repeats the ambiguity instead of giving them one shared test.
wrong_explanations.B: IT can help classify incidents, but deciding how the firm meets a legal duty belongs to the obligation's business owner, not the IT function.
wrong_explanations.D: A narrow test chosen without the obligation's owner may leave out incidents the rule treats as significant, such as an outage with no data lost.

tips: Eliminate: B gives a legal reporting decision to IT instead of the obligation's owner, and D sets a narrow test without that owner, missing incidents with no data lost.
Final two: C beats A because handlers already read the same wording and still disagree; only criteria set by the obligation's owner give them one test to apply.
Exam cue: when a legal duty leaves a term open and practice varies, the obligation's owner sets the firm's criteria; training and reminders follow, not lead.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Strategy, goals and objectives. Online memorial pages and the privacy appetite
questions.question: A funeral services company's board approved vendor-hosted online memorial pages as a strategy; even with every planned control, the pages' target privacy risk exceeds the board's appetite. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Take the strategy's conflict with the appetite to the board
options.B: Narrow the strategy's scope with the pages' owner to fit appetite
options.C: Reset the board's privacy appetite with the pages' owner
options.D: Make the pages' hosting vendor owner of their privacy risk

questions.key_concept: When planned treatment cannot bring an approved strategy within appetite, the board that set both decides what changes: strategy, appetite or investment.
questions.pre_read: Notice which two decisions now conflict, and who made each of them.
questions.correct_explanation: The board approved both the strategy and the appetite, and the analysis shows they cannot both hold: with every planned control, the pages stay above appetite. The board settles that, by changing the strategy, revisiting the appetite or funding more treatment. Narrowing the scope with the pages' owner is the runner-up: it may fit appetite, but it rewrites a strategy the board approved without the board.

wrong_explanations.B: A smaller scope may fit appetite, but changing an approved strategy is the board's decision; the owner and analyst would be rewriting it without the board.
wrong_explanations.C: The board sets risk appetite; neither the pages' owner nor the analyst can reset it to make a strategy fit.
wrong_explanations.D: A vendor can carry some costs, but accountability for families' data stays with the company; a vendor cannot own the company's risk.

tips: Eliminate: C has the owner and analyst reset an appetite the board set, and D hands the company's accountability for families' data to a vendor.
Final two: A beats B because the conflict is between two board decisions, the strategy and the appetite; trimming the strategy without the board settles it at the wrong level.
Exam cue: when planned treatment cannot bring an approved strategy within appetite, take the conflict to the board that set both rather than trimming either yourself.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. Automation proposals after a failed pilot
questions.question: A brick maker's plant managers reject every automation proposal since an approved kiln-automation pilot failed and cost its two sponsors their jobs; board appetite welcomes moderate efficiency risk. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Rate each rejected automation proposal's risk with its business owner
options.B: Name the CIO owner of automation decisions at the plants
options.C: Train plant managers on the board's appetite statement
options.D: Ask executives to judge failures by the decisions behind them

questions.key_concept: Leaders shape the risk people actually take through what they punish; penalizing well-judged failures makes staff avoid risks the appetite welcomes.
questions.pre_read: Ask what changed the managers' behavior, and who controls that cause.
questions.correct_explanation: The rejections began when an approved pilot's failure cost its sponsors their jobs. Executives shape the tolerance people act on through what they penalize, so managers now avoid risks the board's appetite welcomes. Asking executives to judge failures by the decisions behind them removes that cause. Rating each proposal is the runner-up: it shows a proposal fits appetite, but fear of sanctions, not missing ratings, drives the rejections.

wrong_explanations.A: A rating can show a proposal fits appetite, but managers reject proposals for fear of sanctions after the pilot, and a rating does not remove that fear.
wrong_explanations.B: Plant automation serves production objectives, so its decisions belong to the business; naming IT their owner leaves the managers' fear in place.
wrong_explanations.C: Training explains the written appetite, but managers act on what executives punished after the pilot, which outweighs the statement.

tips: Eliminate: B moves business decisions to IT and leaves the cause untouched, and C trains on a written appetite that the sanctions after the pilot already outweigh.
Final two: D beats A because the rejections come from how executives punished an approved failure; rating each proposal adds analysis but leaves that fear in place.
Exam cue: when people avoid risks the appetite welcomes, look at what leaders punished; culture follows how failure is treated more than the written appetite.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. Cloud ban after an appetite change
questions.question: Which of the following should the risk analyst recommend as BEST when an office cleaning contractor's board raises its technology risk appetite but its IT standard still bans all cloud apps?

options.A: Rate each requested cloud app's risk against the new appetite
options.B: Refer the standard to its owner to match the new appetite
options.C: Lift the standard's ban on cloud apps across the firm
options.D: Publish the new cloud-app rules as an advisory guideline for teams

questions.key_concept: Policies and standards trace back to risk appetite; when the board changes its appetite, owners review the standards it affects and realign them.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the board will now accept with what the standard still requires.
questions.correct_explanation: Standards should keep risk within appetite without being stricter than it requires. The board has raised its appetite, so a ban set under the old one may now block risks the board accepts, and the standard's owner should review and realign it. Rating each requested app is the runner-up: it measures apps against the new appetite, but the mandatory standard still bans them, so even an app that fits cannot be used.

wrong_explanations.A: A rating shows whether an app fits the new appetite, but the mandatory standard still bans every cloud app until its owner changes it.
wrong_explanations.C: A higher appetite is not unlimited; dropping the ban leaves cloud apps with no rules, not with rules set to the new appetite.
wrong_explanations.D: A guideline is advisory, so teams may depart from its cloud rules, and the mandatory standard would still ban the apps it describes.

tips: Eliminate: C drops the control instead of setting it to the new appetite, and D puts needed rules in an advisory guideline while the standard's ban stays.
Final two: B beats A because the mandatory standard still bans every cloud app; rating apps one by one cannot let teams use them until the rule itself is realigned.
Exam cue: when appetite moves, the rules beneath it move too, through their owners; a standard stricter or looser than appetite is the gap to fix.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Business processes and resilience. Tug dispatch on an AI service
questions.question: A harbor tug operator assigns tugs to arriving ships through a vendor's AI scheduling service; its dispatch continuity plan says only to call IT if the service fails. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Have the dispatch process owner decide the manual fallback
options.B: Make the AI service's owner in IT design a fallback for dispatch
options.C: Add a second AI scheduling vendor as a standby
options.D: List the service's restore steps in the IT recovery plan

questions.key_concept: A process relying on an AI service needs a manual fallback its process owner decides; IT and the vendor restore the service.
questions.pre_read: Ask what dispatchers would actually do during an outage, and who should decide it.
questions.correct_explanation: How dispatch carries on without the AI service, such as which ships get tugs first and what delay is acceptable, is a business decision, so the dispatch process owner decides the manual fallback and IT supports it. The service's owner in IT is the runner-up: IT can restore the service and advise, but it does not own the dispatch process or decide what service level the business can accept.

wrong_explanations.B: IT owns restoring the AI service, but how tugs are assigned without it, and at what service level, is the dispatch process owner's decision.
wrong_explanations.C: A second service is a solution picked before the process owner has set what dispatch needs, and dispatchers still have no manual method if both fail.
wrong_explanations.D: The IT recovery plan restores the service; it does not tell dispatchers how to keep assigning tugs while the service is down.

tips: Eliminate: C picks a technical standby before the process owner sets what dispatch needs, and D restores the service but leaves dispatchers with no way to work meanwhile.
Final two: A beats B because a fallback decides how the business runs without the service; that is the process owner's call, while IT restores and supports.
Exam cue: when an AI service a process depends on fails, the process owner decides the fallback and the service level it must keep; IT and vendors deliver the technology.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). One IT entry in the enterprise register
questions.question: A honey cooperative's enterprise register lists one IT risk, 'systems failure', owned by the IT manager, though the systems run member payments and export certificates. Which of the following is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Split it into one scenario for each IT system
options.B: Add the finance manager to it as a joint business owner
options.C: Rate it on the IT department's own impact scale
options.D: Recast it as business scenarios held by the process owners

questions.key_concept: In ERM, IT risk is stated by its effect on business objectives, as scenarios owned by the managers whose processes it threatens.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a leader reading this entry could compare or decide from it.
questions.correct_explanation: One 'systems failure' entry owned by IT hides what the cooperative stands to lose, such as late member payments and blocked exports. Recast as scenarios, each held by the manager whose process and objective it threatens, the risks can be rated on the enterprise scale, compared and decided. Splitting by system is the runner-up: it adds detail, but the entries still describe IT components owned by IT, not the business harm leaders weigh.

wrong_explanations.A: Entries per system add technical detail, but they still describe IT components owned by IT, not the payment and export harm leaders must weigh.
wrong_explanations.B: Accountability for a risk sits with one owner; a joint owner blurs who decides, and the entry still hides which objectives are at risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Enterprise risks are compared on one enterprise scale; an IT-only scale leaves this risk hard to rank against the rest of the register.

tips: Eliminate: B splits accountability between two owners, and C rates an enterprise entry on a scale the rest of the register does not use.
Final two: D beats A because enterprise risk is stated by its effect on business objectives; splitting by system adds detail but keeps the entry technical and IT-owned.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. Site managers' access reviews
questions.question: A quarry operator's site managers want to drop their reviews of who can edit weighbridge records, since the risk team and internal audit each test them yearly. What is the risk analyst's BEST advice?

options.A: Rely on the risk team's and internal audit's tests
options.B: Move the site managers' reviews to the second-line risk team
options.C: Keep the site managers' own reviews of weighbridge access
options.D: Make internal audit the owner of weighbridge access reviews

questions.key_concept: Second- and third-line tests check first-line controls; they do not replace them, so management keeps running its own reviews.
questions.pre_read: Note who performs each activity in the stem and what each one is for.
questions.correct_explanation: The managers' reviews are the control itself, run by first-line management. The risk team and internal audit test whether that control works; if the reviews stopped, their yearly tests would find no control to test and access would go unreviewed between them. Relying on their tests is the runner-up: it looks efficient, but other lines check the first line's controls rather than replace them.

wrong_explanations.A: The other lines test whether the managers' reviews work; with the reviews stopped, their tests would find no control and access would go unreviewed for months.
wrong_explanations.B: Running a first-line control would leave the risk team challenging its own work, and site managers would stop owning access to their records.
wrong_explanations.D: Internal audit gives independent assurance; owning a control it also tests would end that independence.

tips: Eliminate: B has the second line run a first-line control it must challenge, and D makes internal audit own a control it independently assures.
Final two: C beats A because the other lines test the managers' reviews; they check the control, they do not replace it.
Exam cue: second- and third-line testing checks first-line controls and does not stand in for them; the first line keeps running its own.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). AI risks rated by each unit's method
questions.question: An egg producer's farm, grading and sales units rate AI risks by their own methods, so its enterprise report cannot compare or combine them with other risks. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Rate the AI risks by each tool owner's judgment
options.B: Have the three units rate AI risks on the enterprise method
options.C: Create a separate AI rating method for the three units
options.D: Use the AI vendors' own risk scores in the enterprise report

questions.key_concept: AI risks are rated on the enterprise's common method, so they can be ranked and combined with the enterprise's other risks.
questions.pre_read: Note what the enterprise report must be able to do with the AI ratings.
questions.correct_explanation: AI risks are business risks, so they belong on the enterprise's common rating method, with AI-specific scenarios, where they can be ranked and combined with the other risks against appetite. A separate AI rating method is the runner-up: it would let the three units compare AI risks with each other, but AI exposure would still sit on its own scale, apart from the other enterprise risks the report must rank.

wrong_explanations.A: Tool owners' judgments differ by person and unit, so the ratings still could not be compared or combined with the enterprise's other risks.
wrong_explanations.C: A separate AI method lets the units compare AI risks with each other, but not with the other enterprise risks the report must rank and combine.
wrong_explanations.D: Vendors score their tools on their own methods and without the producer's context, so the scores still sit outside the enterprise scale.

tips: Eliminate: A leaves ratings to each tool owner's judgment, and D takes vendors' scores built on their own methods; neither puts AI risks on one scale.
Final two: B beats C because a separate AI method still leaves AI risks unable to sit beside the enterprise's other risks; the enterprise method lets them be ranked and combined.
Exam cue: when AI risks cannot be compared with other risks, rate them on the enterprise's common method; AI-specific factors shape the scenario, not a separate scale.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Organizational structure, roles and responsibilities. Risk reviews that run late
questions.question: A school bus operator's risk analyst finds managers named as risk owners finished 40% of their reviews on time; their role descriptions set no risk duties. Which of the following is the analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Report each late review to the risk committee
options.B: Give the review role to the second-line risk team as owner
options.C: Add risk-owner duties to the managers' role descriptions
options.D: Set longer deadlines for the managers' review duties

questions.key_concept: Risk ownership holds when its duties are written into the owners' roles; escalating each lapse treats the symptom while the cause stays.
questions.pre_read: Ask why the reviews run late before choosing how to respond to them.
questions.correct_explanation: The stem gives the cause of the late reviews: the managers' role descriptions set no risk duties, so the reviews lose out to work their roles do require. Writing risk-owner duties into those descriptions makes ownership part of the job they answer for. Reporting each late review to the committee is the runner-up: escalation chases each slip, but the next round runs late again while the roles say nothing about risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Escalation answers each slip, but the roles still set no risk duties, so the next round of reviews would run late the same way.
wrong_explanations.B: The risk team challenges owners' reviews; running them itself would take ownership away from the managers whose areas carry the risks.
wrong_explanations.D: Longer deadlines raise the on-time figure without making anyone answer for the reviews; the risks would simply be reviewed later.

tips: Eliminate: B moves the owners' reviews to the second line that must challenge them, and D lifts the on-time figure by allowing more time, not by fixing who answers.
Final two: C beats A because the stem shows the cause, no role sets the duty; escalating each late review treats the symptom while the roles stay silent.
Exam cue: when people named in a risk role keep missing its duties, check whether the duties are written into their roles; accountability needs a place in the job itself.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. Class of a system holding mixed data
questions.question: A dry-cleaning chain's booking system, mostly price lists but also saved card details, was classified public by its owner. Which of the following should the risk analyst advise as the BEST basis for its class?

options.A: The most sensitive type of data that the system holds
options.B: The owner's view of sensitivity once card details are protected
options.C: The type of data that fills most of the system
options.D: The owner's view of what the system is mainly used for

questions.key_concept: A system takes the class of the most sensitive data it holds; classification sets the protection data needs and is not judged net of it.
questions.pre_read: List the kinds of data the system holds before weighing how it was classified.
questions.correct_explanation: A system is classified at the level of the most sensitive data it holds, the high water mark, because its access, backup and handling rules cover all its data together. The owner's view of sensitivity once the card details are protected is the runner-up: classification is what decides the protection data needs, so setting it net of that protection is circular, and the card controls would lose the class they rest on.

wrong_explanations.B: Classification decides the protection data needs; setting it net of that protection is circular and drops the requirement the card controls rest on.
wrong_explanations.C: Most records being price lists does not lower the harm of exposing card details; one sensitive data type sets the level for the system.
wrong_explanations.D: The owner decides the class, but by the data's sensitivity under the scheme, not by what the system is mostly used for.

tips: Eliminate: C classifies by volume and D by the system's main use; the class follows the sensitivity of the data held, whatever its share of the records.
Final two: A beats B because a class sets the protection required; rating sensitivity after that protection is in place makes the requirement disappear.
Exam cue: a system holding several kinds of data takes the class of its most sensitive data, the high water mark; the class is judged before controls, not net of them.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. Profile refreshed on the calendar alone
questions.question: A glass recycler updates its risk profile only in December, so its board has not seen a new plant's risks, and saw last year's cloud move months late. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Refresh the profile now with the new plant's risk owners
options.B: Automate the profile's December build from the register
options.C: Report each business change to the board as it occurs
options.D: Set events that trigger a profile update between cycles

questions.key_concept: A profile tied only to the calendar lags business change; set the events that trigger an update between scheduled cycles.
questions.pre_read: Look for what the two gaps in the board's view have in common.
questions.correct_explanation: The new plant's risks and last year's cloud move share one cause: the profile is updated only on the calendar. Setting the events that trigger an update between cycles, such as a new site, a platform move or a major incident, keeps the profile current as the business changes. Refreshing now with the new plant's risk owners is the runner-up: it closes today's gap, but the next change would again wait for December.

wrong_explanations.A: Refreshing now closes this gap, but the profile would again wait for December the next time the business changes.
wrong_explanations.B: Automating the build makes December's profile faster to produce, but it still appears once a year, after the changes it should show.
wrong_explanations.C: The board needs changes in exposure against appetite, not a stream of business changes; the updated profile is what turns change into that view.

tips: Eliminate: B speeds up a profile that still appears once a year, and C sends the board raw business changes rather than an updated profile against appetite.
Final two: D beats A because both gaps share one cause, a profile tied to the calendar; refreshing now fixes this one, while triggers fix the next.
Exam cue: refresh the profile now for one missed business change; when it keeps missing changes because it runs on the calendar alone, set the events that trigger updates between cycles.
