questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Rare scenario with a worst case beyond capacity
questions.question: A spice importer rates ransomware on its lot-traceability system rare and so within appetite, though its worst case, a six-week import halt, would exceed its risk capacity. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Make the IT manager owner of the ransomware scenario
options.B: Escalate the worst case against capacity to senior management
options.C: Add standby capacity at a second site for traceability
options.D: Transfer the worst case to a cyber insurer

questions.key_concept: A rare scenario rated within appetite still goes to leaders when its worst case would exceed the enterprise's risk capacity.
questions.pre_read: Compare the scenario's rating with its worst-case loss and the firm's limits.
questions.correct_explanation: Capacity is the loss the firm could absorb and survive; a worst case beyond it threatens the firm itself, whatever a rare likelihood does to the matrix rating. Leaders who set appetite need to see that and decide how to respond. Adding standby capacity at a second site is the runner-up: it may prove the right response, but choosing it now commits money to one treatment before senior management has weighed the threat to capacity.

wrong_explanations.A: Naming IT as owner moves a business risk away from the managers whose imports would stop, and the threat to capacity stays unreported.
wrong_explanations.C: A standby site may be the right response later, but choosing it now picks a costly treatment before the leaders who set appetite have weighed the worst case.
wrong_explanations.D: Insurance can pay part of the cost, but accountability for the risk stays with the importer, and a policy does not restart imports during a halt.

tips: Eliminate: A gives a business risk to IT, and D treats insurance as moving the risk itself; accountability stays with the importer.
Final two: B beats C because a worst case beyond capacity is for the leaders who set appetite to weigh; the analyst reports it before anyone picks a treatment.
Exam cue: a rating within appetite does not clear a scenario whose worst case exceeds capacity; take that worst case to leaders before a treatment is chosen.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. New version of a voluntary framework
questions.question: Four months before a uniform supplier's yearly review of its voluntary framework, a mostly reworded new version is released; no contract, law, threat or business change requires it. What is the risk analyst's BEST advice?

options.A: Start a gap review of the current controls against the new version
options.B: Add the new version to the obligations register
options.C: Have the framework's owner weigh it at the planned review
options.D: Move the controls to the framework's new version as published

questions.key_concept: A voluntary framework's new version creates no obligation; unless a threat or material change makes it urgent, its owner weighs it at the planned review.
questions.pre_read: Check whether anything in the stem makes the new version binding or urgent.
questions.correct_explanation: A framework followed by choice is a reference, not an obligation, so a mostly reworded new version is no reason to act off-cycle. The yearly review, four months away, is where the framework's owner weighs what the version changes and whether to adopt it. A gap review now is the runner-up: it is the right work, but with no obligation, threat or material change making it urgent, it belongs in the planned review.

wrong_explanations.A: A gap review is the right work, but with no obligation, material change or threat making it urgent, it belongs in the planned review four months away.
wrong_explanations.B: No contract or law requires the framework, so its new version creates no obligation; listing it as one misstates what the firm must meet.
wrong_explanations.D: Moving the controls to the version as published skips tailoring it to the firm's risks and the approval a framework change needs.

tips: Eliminate: B treats a voluntary framework as a legal duty, and D adopts the new version wholesale without tailoring it to the firm's risks.
Final two: C beats A because a mostly reworded version of a voluntary framework creates no obligation or urgency; a gap review is right but belongs in the planned review.

Exam cue: a voluntary framework's new edition is no obligation. A mostly reworded one waits for the scheduled review; a material content change, obligation, threat or business change calls for a gap review now.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Organizational structure, roles and responsibilities. Accountable role in an AI model's RACI chart
questions.question: A building society's RACI chart for its AI mortgage-affordability model makes the data science team that built it accountable for its lending decisions' outcomes. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Make the head of mortgage lending accountable as business owner
options.B: Keep the builders accountable, with the business listed as Consulted
options.C: Make the CIO accountable as owner of the model's platform
options.D: Share accountability between the team and the lending risk owner

questions.key_concept: Accountability for the outcomes of an AI model's decisions sits with the business owner of its use; the team that built it stays responsible.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose objective the model's decisions serve, and who only builds or runs it.
questions.correct_explanation: The model's outputs drive lending decisions, so their outcomes belong to the business manager who answers for mortgage lending; RACI gives each outcome one accountable person with that authority. The data science team stays responsible for building, testing and maintaining the model. Keeping the builders accountable is the runner-up: they know the model best, but knowing how it works gives no authority over the lending objective its decisions serve.

wrong_explanations.B: Builders answer for how the model is built, not for lending outcomes they do not control; listing the business as Consulted leaves accountability in the wrong place.
wrong_explanations.C: A senior technology owner runs the platform, not the lending business; accountability for decision outcomes goes to the manager whose objective the decisions serve.
wrong_explanations.D: With two names sharing it, neither fully answers for the outcome; RACI keeps one accountable person per activity, with others responsible or consulted.

tips: Eliminate: C makes the CIO accountable because they own the platform, not the lending objective, and D splits accountability between two parties; RACI allows one accountable person.
Final two: A beats B because the builders know the model best but do not own lending; the head of mortgage lending answers for the model's decision outcomes, while the builders stay Responsible.
Exam cue: in a RACI for an AI system, Accountable goes to the business owner of the decisions it drives; builders and platform teams are Responsible, however senior.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Strategy, goals and objectives. IT strategy drafted inside IT
questions.question: A reinsurer's IT strategy, written by its CIO alone, puts most spending into a data center refresh, while the enterprise strategy calls for faster online quotes to brokers. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Rate the risks to each IT goal with the goal's owner
options.B: Add security requirements to the data center refresh plan
options.C: Make the CIO the risk owner of the online broker quotes goal
options.D: Have senior management map IT goals to enterprise goals

questions.key_concept: IT goals cascade from enterprise goals; an IT strategy set apart from the business is aligned before the risks to its goals are rated.
questions.pre_read: Check whether the IT goals trace to the enterprise strategy before judging anything else.
questions.correct_explanation: Alignment goals (IT goals) should cascade from enterprise goals, so technology spending serves what the business is trying to achieve. A strategy written inside IT that funds a refresh while the enterprise needs faster broker quotes puts that value at risk. Senior management, with business input, maps IT goals to enterprise goals. Rating the risks to each IT goal is the runner-up: it measures risk to goals that may not serve the enterprise strategy.

wrong_explanations.A: Rating risks to goals that were never tied to the enterprise strategy measures risk to the wrong targets; alignment comes first, then each goal's risks are rated.
wrong_explanations.B: Adding requirements protects a project before anyone has shown it serves an enterprise goal; controls follow the objective, not the other way round.
wrong_explanations.C: Broker quoting is a business objective, so its risk sits with the business manager who owns it, not with the CIO who supplies the technology.

tips: Eliminate: B adds controls before tying the project to an objective, and C makes IT the risk owner of a business goal.
Final two: D beats A because IT goals must first trace to enterprise goals; rating the risks to unaligned goals measures risk to the wrong targets.
Exam cue: when IT sets its strategy apart from the business, align IT goals to enterprise goals first; the risk to each goal is rated once the cascade holds.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. Subcontracted crews and the speak-up line
questions.question: A subcontracted crew at a plumbing contractor saw staff share customers' door codes for weeks but had no way to report it: the speak-up line takes employees only. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Train the contractor's staff on handling customers' door codes
options.B: Open the contractor's speak-up line to subcontracted crews
options.C: Route crews' speak-up concerns through each subcontract's owner
options.D: Require each subcontract's owner to add a reporting clause

questions.key_concept: Speak-up routes must reach everyone placed to see a risk, contractors included, with independence and protection from retaliation.
questions.pre_read: Ask why the people who saw the problem stayed silent, then look for the fix to that.
questions.correct_explanation: The crew saw the problem for weeks and stayed silent because no safe route was open to them. Contractors often see what employees miss, so the speak-up line and its protection should cover them too. Routing concerns through each subcontract's owner is the runner-up: it gives crews a route, but through the manager their work depends on, so the independence and protection that help people speak up are lost.

wrong_explanations.A: Training staff on door codes targets the one practice seen; the crew stayed silent because no route reached them, and training leaves that gap open.
wrong_explanations.C: Concerns would pass through the manager who controls the crews' work, so fear of losing it keeps them quiet; a speak-up route needs independence and protection.
wrong_explanations.D: A clause binds the subcontracting firm to report incidents, not its crew members to raise concerns safely; individuals still have no protected route.

tips: Eliminate: A retrains staff on one practice when the gap was the route to report, and D puts a contract duty on firms rather than giving people a safe route.
Final two: B beats C because a speak-up route works when it is independent and protected; one through the manager who controls crews' work keeps them silent.
Exam cue: when people who saw a risk stayed silent, check whether a safe route reached them; speak-up channels cover contractors and suppliers' staff too.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. A standard branches read differently
questions.question: Which of the following should the risk analyst recommend as BEST when a pest control firm's standard requires 'adequate protection' for customer data on tablets, which its branches read differently?

options.A: Rewrite the standard as measurable requirements its owner approves
options.B: Send branch managers a note explaining adequate protection
options.C: Recast the rule as a guideline for branch process owners
options.D: Log each branch's reading as an exception to the standard

questions.key_concept: A standard turns policy into mandatory, measurable requirements; a vague term is restated by the standard's owner so every unit meets one bar.
questions.pre_read: Ask which layer of the policy hierarchy should hold a requirement every branch must meet.
questions.correct_explanation: Standards exist to make policy measurable and mandatory; 'adequate protection' gives branches no bar to meet and compliance checks no basis to judge. Restating it as measurable requirements, such as encryption and screen locks, approved by the standard's owner, sets one bar for every branch. A note to branch managers is the runner-up: it explains the term, but changes nothing the standard requires, so readings and checks still differ.

wrong_explanations.B: A note explains the term but sits outside the approved standard; it binds no one and gives compliance checks nothing measurable to test.
wrong_explanations.C: A guideline advises rather than requires, so turning a mandatory rule into one weakens it; branches could then depart from it with a sound reason.
wrong_explanations.D: Exceptions record approved departures from a clear requirement; logging each branch's reading as one leaves the rule vague and fills the register with non-departures.

tips: Eliminate: C turns a mandatory rule into advice, and D logs differing readings as exceptions, which record departures from a clear rule, not an unclear one.
Final two: A beats B because the requirement must sit, measurably, in the standard itself; a note explains the term but leaves the rule unchanged.
Exam cue: when units read a rule differently, fix the wording at the layer that sets it; standards hold measurable, mandatory requirements, not notes or guidance.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Business processes and resilience. Restore order and the harvest season
questions.question: An agricultural cooperative's continuity plan restores weekly payroll before grain intake; off-season intake is light, but in the six-week harvest an intake outage halts members' deliveries within hours. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Restore grain intake ahead of payroll year-round
options.B: Rank the processes by their average yearly impact
options.C: Give IT discretion over the restore order during an outage
options.D: Vary the restore order by season with the process owners

questions.key_concept: Recovery priority follows when an outage would hurt most; a process critical only at peak times can move up the restore order then.
questions.pre_read: Notice when each process's outage would do the most harm, not only how much harm.
questions.correct_explanation: Intake's impact changes with the season: light off-season, but able to stop members' deliveries within hours at harvest. A restore order that varies by season, agreed with the process owners who set recovery needs, puts each process first when its outage hurts most. Restoring intake ahead of payroll year-round is the runner-up: it protects the harvest but delays weekly pay for little gain the rest of the year.

wrong_explanations.A: A fixed intake-first order protects the harvest but puts weekly payroll behind a lightly used process for most of the year.
wrong_explanations.B: An average spreads the harvest peak across quiet months, so intake ranks low just when an outage would halt deliveries.
wrong_explanations.C: Restore order is a business priority set with process owners in advance; IT carries it out but does not choose it alone mid-outage.

tips: Eliminate: B averages away the harvest peak, and C hands a business priority to IT in the middle of an outage.
Final two: D beats A because intake's impact depends on the season; its recovery need peaks at harvest, but restoring it first all year delays payroll when intake is light.
Exam cue: when a process's impact peaks at certain times, recovery priority follows that timing, set in the plan with process owners rather than fixed by averages.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.2 (Conduct the Business Impact Analysis: recovery criticality rests on the impact of a system disruption and the downtime the process can tolerate); COBIT 2019 DSS04 (Managed Continuity); ISACA Glossary (business continuity plan)

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. Assets valued by the revenue each earns
questions.question: A jewelry retailer's asset owners value IT assets by the revenue each earns directly, so the diamond-certificate records, which every diamond sale needs, rank last. Which of the following should concern the risk analyst MOST?

options.A: Owners rather than IT set the value of each asset
options.B: The values leave out the cost of reissuing the certificates
options.C: The values leave out sales that depend on the records
options.D: The values are not based on the assets' purchase prices

questions.key_concept: An asset is valued by what the business loses without it, including the sales and processes it enables, not only the revenue it earns itself.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the business could not do if each asset were lost, not only what it earns.
questions.correct_explanation: Valuing assets by the revenue each earns directly misses assets that other revenue depends on. Without the certificate records diamonds cannot be sold, so their loss would stop a major revenue stream, yet the ranking puts them last and risks to them would be underrated. Leaving out reissue cost is the runner-up: it is a real gap, but far smaller than the diamond sales the records make possible.

wrong_explanations.A: Owners are the right people to value their assets; the concern is the basis they used for the values, not who set them.
wrong_explanations.B: Reissue cost belongs in the value, but it is small beside the diamond sales that stop while the records are unavailable.
wrong_explanations.D: Purchase price is a weaker basis than business impact; it would rank the records low as well, since they cost little to create.

tips: Eliminate: A questions owners setting the values, which is their role, and D prefers purchase price, a weaker basis than business impact.
Final two: C beats B because the sales that stop without the records far outweigh the cost of reissuing them; both are gaps, one much larger.
Exam cue: value an asset by what the business loses without it, including the processes and sales it enables, not only the revenue it earns itself.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. Request to close an audit finding
questions.question: A paper mill's plant director reports that internal audit's finding on shared control-system passwords is fixed and asks the risk analyst to close it. What is the analyst's BEST response?

options.A: Close the finding on the action owner's report of the fix
options.B: Ask internal audit to confirm the fix in its follow-up
options.C: Test the fix with the risk team, then close the audit finding
options.D: Re-rate the password risk to reflect the reported fix

questions.key_concept: A reported fix for an internal audit finding is confirmed by audit's follow-up before the finding closes; the second line tracks progress meanwhile.
questions.pre_read: Note who raised the finding before deciding who can close it.
questions.correct_explanation: The finding is internal audit's: audit raised it, reports its status to the audit committee and, through its follow-up, confirms management's fix works before closing it. The analyst tracks progress and updates the register once audit confirms. Testing the fix with the risk team is the runner-up: its results can feed audit's follow-up, but closing audit's finding on a second-line test takes over the third line's judgment on its own work.

wrong_explanations.A: The action owner's report says a change was made, not that it works, and closing an audit finding is not the first line's call.
wrong_explanations.C: A second-line test can inform audit's follow-up, but the finding is internal audit's to close; the risk team cannot close it on audit's behalf.
wrong_explanations.D: Re-rating on a reported fix credits a change no one has confirmed works; the rating moves once the fix is shown to be effective.

tips: Eliminate: A closes on the first line's word, and D lowers a rating for a fix nobody has confirmed works.
Final two: B beats C because internal audit raised the finding and confirms its fix through follow-up; a second-line test can inform that, not replace it.
Exam cue: a fix reported for an internal audit finding is confirmed by audit's follow-up before the finding closes; the risk team's own issues close on evidence with the risk owner.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. What the profile adds to the appetite statement
questions.question: A tire retailer's new board member asks what its risk profile shows that the board's approved appetite statement does not. Which of the following is the risk analyst's BEST answer?

options.A: The full list of logged risks, with owners and action notes
options.B: How far a measure can move away from appetite before escalation
options.C: The exposure the business carries now, compared with appetite
options.D: The largest loss the business can absorb and survive

questions.key_concept: The risk profile shows the exposure the enterprise carries now, combined and set against appetite; appetite states how much risk leaders will take.
questions.pre_read: Name the concept each option describes before matching one to the question.
questions.correct_explanation: Appetite states how much risk the board is willing to take; the profile shows how much the business actually carries now, combined from the register and compared with that appetite, so leaders can see where exposure is too high or too low. The full list of logged risks with owners and action notes is the runner-up: that is the register, from which the profile selects and combines the top risks.

wrong_explanations.A: A full list with action notes is the risk register, the detailed working record; the profile selects, combines and prioritizes its top risks into overall exposure.
wrong_explanations.B: That describes tolerance, the measurable limit around appetite that triggers escalation; leaders set it, and the profile does not supply it.
wrong_explanations.D: That describes risk capacity, the outer bound the enterprise could survive; appetite sits inside it, while the profile measures current exposure.

tips: Eliminate: B describes tolerance and D describes capacity; both are limits leaders set or estimate, not a picture of the exposure carried today.
Final two: C beats A because the profile selects and combines register entries into overall exposure against appetite; the full list of logged risks with action notes is the register.
Exam cue: appetite is what leaders will take, tolerance how far a measure may move, capacity what the firm can survive; the profile is what it carries now.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Limits set by three divisions
questions.question: A lighting manufacturer's board set a $2,000,000 yearly appetite for customer data breach losses; its three division heads each then set a $1,000,000 limit of their own. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Measure divisions' breach losses against their owners' own limits
options.B: Keep the division owners' limits and track their combined losses
options.C: Buy insurance for breach losses above the board's appetite
options.D: Ask senior management to reset all three limits to fit appetite together

questions.key_concept: Limits handed down to units must together fit within the appetite above them; the level that allocates appetite resets them before losses occur.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the limits below allow with the limit set above them.
questions.correct_explanation: Tolerances pass down from appetite, so the limits given to units must together fit inside it. Here each division may lose $1,000,000, authorizing $3,000,000 against a $2,000,000 appetite, so senior management, which allocates appetite, should reset them. Keeping the limits and tracking combined losses is the runner-up: it would show the breach once losses arrive, but the division heads would still be acting within limits that allow it.

wrong_explanations.A: Judged against their own limits, all three divisions can stay compliant while together they pass the board's appetite by up to $1,000,000.
wrong_explanations.B: Tracking the total detects a breach after the losses occur; the limits themselves still permit $3,000,000 of loss against a $2,000,000 appetite.
wrong_explanations.C: Insurance moves part of the cost of covered losses, not the limits; the division heads would still be authorized to take more risk than the board accepts.

tips: Eliminate: A judges the divisions by limits that overrun the appetite, and C buys cover instead of fixing limits that authorize more risk than the board accepts.
Final two: D beats B because limits must fit within appetite before losses occur; tracking the combined total shows the breach only after the divisions have acted within their limits.
Exam cue: when unit limits add up to more than the appetite above them, the cascade is broken; take it to whoever allocates the appetite before any loss tests it.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. Vendor AI terms and customer confidentiality
questions.question: An internet provider's support manager wants a vendor's AI ticket summaries; the vendor's terms let it train on ticket data, which the sales director's customer contracts keep confidential. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Raise the conflict with the owner of the customer contracts
options.B: Notify customers that ticket summaries will use AI
options.C: Rate the confidentiality risk for the support manager to decide
options.D: Record the vendor's terms in the register with IT as owner

questions.key_concept: When a supplier's AI terms would break commitments already made to customers, the owner of those commitments decides before the feature is used.
questions.pre_read: Look for what the provider has already promised, and who holds that promise.
questions.correct_explanation: Letting the vendor train on ticket data would break confidentiality already promised to customers: a conflict with an obligation, not a risk the feature's sponsor can weigh and accept. The contracts' owner, the sales director, decides how to resolve it, such as a no-training term or leaving the feature off. Rating the risk for the support manager to decide is the runner-up: it leaves a promise to customers with a sponsor who cannot waive it.

wrong_explanations.B: A notice tells customers about AI use but does not release the provider from its confidentiality terms; whether and how to approach customers is the contracts' owner's call.
wrong_explanations.C: Rating helps, but the support manager sponsors the feature and cannot waive commitments in customer contracts; leaving the decision to them treats a contract breach as a trade-off.
wrong_explanations.D: The conflict is with customer contracts, a business obligation; filing it under IT leaves no one with authority over those commitments deciding before the feature is used.

tips: Eliminate: B gives customers notice but leaves the confidentiality terms broken, and D files a contractual conflict under IT, which does not hold customer commitments.
Final two: A beats C because the vendor's terms clash with commitments already made; the contracts' owner decides, while the support manager cannot weigh away a promise to customers.
Exam cue: when a supplier's AI terms clash with what the firm has promised its own customers, take the conflict to the owner of those commitments before go-live.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. Register updates timed to audits
questions.question: A ceramics maker's department heads, who own its IT risks, update their register entries only in the week before each internal audit. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Train the department heads on keeping register entries current
options.B: Notify the owners when an entry passes its review date
options.C: Make risk a standing item in executives' operating reviews
options.D: Increase internal audits of the heads' register entries

questions.key_concept: Owners who update risks only for audits show a compliance culture; leaders asking about risk in routine reviews changes that more than training or reminders.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the timing of the updates says about why the owners make them.
questions.correct_explanation: Updates timed to audits show the heads treat the register as an audit task, not part of running their departments. Culture follows what leaders ask about, so making risk a standing item in executives' operating reviews gives the heads a business reason to keep entries current. Training the heads is the runner-up: it improves how they maintain entries, but they already can; what is missing is a reason beyond the audit.

wrong_explanations.A: The heads already update entries well enough for audits, so skill is not the gap; after training, the audit would still be their only reason to update.
wrong_explanations.B: Reminders add another outside prompt; owners who update for audits would update for reminders too, without seeing risk as part of their own work.
wrong_explanations.D: More audits would bring more bursts of updates, deepening the habit of keeping entries current for auditors rather than for decisions.

tips: Eliminate: B adds reminders and D adds audits; both give owners more outside prompts and confirm the register as a compliance task.
Final two: C beats A because the heads already can update entries; leaders asking about risk in routine reviews gives them a reason to, which training does not.
Exam cue: when risk work happens only before audits, look for leaders using it in everyday decisions; training builds ability and reminders add prompts, but neither supplies a motive.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Business processes and resilience. Plan invocation with the director away
questions.question: Only a boatyard's managing director may invoke its continuity plan; when a storm flooded the yard, the director was unreachable at sea for six hours. Which of the following is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Storm criteria that set out when the yard's plan must be invoked
options.B: Flood barriers around the yard's boat lifts and controls
options.C: Recovery-step training for the yard's crews
options.D: A deputy named in the plan, empowered to invoke it

questions.key_concept: A continuity plan names who may invoke it and a deputy with the same authority, so one unreachable person cannot hold up the response.
questions.pre_read: Ask what stopped the plan from starting, and whether each option removes that cause.
questions.correct_explanation: The plan depended on one person to start it, so the yard lost six hours when that person was unreachable. A deputy named in the plan, with the same authority to invoke it, removes that single point of failure for any event, not just storms. Storm criteria are the runner-up: they state when the plan should start, but with the director at sea no one present could act on them.

wrong_explanations.A: Criteria say when to invoke, but the authority would still sit with one person; with the director at sea, no one present could have used them.
wrong_explanations.B: Barriers may limit flood damage, but the plan would still stall the next time the director, its only invoker, cannot be reached.
wrong_explanations.C: Trained crews still need someone with authority to start the plan; training on recovery steps leaves invocation waiting for the director.

tips: Eliminate: B reduces one hazard's damage, and C trains crews on recovery; neither lets anyone start the plan while the director is away.
Final two: D beats A because the gap is who may invoke, not when; criteria leave the decision with one unreachable person, while a named deputy can act on them.
Exam cue: look for single points of failure in a continuity plan's people as well as its systems; the authority to invoke needs a named deputy.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 4.2.1 (Activation Criteria and Procedure: the individual with authority to activate the plan is designated clearly in it, and a successor is identified to assume that authority if necessary); COBIT 2019 DSS04 (Managed Continuity); ISACA Glossary (business continuity plan)

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). IT department's own appetite statement
questions.question: A pawnbroker's IT department published its own risk appetite allowing two-day outages of the customer loan system; the board's appetite allows four hours for any customer-facing service. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Keep IT's appetite for internal systems customers do not use
options.B: Derive every IT outage limit from the enterprise appetite
options.C: Give the loan-system owner the choice of statement
options.D: Rate loan-system outages against IT's own limit

questions.key_concept: Appetite is set once for the enterprise by its leaders; IT applies it through limits derived from it, not through an appetite of its own.
questions.pre_read: Note who wrote each statement and which one the enterprise's leaders approved.
questions.correct_explanation: Leaders set appetite once for the enterprise; limits for each area, IT included, are derived from it, with outage limits agreed with the business owners of the services. IT's statement lacks that authority and allows the customer loan system twelve times the outage the board accepts. Keeping IT's appetite for internal systems is the runner-up: those systems still support enterprise objectives, so their limits come from the board's appetite too.

wrong_explanations.A: Internal systems still serve enterprise objectives; a separate IT appetite for them keeps a second, unapproved yardstick beside the board's.
wrong_explanations.C: Risk owners apply the enterprise appetite to their risks; they do not choose which appetite applies to them.
wrong_explanations.D: Rating against IT's two-day limit judges a customer-facing outage by a yardstick the board did not set, one that allows twelve times its four hours.

tips: Eliminate: C lets an owner pick an appetite, and D rates outages against a limit the board did not approve.
Final two: B beats A because appetite is set once at the top; internal systems also get limits derived from it, not from an appetite IT writes.
Exam cue: when a department writes its own appetite, bring its limits under the appetite enterprise leaders approved; disciplines apply appetite rather than set it.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Strategy, goals and objectives. Assessment scope and a pending strategy
questions.question: A textbook publisher's board votes on its new strategy in six weeks; the IT risk assessment starts in four months, and its scope is not needed before then. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Wait for the approved strategy before setting the scope
options.B: Base the scope on the strategy's current draft
options.C: Scope it around the systems with the most open audit findings
options.D: Have the IT system owners name the areas to cover

questions.key_concept: An assessment is scoped from approved objectives; when approval comes before the work starts and nothing forces an earlier scope, wait for it.
questions.pre_read: Note the dates in the stem, then ask what each option would build the assessment's scope around.
questions.correct_explanation: An assessment's scope follows the objectives it protects, and the board settles those objectives in six weeks, long before the scope is needed. Waiting costs nothing and avoids scoping around goals the board may still change. Basing the scope on the current draft is the runner-up: practitioners do scope on drafts when the work cannot wait, but here it can, and a draft risks rework or a scope aimed at dropped goals.

wrong_explanations.B: Scoping on a draft makes sense when the work must start first; here the approved strategy arrives months before the assessment, so the draft only adds rework risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Open audit findings describe technical weaknesses, not what the business is trying to achieve; scoping around them starts from vulnerabilities instead of objectives.
wrong_explanations.D: IT system owners would scope by the systems they run, not by the strategy's objectives, leaving the business leaders who own those objectives out.

tips: Eliminate: C starts from audit findings and D from IT system owners' views; both scope by technology rather than by the objectives the assessment protects.
Final two: A beats B because the approved strategy arrives before the scope is needed; scoping on the draft gains no time and risks rework if the board changes it.
Exam cue: when objectives will be approved before an assessment must be scoped, and nothing forces an earlier start, scope on the approved version rather than a draft.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Organizational structure, roles and responsibilities. Register kept in different formats
questions.question: A money transfer operator's units use different templates for its enterprise register, two with no supplier-risk category. Which of the following should the risk analyst recommend as MOST responsible for fixing this?

options.A: The IT department, which hosts the register software
options.B: The risk owners, for the risks that they record
options.C: The chief risk officer, who runs the risk function
options.D: Internal audit, which gives assurance on the register

questions.key_concept: The role running the risk function, often the chief risk officer, keeps one register template with the approved categories; owners answer for their entries.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the problem sits in single entries or in how the register is built across units.
questions.correct_explanation: Templates that differ by unit, two missing a risk category, are problems of the register's design, which belongs to the role running the risk process: the chief risk officer puts one template, with the approved categories, in every unit, and NIST IR 8286 Rev. 1 gives register upkeep to the enterprise risk officer. The risk owners are the runner-up: they answer for their own entries, but no owner can set the template other units use.

wrong_explanations.A: Hosting the software makes IT responsible for the tool working, not for the templates and categories the units record risks in.
wrong_explanations.B: Owners keep their own entries current, but templates and categories are set across units; owners adding supplier risks would still leave the templates inconsistent.
wrong_explanations.D: Internal audit can report on the register's quality, but running it would have audit assessing its own work; it stays independent of the process.

tips: Eliminate: A gives the job to the team hosting the tool and D to internal audit, whose role is independent assurance; neither runs the risk process.
Final two: C beats B because the risk function keeps one template, with the approved categories, across units; owners answer for the entries they make in it.
Exam cue: when units' register templates differ, look to the role that runs the risk process to align them to the approved categories; owners answer for their own entries.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. Standards citing a replaced policy
questions.question: An eyewear retailer replaced its security policy last year, but its 12 security standards still cite the old one, and some store managers say they no longer apply. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Rewrite the 12 standards from scratch with their owners
options.B: Notify store managers that the standards still apply
options.C: Recast the 12 standards as advisory guidelines
options.D: Reissue each standard under the current policy

questions.key_concept: Each standard draws its authority from an approved policy; when the policy is replaced, standards are reissued under the new one so they still bind.
questions.pre_read: Ask where a standard's authority comes from, and what changed above it.
questions.correct_explanation: Standards draw their authority from the approved policy above them; once that policy was replaced, standards citing the old one lost a traceable mandate, which is why managers can dispute them. Reissuing each under the current policy restores the link and lets its owner confirm it still fits. Notifying managers that the standards apply is the runner-up: it settles today's argument, but the standards still cite a retired policy, so the dispute can return.

wrong_explanations.A: Nobody has faulted the requirements themselves; rewriting all 12 from scratch spends effort on sound rules when only their link to the policy needs fixing.
wrong_explanations.B: A notice settles today's dispute but leaves the standards citing a retired policy, so new managers and auditors would meet the same gap.
wrong_explanations.C: Guidelines are advisory; recasting mandatory security rules as guidelines would make the managers' claim true instead of closing the gap.

tips: Eliminate: A rewrites rules nobody has faulted, and C turns mandatory standards into advice; neither restores the link between the standards and the current policy.
Final two: D beats B because the standards' authority comes from the policy they cite; a notice asserts that they apply, while reissuing them under the current policy fixes the link.
Exam cue: when a policy is replaced, check that the standards below it now trace to the new one; each layer takes its authority from the approved layer above.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Business processes and resilience. Manual workaround for an AI scheduler
questions.question: A heat pump installer's AI tool schedules 300 visits daily; the manual workaround was never run at that volume, and most dispatchers, hired since go-live, never used it. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Exercise the workaround for a full day with the process owner
options.B: Train the dispatchers on the manual workaround's written steps
options.C: Negotiate a higher uptime commitment through the vendor's contract owner
options.D: Add an alert to IT when the AI tool's response slows

questions.key_concept: A manual workaround counts only once the people who would run it show, in an exercise, that it carries the needed service level.
questions.pre_read: Ask what nobody yet knows about the workaround, and which option would find out.
questions.correct_explanation: The workaround has never carried 300 visits a day, and most of the people who would run it have never used it, so nobody knows whether it keeps service going. A full-day exercise with the process owner shows whether it meets the service level the owner needs, and trains the dispatchers as it runs. Training alone is the runner-up: it teaches the steps but cannot show the workaround copes at that volume.

wrong_explanations.B: Training prepares dispatchers to take part, but cannot show whether hand scheduling copes with 300 visits a day; an exercise shows that and trains them too.
wrong_explanations.C: A stronger uptime commitment makes outages rarer, but the tool can still fail, and the manual route it falls back on stays unproven.
wrong_explanations.D: An alert tells IT sooner that the tool is failing, but detection does not keep visits scheduled; the dispatchers still need a workaround they can run.

tips: Eliminate: C makes outages rarer and D detects them sooner; both work on the AI tool and leave the people-run workaround unproven.
Final two: A beats B because training teaches the steps, while a full-day exercise shows whether the dispatchers can carry the daily volume, and trains them too.
Exam cue: when a continuity workaround depends on people who have never run it at full load, exercise it with the process owner before counting on it.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. Overlapping second-line questionnaires
questions.question: A salmon farm's compliance, security and risk teams each send site managers a yearly questionnaire; the three overlap by 70%, and answers are now rushed. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Hand the three questionnaires to internal audit to run
options.B: Combine the three teams' questionnaires into one shared review
options.C: Spread the three questionnaires across different quarters
options.D: Merge the compliance, security and risk teams into one function

questions.key_concept: Second-line functions coordinate what they ask of the first line; one shared review removes duplicate demands while each function keeps its own role.
questions.pre_read: Find what causes the rushed answers, then weigh how much each option changes to remove it.
questions.correct_explanation: The rushed answers come from three uncoordinated requests asking site managers largely the same things. Combining them into one shared review removes the 70% overlap while compliance, security and risk keep their own roles and reporting. Spreading the questionnaires across quarters is the runner-up and a common quick fix: it eases the peak, but managers still answer the same questions three times a year.

wrong_explanations.A: Internal audit gives independent assurance; running the second line's monitoring would leave it auditing its own work, and the overlap would remain.
wrong_explanations.C: Spacing the questionnaires lightens each sitting, but managers still answer most questions three times, so the duplicate demand that drives rushed answers stays.
wrong_explanations.D: The overlap comes from uncoordinated requests, not from having three functions; separate second-line teams can coordinate without a reorganization.

tips: Eliminate: A moves second-line monitoring to the third line, and D reorganizes three functions when the problem is their uncoordinated requests.
Final two: B beats C because one shared review removes the duplicated questions; spreading them across quarters only spaces out the same triple burden.
Exam cue: when several second-line teams ask the first line overlapping questions, coordinate the requests into one; duplicated demands degrade the answers every team relies on.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. Rating changed at acceptance
questions.question: A tannery's plant director accepted a dosing-system risk rated 16 of 25, within appetite, and re-rated it 6 though nothing else changed. Which of the following should the risk profile MOST appropriately show?

options.A: The plant director's rating of 6, given at acceptance
options.B: The risk moved off the profile onto its owner's accepted-risks list
options.C: The rating of 16, with the director's acceptance noted
options.D: The risk shown as transferred to its owner, the plant director

questions.key_concept: Acceptance records the owner's decision to carry a risk; it changes neither likelihood nor impact, so the profile keeps the rating and notes the acceptance.
questions.pre_read: Check what, if anything, changed the risk's likelihood or impact between the two ratings.
questions.correct_explanation: Acceptance is the owner's decision to carry a risk, not a control: with nothing else changed, likelihood and impact are as they were at 16. The profile shows the exposure carried, so it keeps 16 and notes the acceptance, and the analyst raises the unexplained drop with the director. The director's 6 is the runner-up, as owners validate their ratings, but a rating rests on likelihood and impact, and neither moved.

wrong_explanations.A: Owners decide whether to accept, but a lower rating needs a change in likelihood or impact; with neither changed, 6 understates what the tannery now carries.
wrong_explanations.B: Accepted risks are still exposure the business carries; moving them off the profile hides part of the position leaders compare with appetite.
wrong_explanations.D: Transfer shifts part of the loss to another party, such as an insurer; acceptance keeps the whole risk inside the tannery, with its owner.

tips: Eliminate: B takes an accepted risk off the profile, though it is still exposure, and D confuses acceptance with transfer, which moves loss to another party.
Final two: C beats A because acceptance is a decision, not a control; with likelihood and impact unchanged, the rating stays at 16 whoever accepts it.
Exam cue: when a rating drops at acceptance with nothing else changed, keep the earlier rating and record the acceptance; ratings move with likelihood and impact, not with the decision.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. Per-record penalty in a customer contract
questions.question: A housing developer's contract would make a glazier pay $150 per homebuyer record exposed in a breach, uncapped. Which of the following BEST lets the risk analyst size the term's maximum cost?

options.A: The largest breach loss the glazier has suffered so far
options.B: The number of homebuyer records the glazier will hold for the developer
options.C: The average cost per breached homebuyer record across the industry
options.D: The total value of the developer's contract to the glazier

questions.key_concept: A contract term that prices each affected record has a maximum cost set by how many records it covers; size it before the owner signs.
questions.pre_read: Note what the term fixes and what it leaves open before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The term fixes the price of each exposed record at $150 with no cap, so the most it could cost is that price times the records the glazier would hold for the developer: here a count is the right measure. The contract's total value is the runner-up because many contracts cap liability at the fees paid, but this term has no cap; value shows what the deal earns, not what it could cost.

wrong_explanations.A: Past breach losses came from other contracts and data; this term prices records the glazier has not yet received, so history cannot set its maximum.
wrong_explanations.C: An industry average estimates breach costs in general, but this term already fixes the price per record; what is unknown is how many records it applies to.
wrong_explanations.D: Contract value shows what the deal earns; with no cap in the term, the liability grows with the records held, not with the fees, and can far exceed them.

tips: Eliminate: A uses past losses and C an industry cost per record; the term itself fixes the price, so neither sizes what this term could cost.
Final two: B beats D because an uncapped per-record term grows with the records held; contract value is what the deal earns, a common cap this term lacks.
Exam cue: when a contract term prices each record or unit affected, size its maximum from the count it applies to; earnings and loss history do not bound it.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Strategy, goals and objectives. Risk report arranged by system
questions.question: An olive oil producer's board set three objectives for the year, but the risk report it receives lists IT risks only by the system each affects. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Tell system owners which board objectives their risks affect
options.B: Add the affected systems' replacement costs to the report
options.C: Group the reported IT risks under their owners' business units
options.D: Map each reported risk to the board objective it threatens

questions.key_concept: Risk reported to leaders is tied to the objectives they set, so they can see which goals are at risk, not only which systems.
questions.pre_read: Note what the board set for the year and what the report is arranged around.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk is the effect of uncertainty on objectives, and the board set three for the year; a report by system shows where problems sit, not which goals they threaten. Mapping each risk to the objective it threatens lets directors see what is at stake. Grouping by each owner's unit is the runner-up: it adds accountability, but directors would still have to work out which of their objectives each risk puts at risk.

wrong_explanations.A: System owners learn the link, but the board's report stays arranged by system, so the directors who set the objectives still cannot see which are at risk.
wrong_explanations.B: Replacement costs value the systems, not the risks; they do not show which of the board's objectives a risk threatens or by how much.
wrong_explanations.C: A view by unit shows who answers for each risk, but objectives can span units, so the board still cannot read the risk to each of its objectives.

tips: Eliminate: A informs system owners but leaves the board's report unchanged, and B adds replacement costs, which value the systems, not the objectives at stake.
Final two: D beats C because the board set objectives and needs risk shown against them; grouping by each owner's unit adds accountability but not that view.
Exam cue: when leaders steer by objectives they have set, report risk against those objectives; systems and units show where a risk sits, not what it threatens.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. Rating a process one designed
questions.question: Before joining the risk team, a kitchen fitter's risk analyst designed its job-scheduling process; the head of risk now asks the analyst to rate that process's risks. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Disclose the design role to the head of risk before rating
options.B: Rate the process, then ask a colleague to review the rating
options.C: Hand the rating over to internal audit to perform
options.D: Rate the process jointly with its owner

questions.key_concept: A practitioner asked to rate work they designed discloses that role before starting, so whoever assigned it can reassign the work or add a review.
questions.pre_read: Notice the analyst's earlier role and when each option deals with it.
questions.correct_explanation: Rating a process one designed threatens objectivity, and the Code asks for objectivity and disclosure of facts that could distort results. Disclosing the design role first lets the head of risk reassign the rating or add an independent review. Rating it, then asking a colleague to review it, is the runner-up: review is a safeguard, but it follows a rating the design may have shaped, and the head of risk never learns of the conflict.

wrong_explanations.B: A colleague's review helps, but it comes after a rating the design may have shaped, and the head of risk never hears of the conflict to choose a safeguard.
wrong_explanations.C: Internal audit gives independent assurance as the third line; taking on the second line's risk rating would draw it into management's work.
wrong_explanations.D: Rating with the owner adds the first line's view, but the owner runs the process being rated, so it adds no independence, and the analyst's role stays undisclosed.

tips: Eliminate: C hands second-line rating work to internal audit, the third line, and D adds the process owner, who runs the process and leaves the design role undisclosed.
Final two: A beats B because FIRST means before the rating: disclosure lets the head of risk reassign or review it; a self-arranged review leaves them unaware.
Exam cue: when a practitioner is asked to assess their own past work, disclose it before starting so the assigner can choose a safeguard; a check arranged afterward leaves the assigner unaware.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. A standard missed at newer sites
questions.question: A self-storage operator's standard requires default passwords changed on each gate-access controller; IT changed them at 40 older sites but missed six newer ones. Which of the following is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Grant the six sites an exception with the operations director as owner
options.B: Rate the exposure at the six sites before changing anything
options.C: Change the default passwords on the six newer sites' controllers
options.D: Have the standard's owner limit the rule to the older sites

questions.key_concept: A mandatory standard missed in rollout is simply applied where it was missed; exceptions are for rules that cannot be met for now.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the newer sites could meet the standard and what kept them from meeting it.
questions.correct_explanation: The standard already requires default passwords to be changed, and the six newer sites were simply missed in IT's rollout. Changing the passwords on those controllers, as the rollout should have done, closes a gap the standard already rules on. Rating the six sites' exposure first is the runner-up: analysis comes before new controls, but this control is already required, and factory default passwords are widely known.

wrong_explanations.A: Exceptions cover rules that cannot be met for now; changing a default password is quick, so an exception would accept a risk no one needs to carry.
wrong_explanations.B: Rating comes before choosing new controls, but the standard already requires this one; re-rating six sites delays a simple fix while known defaults stay in place.
wrong_explanations.D: Limiting the rule to older sites rewrites the standard around a rollout miss; the newer controllers carry the same well-known default passwords.

tips: Eliminate: A uses an exception where compliance is quick and possible, and D rewrites the standard to fit a rollout miss; neither closes the gap.
Final two: C beats B because the standard already requires the change and the sites were simply missed; rating them first only delays a required, simple control.
Exam cue: when a mandatory standard was missed in rollout rather than found unworkable, apply it where it was missed; save exceptions for rules that cannot be met for now.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. A vendor's device on the farm network
questions.question: A mushroom grower's climate-control vendor installed its own remote-monitoring gateway on the farm network; the asset inventory leaves it out because the vendor owns the device. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Cover the gateway through the vendor contract's security terms
options.B: List vendor-owned devices in the inventory with internal owners
options.C: Disconnect the gateway until the vendor proves that it is secure
options.D: Record the gateway just on IT's network diagram

questions.key_concept: What sits on the enterprise's network or holds its data belongs in the inventory with an internal owner, whoever holds legal title to it.
questions.pre_read: Notice where the device sits and what rule kept it out of the inventory.
questions.correct_explanation: The gateway sits on the farm network and links the climate system to the outside, so its risk is the farm's, whoever holds title to it. Listing vendor-owned devices in the inventory with internal owners fixes the rule that left it out and brings it into risk assessment. Covering it through the contract's security terms is the runner-up: terms set the vendor's duties but leave the gateway outside the farm's own view and ownership.

wrong_explanations.A: Contract terms bind the vendor, but the farm still carries the risk; without an inventory entry and an owner, no one assesses or watches the gateway.
wrong_explanations.C: Disconnecting picks a response before the risk is analyzed and cuts the monitoring the farm relies on; the gap is in the inventory, not the device.
wrong_explanations.D: A network diagram shows connections, not an owner, class or risk rating, so the gateway would stay out of assessments that start from the inventory.

tips: Eliminate: C disconnects before any analysis, cutting monitoring the farm uses, and D records the gateway as a line on a diagram with no owner or rating.
Final two: B beats A because the gateway sits on the farm network, so the inventory rule must cover it, with an owner; contract terms set only the vendor's duties.
Exam cue: legal title does not set inventory scope; list what sits on the enterprise's network or holds its data, with an internal owner, whoever owns the device.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). Slow adoption of AI
questions.question: A savings cooperative's register covers only harms from using AI, not the loan growth it loses to rivals whose AI tools approve loans in minutes. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Refer the lost growth to its business owner as a sales matter
options.B: Keep AI opportunities in a separate innovation register
options.C: Fund an AI loan-approval tool to match rivals' speed
options.D: Rate slow AI adoption with its business owner as an IT risk

questions.key_concept: Value lost by adopting technology too slowly is IT risk, benefit or value enablement in Risk IT's terms, rated and owned like any other.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the register covers with what the cooperative is losing.
questions.correct_explanation: ERM covers upside as well as loss, and Risk IT counts value missed through slow use of technology as benefit or value enablement risk. Rating slow AI adoption with its business owner puts it in the register beside the harms of using AI, so leaders weigh both sides. Referring the lost growth to the owner as a sales matter is the runner-up: the owner is right, but the risk stays unrated and outside the register.

wrong_explanations.A: The business owner should hold it, but as a sales matter it stays outside the register, so leaders never weigh it against the harms of using AI.
wrong_explanations.B: A separate register keeps AI's upside apart from the risks leaders compare, so neither side can be weighed against the other or against appetite.
wrong_explanations.C: Funding a tool picks a response before the risk of slow adoption is rated, and spending decisions belong to leaders, not the risk analyst.

tips: Eliminate: B splits AI opportunities into a separate register leaders do not compare, and C funds a tool before the risk of slow adoption is rated.
Final two: D beats A because value lost to slow adoption is IT risk to rate with its owner; as a sales matter it stays outside the register leaders weigh.
Exam cue: when a register lists only the harms of using a new technology, look for the value lost by not using it, and rate that with its owner too.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. Two lines' tests disagree
questions.question: A piano maker's risk team rated its backup control effective in March; internal audit, testing it in May, rated it ineffective. Before the board's risk report, what should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Compare both tests' scope and dates with audit and the control's owner
options.B: Retest the control with a larger sample from the risk team
options.C: Report internal audit's later rating to the board as it stands
options.D: Report whichever rating the control's owner accepts

questions.key_concept: When two lines' tests of one control disagree, compare their scope, samples and timing before reporting, so the board gets one explained result.
questions.pre_read: Note who tested the control, when, and what is still unknown about why the results differ.
questions.correct_explanation: Two tests two months apart reached opposite results, and nothing yet shows whether the control broke after March or the tests covered different ground. Comparing scope and dates with internal audit and the control's owner explains the gap, so the board gets one reasoned view. Reporting internal audit's later rating is the runner-up: it may prove right, but sent alone it leaves the earlier result unexplained and the cause unknown.

wrong_explanations.B: A bigger sample from the same team sets audit's evidence aside; if the tests differ in scope or timing, retesting may repeat the gap.
wrong_explanations.C: Audit's later result may well stand, but reporting it before the difference is understood leaves the board unsure what changed or which result fits.
wrong_explanations.D: The control's owner answers for the control; letting them pick the reported rating puts preference in place of evidence and undercuts both tests.

tips: Eliminate: B retests without weighing audit's evidence, and D lets the control's owner choose the result, putting preference in place of evidence.
Final two: A beats C because the tests ran months apart and the cause of the gap is unknown; audit's result may stand, but the board needs it explained.
Exam cue: when two assurance results on one control conflict, reconcile their scope, sample and timing with the testers and the control's owner before reporting either result.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Appetite words and limit disagree
questions.question: A hardware store chain's board states a low appetite for online fraud but allows $1,500,000 of losses a year, which its impact scale rates severe. Which of the following is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Monitor online fraud against the $1,500,000 limit with its risk owner
options.B: Apply a lower limit, set by the risk team, to online fraud
options.C: Raise the mismatch with the board that set the fraud appetite
options.D: Treat the $1,500,000 limit as a tolerance above the appetite

questions.key_concept: When an appetite statement and its limit disagree, the body that set them reconciles them; the practitioner neither picks one nor rewrites them.
questions.pre_read: Compare the board's statement with its limit, using the scale the stem gives.
questions.correct_explanation: The board's words say low appetite, but its limit allows losses the chain's own scale rates severe, so the two cannot both guide decisions. Only the board, which set the appetite, can say which it meant. Monitoring against the $1,500,000 limit with the risk owner is the runner-up: the figure is measurable, but working to it quietly accepts severe yearly losses the board's statement rules out.

wrong_explanations.A: The limit is measurable, but working to it treats severe yearly losses as acceptable when the board's own statement says its appetite is low.
wrong_explanations.B: Appetite is set by the board; a limit the risk team sets replaces the board's figure with the team's own reading of the board's words.
wrong_explanations.D: Calling the limit a tolerance relabels the board's figure without asking it; tolerance is a limited deviation, and severe losses still contradict a low appetite.

tips: Eliminate: B has the risk team set the board's limit, and D relabels it as a tolerance; both settle the board's mismatch without the board.
Final two: C beats A because the statement and the limit disagree; working to the number alone picks one side of a choice that belongs to the board.
Exam cue: read an appetite statement's words against its limits and the impact scale; when they disagree, the board that wrote them says which it meant.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Organizational structure, roles and responsibilities. Owner asks the analyst to apply a control
questions.question: A foreign exchange bureau's card-fraud risk owner chose the risk analyst's costed option of blocking web orders from three countries and asks the analyst to apply the block. What is the analyst's BEST response?

options.A: Apply the block through the bureau's change process
options.B: Pass the block to IT operations as a firewall change
options.C: Estimate the fraud the block would stop before applying it
options.D: Get the chief risk officer's approval before the block goes in

questions.key_concept: Once the owner chooses a response, the practitioner hands the change to the first-line team that makes it, and goes on advising and monitoring.
questions.pre_read: Note what has already been decided and whose job the remaining work is.
questions.correct_explanation: The owner has already chosen from costed options, so what remains is putting the block in place. Blocking web orders is a technical control, and IT operations makes firewall changes as the first line, so the change goes to them. Applying the block through the change process is the runner-up: the change would be controlled, but the analyst would then run a control the risk function later monitors, mixing first-line work with the second line's.

wrong_explanations.A: Change control keeps the change orderly, but the analyst would be running a control the risk function later monitors; making firewall changes is IT's first-line work.
wrong_explanations.C: The costed options already set out what the block would save and cost; estimating it again repeats analysis the owner has already used to decide.
wrong_explanations.D: The owner chose within their role as risk owner; the chief risk officer runs the risk function, and this chosen response needs no further approval from them.

tips: Eliminate: C re-estimates what the costed options already showed, and D adds a chief risk officer approval that a response chosen within the owner's authority does not need.
Final two: B beats A because the analyst advises and monitors but does not run controls; IT operations makes firewall changes, however carefully the analyst would apply one.
Exam cue: when the owner has chosen a response from completed analysis and asks the practitioner to put it in place, hand the work to whoever runs that control.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. Request to fix an exposure quietly
questions.question: An electrical contractor's project director wants client building-access codes, found exposed in a public folder, fixed quietly; the client contract requires notice of any exposure. What is the risk analyst's BEST response?

options.A: Report the exposure through the contractor's incident process
options.B: Delete the exposed building-access codes from the public folder
options.C: Send the client's security team the exposure details
options.D: Have IT log the folder fix as a routine change request

questions.key_concept: A known exposure goes into the incident process, not a quiet fix or a lone disclosure, so those authorized can give the notice owed.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what the director wants against what the contract requires, and who handles notice.
questions.correct_explanation: Fixing a known exposure quietly would hide a significant fact and break the contract's notice term. Reporting it through the incident process puts containment and the notice decision with the people authorized to handle them. Deleting the codes is the runner-up: it stops further exposure, but codes already seen stay valid until the client changes them, and done quietly no notice is sent.

wrong_explanations.B: Removing the codes stops further exposure, but codes already seen stay valid until the client changes them, and done quietly the notice the contract requires goes unsent.
wrong_explanations.C: The client must hear, but through the contractor's process; an analyst writing to the client alone releases company information without the authority to do so.
wrong_explanations.D: A routine change records the fix but not the exposure, so the incident and the notice the contract calls for stay hidden.

tips: Eliminate: C has the analyst contact the client outside the contractor's process, and D files the exposure as a routine change, which records the fix but not the incident.
Final two: A beats B because deleting the codes stops further exposure but hides it from the client, whose codes stay valid; the incident process has the required notice decided by those authorized.
Exam cue: when someone wants a known exposure fixed quietly, take it into the incident process; containment on its own does not meet a duty to report.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. Protection set by data class
questions.question: A pipe maker protects servers by data class, so its production-scheduling server, which holds only public data, gets the lowest tier, though the plant stops without it. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Reclassify the server's data as restricted, with its owner's approval
options.B: Set the server's tier by what the business paid for it
options.C: Keep the server on the tier its data class sets
options.D: Base server tiers on business criticality as well as data class

questions.key_concept: A data class reflects sensitivity; protection also follows business criticality, so a system holding public data can still need strong availability controls.
questions.pre_read: Separate how sensitive the server's data is from how much the business needs the server.
questions.correct_explanation: The tier rule looks only at how sensitive the data is, so a server the plant cannot run without gets the least protection. Basing tiers on business criticality as well fixes the rule for this server and any like it. Reclassifying the data as restricted is the runner-up: it would raise the tier, but it labels public data as sensitive, adds handling it does not need and leaves other critical systems under the same gap.

wrong_explanations.A: A higher class would lift the tier, but even with the owner's approval it mislabels public data and leaves the rule's gap for other critical systems.
wrong_explanations.B: Purchase price ignores what the plant loses while the server is down, which is the harm its protection should match.
wrong_explanations.C: The data class says how sensitive the data is, not how much the plant depends on the server, so the tier stays far below its importance.

tips: Eliminate: B values the server by its purchase price, not the harm of losing it, and C keeps a tier set by data sensitivity while the plant depends on the server.
Final two: D beats A because the data really is public; the gap is in a rule that ignores criticality, and a false class would fix one server by mislabeling it.
Exam cue: when an important system gets weak protection because its data is not sensitive, add criticality to the rule; do not relabel the data to force a higher tier.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. Process scores in the board's profile
questions.question: A feed mill's board gets an 'IT risk profile' that lists each IT process's maturity level, all now 3 or higher out of 5. Which of the following should concern the risk analyst MOST?

options.A: The levels have no targets tied to the mill's own risks
options.B: Level 3 sits below the sector's typical maturity
options.C: Maturity levels do not show the risk the mill carries
options.D: The report rates IT processes rather than systems

questions.key_concept: A risk profile shows the exposure the enterprise carries; process maturity shows capability and cannot stand in for it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the board could decide from the measure it is shown.
questions.correct_explanation: A risk profile tells the board how much risk the mill carries, so it can judge that against appetite and choose responses. Maturity levels describe how well IT processes are run, and a mature process can still face high risk. Missing risk-based targets is the runner-up: targets would make the scores more useful, but even with them the board would still have no view of the mill's exposure.

wrong_explanations.A: Risk-based targets would improve how maturity is managed, but the board would still see capability scores, not the exposure a profile should show.
wrong_explanations.B: Comparing with other mills changes the yardstick, not the measure; the board still would not see the mill's own risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Processes and systems are both workable units; the problem is that the report measures capability, not risk, at whatever level it reports.

tips: Eliminate: B compares the scores with other mills, and D swaps processes for systems; either way the report still measures capability, not risk.
Final two: C beats A because targets would sharpen a capability measure without turning it into exposure; the board still could not set the mill's risk against its appetite.
Exam cue: when a report called a risk profile shows maturity, compliance or activity scores, ask whether it shows the exposure carried, set against appetite.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Getting breaches to deciders
questions.question: Which of the following should the risk analyst recommend to BEST ensure a vehicle licensing agency's tolerance breaches reach the right decision-makers in time?

options.A: A KRI dashboard that every manager can view
options.B: Escalation routes and deadlines set for tolerance breaches
options.C: A monthly summary of breaches for the executive risk committee
options.D: Training for risk owners on their tolerance limits

questions.key_concept: Breaches reach the right level in time when the framework sets, in advance, who hears of each breach and how fast.
questions.pre_read: Look for what makes a breach reach someone who decides, within a set time.
questions.correct_explanation: A breach needs a decision from the risk owner, or from the level that set the limit, while there is still time to act. Escalation routes and deadlines set in advance say who must hear of a breach and how fast. A monthly summary for the executive risk committee is the runner-up: it keeps oversight informed, but a breach can wait weeks for it, and the committee may not be the level that decides.

wrong_explanations.A: A dashboard lets managers see breaches but makes no one responsible for raising them, so a breach can sit in plain view with no decision.
wrong_explanations.C: Committee oversight matters, but a monthly summary can arrive weeks after a breach, and the decision may belong to the owner or another level.
wrong_explanations.D: Owners who know their limits still need a set route and deadline for raising a breach; training adds knowledge, not a path.

tips: Eliminate: A shows breaches to many managers without making anyone raise them, and D teaches owners their limits without giving breaches a route.
Final two: B beats C because a breach needs a decision while action is still possible; a monthly summary reports it later, to a body that may not decide.
Exam cue: for breaches that must reach deciders in time, look for a route and deadline set in advance; dashboards, training and periodic summaries inform but cannot ensure a timely decision.
