questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. AI chatbot used in several countries
questions.question: A flooring retailer runs an AI chatbot from its home country for online shoppers in four other countries, whose AI rules require different things. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Apply the AI rules of the retailer's home country to the chatbot
options.B: Apply the strictest country's AI rules across the business
options.C: Make IT the owner of the chatbot's AI compliance duties
options.D: Record the chatbot's duties by country of use under its business owner

questions.key_concept: AI duties can arise from where a system is used and whom it affects; each country's duties are recorded as owned obligations, with legal input.
questions.pre_read: Note where the chatbot is used and how the countries' rules differ.
questions.correct_explanation: AI rules can apply where a system is used and to the people it affects, so each of the four countries can add its own duties. Recording them by country, with legal input, in the obligations register under the chatbot's business owner shows each duty and who must meet it. Applying the strictest country's rules is the runner-up: it sounds safe, but when the rules require different things, no one country's set covers the others.

wrong_explanations.A: Rules follow the shoppers the chatbot serves, not only where the retailer is based, so home-country rules can miss duties in the other four countries.
wrong_explanations.B: When rules require different things, no single country's set is strictest in every respect, so applying one leaves other countries' duties unmet.
wrong_explanations.C: IT runs the chatbot, but meeting legal duties for its use is a business obligation; the business owner answers for it, with IT's help.

tips: Eliminate: A follows where the retailer is based rather than where shoppers are, and C hands a business obligation to IT, which runs the chatbot.
Final two: D beats B because the four countries' rules require different things; one country's set cannot cover duties it does not contain, while recording by country shows each.
Exam cue: when an AI system serves people in several jurisdictions, map duties by where it is used and whom it affects, as owned obligations, before choosing how to comply.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Strategy, goals and objectives. What an IT risk program is for
questions.question: A consulate's new consul general asks the risk analyst what its IT risk program is for. Which of the following is the analyst's BEST answer?

options.A: Supporting the consulate in achieving its mission objectives
options.B: Reducing the number of security incidents the consulate suffers
options.C: Meeting the security objectives set for its systems
options.D: Complying with the host country's data protection laws

questions.key_concept: IT risk management exists to help the enterprise achieve its objectives, keeping risk within appetite rather than driving incidents toward zero.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each option treats as the end and what it treats as a means.
questions.correct_explanation: IT risk management exists to support what the enterprise sets out to achieve: it weighs the uncertainty that could help or hinder the consulate's mission, so leaders take the risks worth taking and treat the rest. Fewer security incidents is the runner-up: incidents matter by their effect on those objectives, and a program judged by incident numbers can spend on minor events and hold back work the mission needs.

wrong_explanations.B: Incidents matter by their effect on the mission; a program aimed at fewer incidents can over-control minor events and slow work the consulate needs done.
wrong_explanations.C: Security objectives for systems are means, set to serve the consulate's mission; treating them as the program's purpose puts the technical goal ahead of what it protects.
wrong_explanations.D: Legal compliance is one obligation the program helps meet, not its purpose; being compliant does not show that risks to the mission are low.

tips: Eliminate: C treats system security objectives as ends, though they serve the mission, and D takes one obligation, legal compliance, as the whole purpose.
Final two: A beats B because incidents matter by their effect on objectives; a program judged by incident numbers can over-control and hinder the mission it serves.
Exam cue: when asked what risk management is for, choose the enterprise's objectives over any technical, compliance or incident measure, which are means or results.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Organizational structure, roles and responsibilities. A committee member's own request
questions.question: The head of tax at an accountancy practice, a voting risk committee member, asks the committee to approve delaying a client-portal fix beyond their own approval limit. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Return the request to the head of tax to decide
options.B: Record the head of tax's interest in the committee's minutes
options.C: Exclude the head of tax from the committee's vote on it
options.D: Pass the head of tax's vote to a tax team deputy

questions.key_concept: A committee member whose own request is being decided declares the interest and steps out of that vote, so the decision stays objective.
questions.pre_read: Note whose request the committee is deciding and who votes on it.
questions.correct_explanation: A member voting on their own request has a conflict of interest, so the head of tax steps out of that vote while the rest of the committee decides within its authority. Recording the interest in the minutes is the runner-up: declaring a conflict is the right first step, but if the head of tax still votes, the decision on their own delay is not objective.

wrong_explanations.A: The delay exceeds what the head of tax may approve, which is why it reached the committee; sending it back bypasses the authority level the risk needs.
wrong_explanations.B: Declaring the interest is needed, but on its own it leaves the head of tax voting on their own request, so the decision is still not objective.
wrong_explanations.D: A deputy from the tax team reports to the head of tax and shares the interest, so passing the vote to them keeps the conflict in the decision.

tips: Eliminate: A sends the delay back to the person whose limit it exceeds, and D passes the vote to a deputy who answers to that same person.
Final two: C beats B because declaring a conflict does not remove it; the head of tax must also step out of the vote on their own request.
Exam cue: when a committee decides a member's own request, look for the member stepping out of the vote; declaring the interest alone is not enough.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. A policy past its review date
questions.question: A rope maker's data policy passed its review date eight months ago, and a plant manager now says its rules no longer bind plant staff. What is the risk analyst's BEST response?

options.A: Treat the policy as guidance until senior management approves its review
options.B: Advise that the policy stays in force during its overdue review
options.C: Suspend the policy until a reviewed version is approved
options.D: Review the policy within the risk team and reissue it

questions.key_concept: Unless it sets an expiry, a policy stays in force until replaced or withdrawn; a missed review date calls for the review, not a pause.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the missed date says about the review process from what it says about the rules.
questions.correct_explanation: A policy states management's intent and, unless it says otherwise, stays in force until its approvers replace or withdraw it; a missed review date is a lapse in upkeep, not a release from the rules. So the policy keeps applying while its owner completes the overdue review. Treating it as guidance meanwhile is the runner-up: it sounds measured, but it makes mandatory rules optional for the very staff who doubt them.

wrong_explanations.A: Guidance is advisory, so staff could depart from rules management still intends; a late review does not change what the approved policy requires.
wrong_explanations.C: Suspending the policy leaves the data it protects with no rules while the review runs, a gap that no one has assessed or accepted.
wrong_explanations.D: The analyst can feed the review, but the policy owner leads it and senior management approves the result; a policy the risk team reissues lacks that authority.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves the data with no rules while the review runs, and D has the risk team reissue a policy that senior management approves.
Final two: B beats A because a late review does not cancel management's intent; treating the rules as guidance makes them optional until senior management approves the review.
Exam cue: an overdue policy review is a lapse to close through the policy's owner, not a reason to treat the policy's rules as lapsed.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.PO-02 (policy for managing cybersecurity risks is reviewed, updated, communicated and enforced to reflect changes); ISACA Glossary (policy)

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Business processes and resilience (DRP, BCP). A plan slower than the process it feeds
questions.question: A tea blender's packing process must restart within a day to meet supermarket orders, but the plan for the blending line feeding it restores blending in five days. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Raise packing's need with the blending line's process owner
options.B: Build a stock of blended tea to cover the five-day gap
options.C: Ask IT to cut the blending line's system recovery to one day
options.D: Take five days as packing's restart target

questions.key_concept: When one process needs another to restart, its need sets what the other must deliver; the other process's owner decides how.
questions.pre_read: Trace what the packing process needs from the blending line, and who decides how fast blending returns.
questions.correct_explanation: Packing cannot restart in a day while the blending it depends on takes five, so the plans do not fit. Packing's need sets what blending must deliver, and the blending line's process owner decides how, so the analyst takes that one-day need to them. Building a stock of blended tea is the runner-up: it may be the right fix, but it picks the response before the owner has weighed it.

wrong_explanations.B: A buffer stock is one possible fix, with costs of its own; choosing it now settles the blending line's response before its owner has weighed the options.
wrong_explanations.C: Restoring systems is the disaster recovery part; the line also needs its machines, people and supplies, and what it must deliver is set by the business, not IT.
wrong_explanations.D: Packing's one-day need comes from its supermarket orders; moving its target to fit the blending plan hides the gap instead of closing it.

tips: Eliminate: C hands a business recovery need to IT as a systems job, and D bends packing's target to fit the slower plan rather than the orders it serves.
Final two: A beats B because the blending line's owner decides how its recovery meets packing's need; a stock of tea is one option for them to weigh.
Exam cue: when one process's plan cannot meet a dependent process's need, take the need to the owner of the process depended on before any fix is chosen.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). Framework kept by IT security
questions.question: A solar farm operator's approved enterprise risk framework is maintained by its IT security team, which also rates its own security risks under it. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Add a chief risk officer review of IT security's framework changes
options.B: Split the framework into separate IT and business versions
options.C: Give internal audit the job of maintaining the framework
options.D: Move upkeep of the framework to the chief risk officer's function

questions.key_concept: The enterprise risk function, usually under the chief risk officer, keeps the enterprise risk framework; a team rated under its rules should not maintain them.
questions.pre_read: Note who keeps the framework and whose risks are rated under it.
questions.correct_explanation: An enterprise framework sets how every unit's risks are rated, so the function running enterprise risk management, usually under the chief risk officer, keeps it, and senior management approves changes. A team keeping rules it is itself rated under cannot apply them objectively, and its view is narrower than the enterprise's. A chief risk officer review of IT security's changes is the runner-up: it adds oversight, but the rules stay with the team they judge.

wrong_explanations.A: A review catches some changes, but IT security still keeps the rules its own risks are rated under, and the framework stays shaped by one team's view.
wrong_explanations.B: Separate IT and business versions recreate the silo that ERM removes; risks rated under different frameworks cannot be compared or combined.
wrong_explanations.C: Internal audit gives independent assurance over the framework; maintaining it would be a management duty that undermines that independence.

tips: Eliminate: B splits one framework into silos whose risks cannot be compared, and C gives internal audit a management duty it must stay independent of.
Final two: D beats A because oversight of changes leaves the rules with the team they are applied to; the enterprise risk function keeps them for every unit.
Exam cue: the enterprise risk function keeps the enterprise framework and senior management approves it; a team rated under the rules should not be their keeper.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. Validators inside an AI model unit
questions.question: An annuity provider's data science unit builds its AI pricing models, and validators inside the unit sign them off, which the chief risk officer counts as second-line review. What is the risk analyst's BEST advice?

options.A: Count the validators' sign-off as the second line's model review
options.B: Treat the sign-off as independent assurance for the board
options.C: Treat the sign-off as first-line testing for the risk team to challenge
options.D: Have the unit's head vouch for the validators' objectivity

questions.key_concept: Validators who report into the unit that builds AI models do first-line self-testing; an objective second line still challenges their results.
questions.pre_read: Note whom the validators report to and whose models they check.
questions.correct_explanation: Validators who report into the unit that builds the models are part of that unit's own checking, the first line, however good their work. Their sign-off is useful first-line testing, and the chief risk officer's risk team still challenges its results from outside the unit. Counting it as second-line review is the runner-up: the validators do validate, but their reporting line ties them to the builders, so nothing outside the unit questions the models.

wrong_explanations.A: The validation is real work, but validators inside the data science unit answer to the head whose team built the models, so their sign-off is not objective challenge.
wrong_explanations.B: Independent assurance to the board comes from the third line, outside management; a team inside the unit that builds the models cannot give it.
wrong_explanations.D: The unit's head leads the work under review, so their word cannot make the validators objective; the reporting line decides which line a team sits in.

tips: Eliminate: B gives a team inside the building unit the third line's independent role, and D asks the head whose models are checked to vouch for the checkers.
Final two: C beats A because validators reporting into the building unit test their own unit's work; second-line challenge has to come from outside that unit.
Exam cue: place a review team by its reporting line, not its name; validators answering to the builders' head are first line, and the second line still challenges.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. Store risks dropped after a move to SaaS
questions.question: A jeweler's risk analyst finds its profile dropped the online store's card-data and outage risks once the store moved to a SaaS platform. Which of the following should the profile MOST appropriately show?

options.A: The provider's own ratings of the risks on its platform
options.B: The store's risks rated by their effect on the jeweler
options.C: A note naming the provider as owner of the store's risks
options.D: The platform's uptime against the jeweler's contracted service level

questions.key_concept: Outsourcing moves the work, not the exposure; an outsourced activity's risks stay in the profile, rated by their effect on the enterprise.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose sales, customers and obligations the store's risks would still hit.
questions.correct_explanation: Moving the store to a SaaS platform moved the work, not the jeweler's exposure: lost sales, card-scheme penalties and lost customer trust still fall on the jeweler. The profile keeps the store's risks, rated by their effect on the jeweler, with the provider's controls credited where evidence supports them. The provider's own ratings are the runner-up: they keep the risks visible, but they measure harm to the provider's platform, not to the jeweler.

wrong_explanations.A: The provider rates risks to its own platform and business; the jeweler's profile needs the harm to the jeweler's sales and customers, which those ratings do not measure.
wrong_explanations.C: Outsourcing moves the work, not accountability; the provider cannot own risks to the jeweler's objectives, and a note gives leaders no exposure to weigh.
wrong_explanations.D: Uptime against a service level measures the provider's performance, not the jeweler's exposure; a platform can meet its service level while card data leaks.

tips: Eliminate: C hands ownership of the jeweler's risks to the provider, and D reports the provider's service performance where the jeweler's exposure belongs.
Final two: B beats A because the profile shows the jeweler's exposure; the provider's ratings measure harm to its platform, not to the jeweler's sales and customers.
Exam cue: when an activity moves to a provider, its risks stay in the enterprise's profile, rated by the harm they would do to the enterprise.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. AI-written sales messages under target pressure
questions.question: Pressed by the sales director's monthly targets, a card issuer's staff prompt an approved AI writing tool to inflate card rewards in messages to prospects. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Add a filter that blocks unsupported reward claims in AI drafts
options.B: Rate the risk of the inflated claims with the sales director
options.C: Make the tool's owner bar reward figures from its prompts
options.D: Report the inflated claims to the code of conduct's owner

questions.key_concept: Staff who use an AI tool to mislead customers under target pressure create conduct risk, taken first to the code of conduct's owner.
questions.pre_read: Ask who chose the misleading wording: the tool, or the people using it.
questions.correct_explanation: The tool writes what staff ask for; the staff are choosing to overstate rewards to meet targets. That is conduct risk, so the analyst reports it first to the code of conduct's owner, who can investigate, correct messages already sent and look at the targets. Rating the risk with the sales director is the runner-up: analysis helps, but the director sets the targets driving the conduct, and misconduct under way needs the conduct route.

wrong_explanations.A: A filter treats the tool as the cause; staff who choose to overstate rewards can reword drafts or write messages themselves, and the misled prospects stay uncorrected.
wrong_explanations.B: The sales director sets the targets driving the conduct, so rating it with them leaves the source of the pressure judging it, while misconduct already under way goes uninvestigated.
wrong_explanations.C: Restricting prompts is a tool fix for a people problem: it also blocks accurate reward details, and staff can still overstate rewards outside the tool.

tips: Eliminate: A and C fix the tool, a filter or a prompt rule, while the staff choosing to mislead can still word messages themselves.

Final two: D beats B because staff are already misleading prospects under the director's targets; the conduct route investigates, while rating it with the target-setter leaves the pressure judging itself.
Exam cue: when people knowingly misuse an AI tool to mislead customers, treat it as conduct risk and take it first to the code of conduct's owner; tool controls can follow.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. Files held on another owner's platform
questions.question: A management consultancy's head of knowledge, who owns its document platform, is asked to release a former client's files, owned by that client's engagement partner, for a pitch. What is the risk analyst's BEST advice?

options.A: Give the decision to IT as the platform's technical owner
options.B: Give the decision to the engagement partner who owns the files
options.C: Give the decision to the head of knowledge as the platform's owner
options.D: Release the files once the former client's name is removed

questions.key_concept: A system's owner runs the platform, but data held on it keeps its own owner, who decides who may receive it.
questions.pre_read: Separate who owns the platform from who owns the files stored on it.
questions.correct_explanation: Owning a platform makes the head of knowledge answerable for the system, not for every file on it. The former client's files have their own owner, the engagement partner, who knows what the client agreed and decides who may receive them. Giving the decision to the head of knowledge is the runner-up: a system can hold many owners' data, and owning the system does not carry the right to release it.

wrong_explanations.A: IT runs and safeguards the platform as custodian; calling it the technical owner does not give it the business decision on who may receive a client's files.
wrong_explanations.C: The head of knowledge owns the platform, not the files on it; the files' owner, the engagement partner, decides who may receive them.
wrong_explanations.D: Removing the name decides the release without the files' owner; the files' content can still identify the client or break what the client was promised.

tips: Eliminate: A gives a custodian the owner's decision, and D releases the files after removing a name, deciding without the files' owner.
Final two: B beats C because the files have their own owner; owning the platform that stores them does not carry the decision on who may receive them.
Exam cue: a system and the data on it can have different owners; whoever owns the data decides who receives it, wherever it is stored.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). IT loss records outside the enterprise loss data
questions.question: A window maker's IT team logs outage and data-loss costs only in its service desk tool; the enterprise loss database that calibrates every risk type's ratings holds none. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Feed IT losses into the enterprise's shared loss database
options.B: Calibrate IT ratings from the service desk's own loss records
options.C: Estimate IT likelihoods from published industry loss surveys
options.D: Take IT losses to the IT steering committee as a separate report

questions.key_concept: IT loss events belong in the enterprise's shared loss data, so IT risks are rated on the same evidence as other risks.
questions.pre_read: Notice which loss data the enterprise uses to rate its other risks, and what it holds about IT.
questions.correct_explanation: The enterprise calibrates every risk type from one loss database, and IT losses are missing from it, so IT ratings rest on different evidence and the enterprise view understates IT losses. Feeding IT losses into the shared database fixes both. Calibrating IT ratings from the service desk's records is the runner-up: it uses the window maker's own losses, but keeps IT on a separate evidence base, outside the data leaders use for every other risk.

wrong_explanations.B: The service desk records are real losses, but rating IT from them alone keeps IT on its own evidence base, and the enterprise database still shows no IT losses.
wrong_explanations.C: Industry surveys can supplement internal data, but estimating from them sets aside the window maker's own recorded losses and leaves the enterprise database without IT events.
wrong_explanations.D: A separate report to an IT committee keeps IT losses outside enterprise risk management, so they are not weighed beside other risks.

tips: Eliminate: C swaps the firm's own recorded losses for outside surveys, and D routes IT losses to an IT committee outside enterprise risk management.
Final two: A beats B because the enterprise rates every risk type from one loss database; rating IT from service desk records keeps IT on a separate evidence base.
Exam cue: IT risk is part of enterprise risk, so its loss events go into the same loss data the enterprise uses to rate every other risk.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. Board question on a rise in exposure
questions.question: A trout farm's board asks why technology risk exposure jumped in its latest risk profile. Which of the following should the risk analyst provide as the BEST answer?

options.A: Total technology exposure now beside its previous total
options.B: A count of technology risks rated high, then and now
options.C: Records of technology control tests and their results
options.D: The risks whose ratings rose, and what made them rise

questions.key_concept: To explain a change in the profile, show which risks moved and why; a net total shows that exposure changed, not what drove it.
questions.pre_read: Note what the board asked: whether exposure rose, or why it did.
questions.correct_explanation: The board already knows exposure rose; it asked why. Naming the risks whose ratings rose, and what changed for each, such as a new threat, a failed control or a new activity, tells leaders where to act. Total exposure beside the previous total is the runner-up: it confirms and sizes the rise, but a net figure cannot say which risks drove it, and a large rise in one risk can hide behind small falls elsewhere.

wrong_explanations.A: Comparing totals restates what the board already saw; it cannot show which risks drove the rise or why, so leaders cannot tell where to act.
wrong_explanations.B: A count of high-rated risks hides how large each one is; exposure can rise sharply with no change in how many risks are rated high.
wrong_explanations.C: Control tests show activity, not exposure; a list of tests cannot say which risks rose or what caused them to rise.

tips: Eliminate: B counts high-rated risks, which says nothing of their size, and C lists control testing, which shows activity rather than exposure.
Final two: D beats A because the board asked why exposure rose; totals confirm the rise, while the risks that moved, and their causes, explain it.
Exam cue: when leaders ask why the profile changed, answer with the risks that moved and what moved them; net totals and counts show that it changed, not why.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Appetite stated as an incident count
questions.question: An electoral commission's board proposes stating its cyber risk appetite as no more than five security incidents a year, of any kind. What is the risk analyst's BEST advice?

options.A: Compare the five-incident limit with peer commissions' counts
options.B: Express the appetite as limits on harm to election delivery
options.C: Have IT security set the incident limit in the appetite
options.D: Treat the five-incident limit as the commission's risk capacity

questions.key_concept: Appetite states how much harm to objectives leaders will accept; a count of incidents of any kind weighs trivial and grave events alike.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the proposed limit measures, and whether that is what the commission must protect.
questions.correct_explanation: Appetite is the risk leaders will accept in pursuit of the mission, so it should speak to harm to objectives, here delivering elections voters trust. A count of incidents of any kind treats a blocked phishing email like a tampered results feed. The board still sets the appetite. Comparing the limit with peers is the runner-up: it tunes the number but keeps measuring events rather than harm.

wrong_explanations.A: Peer counts tune the number but keep the wrong measure: incidents of any kind, trivial or grave, still count the same against the limit.
wrong_explanations.C: Appetite is set by the board and senior management; IT security applies it, so having it set the limit moves the decision to the wrong level.
wrong_explanations.D: Capacity is the most loss the commission could survive, an outer bound for appetite; relabeling an incident count as capacity confuses the two.

tips: Eliminate: C hands appetite-setting to IT security, below the board, and D relabels an appetite limit as capacity, the outer bound appetite must sit within.
Final two: B beats A because appetite should measure harm to objectives; a peer-tuned count still weighs a blocked phishing email like a tampered results feed.
Exam cue: an appetite stated as a count of events of any kind measures activity, not harm; advise expressing it as limits on harm to objectives.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. Customer terms missing from a supplier contract
questions.question: A hydroelectric operator's grid contract requires plant-system security controls; its maintenance contractor meets them now, though the contractor's contract, renewing soon, omits them. Which of the following is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Obtain the contractor's signed statement that it meets the terms
options.B: Name the contractor owner of the risk of missing the grid terms
options.C: Write the grid contract's security terms into the renewed contract
options.D: Limit the contractor's remote access to the plant systems

questions.key_concept: Duties an enterprise owes its customers are written into the contracts of suppliers doing the work, so the supplier is bound to keep meeting them.
questions.pre_read: Ask what binds the contractor to keep meeting the grid terms after today.
questions.correct_explanation: The operator stays answerable to the grid operator for the controls, but the contractor who maintains the plant systems has no duty to keep them. Writing the grid terms into the renewed contract binds the contractor and gives the operator remedies if they lapse. The signed statement is the runner-up: it confirms the controls are met now, but it creates no lasting duty, so the contractor could drop them without breaching anything.

wrong_explanations.A: A statement records that the controls are met today; it does not oblige the contractor to keep them or give the operator any remedy if they lapse.
wrong_explanations.B: Outsourcing moves the work, not accountability; the operator still answers to the grid operator, so the contractor cannot own the risk of breaching those terms.
wrong_explanations.D: Restricting access may reduce some risk, but it does not oblige the contractor to keep the controls the grid contract requires on systems it still maintains.

tips: Eliminate: B makes the contractor owner of a duty the operator still holds, and D restricts access without obliging the contractor to keep the required controls.
Final two: C beats A because a signed statement confirms today's position, while terms in the renewed contract bind the contractor to keep meeting them.
Exam cue: when a customer contract requires controls that a supplier operates, pass the terms into the supplier's contract; the enterprise stays accountable either way.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Strategy, goals and objectives. Risk input to an acquisition vote
questions.question: An equipment lessor's board will soon vote on buying a rival; the deal's value depends on moving the rival's leases onto the lessor's platform within a year. What is the risk analyst's BEST contribution?

options.A: Rate the risks that could delay or derail the planned migration
options.B: Assess the rival's security controls against the lessor's standards
options.C: Set the rival's risk appetite beside the lessor's for the board
options.D: Review the rival's past breaches from public news reports

questions.key_concept: Risk input to a strategic decision, such as buying a rival, centers on what could stop the decision delivering the value it is made for.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the board is buying the rival for, and what could stop it.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk input helps most while leaders choose, framed by the objective the choice serves. The deal's value rests on moving the rival's leases onto the lessor's platform within a year, so the analyst rates the risks to that move, such as data quality, contract terms and capacity. Assessing the rival's security controls is the runner-up: it is useful due diligence, but it describes the rival today, not what could stop the deal paying off.

wrong_explanations.B: Control gaps at the rival matter once it is bought, but they describe its current state; the board's vote turns on whether the platform move can deliver the deal's value.
wrong_explanations.C: The lessor's board decides against its own appetite for its own strategy; the rival's appetite ends with the deal and says nothing about whether the platform move will work.
wrong_explanations.D: Public breach reports are partial and look back at the rival's past; they do not show the risks that could stop the platform move the deal depends on.

tips: Eliminate: C sets the rival's appetite beside the lessor's, though the lessor's board decides on its own, and D relies on public breach reports that look back at the rival.
Final two: A beats B because the deal is bought for its value, which rests on the platform move; the rival's controls describe it today, not the risk to that objective.
Exam cue: when leaders weigh a deal or other strategic move, frame risk input around the objective it must deliver; the target's current controls are one input to that view.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. Inputs to a yearly policy review
questions.question: A water board's security policy owner reviews the policy each year by rereading it alone, and it has never changed. Which of the following should the risk analyst recommend as the MOST useful review input?

options.A: Security policies that peer water boards have published
options.B: Page views of the policy on the staff intranet since its release
options.C: Staff survey ratings of how clearly the policy is written
options.D: Exceptions, incidents and compliance results tied to the policy

questions.key_concept: A policy review draws on evidence of how the policy works in practice, such as exceptions, incidents and compliance results, not a reread.
questions.pre_read: Ask what would show the owner whether the policy still works.
questions.correct_explanation: A review should test whether the policy still fits the water board's risks and how work is actually done. Exceptions show where staff cannot meet it, incidents show where it failed to prevent harm, and compliance results show where practice departs from it; together they point to what needs to change. Peer policies are the runner-up: they can prompt questions, but they reflect other boards' risks, not how this policy performs.

wrong_explanations.A: Peer policies reflect other utilities' risks and choices; they can prompt questions, but they show nothing about where this board's policy fails or no longer fits.
wrong_explanations.B: Page views show that staff opened the policy, not whether its rules still match the board's risks or work in practice.
wrong_explanations.C: Clarity ratings help communication, but a clearly written policy can still be out of step with the board's risks, the law or daily practice.

tips: Eliminate: B and C show whether staff opened or understood the policy, not whether its rules still fit the risks and the way work is done.
Final two: D beats A because a review needs evidence of how this policy performs at this board; peer policies reflect other organizations' risks and choices.
Exam cue: to review a policy, look for evidence from its own use, such as exceptions, incidents and compliance results; outside examples and readership figures come second.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.PO-02 (policy for managing cybersecurity risks is reviewed, updated, communicated and enforced to reflect changes); ISACA Glossary (policy)

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Business processes and resilience. Continuity plan after an AI redesign
questions.question: A roofing contractor dropped its dispatchers when a vendor's AI tool began triaging storm calls and booking crews; its continuity plan has dispatchers assign crews if systems fail. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Exercise the plan's manual crew assignment with the call center team
options.B: Add a standby copy of the AI tool at a second site
options.C: Revise the continuity plan to fit the redesigned call process
options.D: Ask the tool's vendor to commit to higher availability

questions.key_concept: When a process is redesigned, such as around an AI tool, its owner revises the continuity plan before it is relied on.
questions.pre_read: Check whether the plan's fallback still matches how the process now runs.
questions.correct_explanation: The plan relies on dispatchers the redesign removed, so it would fail the first time it is used. When a process changes, its continuity plan changes with it: the process owner revises the fallback for the new design, such as who assigns crews and from which records, then exercises it. Exercising the current plan is the runner-up: it can only confirm a known gap, since the role it relies on no longer exists.

wrong_explanations.A: An exercise tests the plan as written; this plan relies on dispatchers who are gone, so exercising it before revision can only confirm the gap already known.
wrong_explanations.B: A standby copy makes losing the tool less likely, but systems can still fail together, and the plan's fallback still relies on dispatchers who are gone.
wrong_explanations.D: A vendor's availability commitment lowers or compensates outage risk; it gives the contractor no way to assign crews while systems are down.

tips: Eliminate: B and D make the AI tool less likely to fail, but a continuity plan must keep crews assigned when it does fail.
Final two: C beats A because the plan relies on a role the redesign removed; exercising it confirms a known gap, while revising it gives the process a fallback that exists.
Exam cue: when a process is redesigned around AI or automation, the process owner revises its continuity plan for the new design before it is exercised or relied on.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. Inventory detail for outage impact
questions.question: Which of the following inventory details BEST helps a detergent maker's risk analyst rate the business impact of an outage of each listed asset?

options.A: Processes that would halt if the asset were down
options.B: Classification of the data that the asset holds
options.C: Replacement cost of the asset from purchase records
options.D: Open vulnerabilities found on the asset in the last scan

questions.key_concept: Linking each inventoried asset to the processes that depend on it lets the impact of its outage be rated by business harm.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the business loses while an asset is down.
questions.correct_explanation: An outage's business impact depends on what stops while the asset is unavailable, so recording the processes that depend on each asset lets the analyst tie it to the impact the business would suffer. Data classification is the runner-up: it shows how sensitive the data is, which drives the impact of disclosure, but an asset holding no sensitive data can still halt production when it is down.

wrong_explanations.B: Classification rates the data's sensitivity, which matters if it is disclosed; an outage's impact depends on which processes stop, and a low-class asset can still halt production.
wrong_explanations.C: Replacement cost is what the asset cost to buy, not what the business loses while it is down; a cheap asset can stop a costly process.
wrong_explanations.D: Open vulnerabilities bear on how likely an outage is, not on how much the business loses once the asset is unavailable.

tips: Eliminate: C values the asset by its price, not by what the business loses, and D counts weaknesses, which bear on likelihood rather than impact.
Final two: A beats B because an outage's impact follows from the processes that stop; classification measures sensitivity, which drives the impact of disclosure, not of downtime.
Exam cue: to rate the impact of an asset's outage, link it to the processes that depend on it; price, open flaws and data class answer other questions.

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. Practice risks left to the risk team
questions.question: An executive search firm's risk team identifies, rates and tracks each practice's risks through yearly interviews; practice leaders see those risks only in the risk team's yearly report. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Run the practices' risk interviews quarterly instead of yearly
options.B: Take full charge of the practices' risks within the risk team
options.C: Ask internal audit to review the practices' risks during its audits
options.D: Build risk review into the agendas of practice management meetings

questions.key_concept: The first line identifies and manages the risks its work creates as part of running it; the second line supports and challenges.
questions.pre_read: Ask who should be identifying and managing the practices' risks day to day.
questions.correct_explanation: Practice leaders run the work that creates these risks, so as the first line they identify and manage them; the risk team sets the method, supports and challenges. Building risk review into practice management meetings puts that work where practice decisions are made. Quarterly interviews are the runner-up: they keep the list more current, but identifying and managing the practices' risks would still sit with the risk team.

wrong_explanations.A: More frequent interviews refresh the risk team's list, but the second line still does the identifying and tracking, and practice leaders still do not manage their risks.
wrong_explanations.B: Taking full charge formalizes the problem: the second line would run first-line risks and could no longer challenge how they are managed.
wrong_explanations.C: Internal audit gives independent assurance on how risks are managed; reviewing the practices' risks in its audits does not make leaders identify or manage them.

tips: Eliminate: B makes the risk team run first-line risks, and C gives internal audit a review that leaves the leaders' role unchanged.
Final two: D beats A because practice leaders must identify and manage their own risks; interviewing them more often leaves that work with the second line.
Exam cue: when the second line identifies and tracks a unit's risks for it, move that work into the unit's own management routine; the second line supports and challenges.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Slowdowns dropped from a downtime count
questions.question: A biscuit baker's board set a six-hour monthly tolerance for online ordering being unavailable; after a tolerance breach, the order system's owner stopped counting slowdowns that halt ordering. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Add server capacity to end the slowdowns that halt ordering
options.B: Report downtime against the tolerance as it was first set
options.C: Log the ordering slowdowns as a separate risk in the register
options.D: Count a slowdown as half an outage toward the tolerance

questions.key_concept: What counts toward a tolerance is set by whoever set the tolerance; an owner who narrows the measure loosens the limit and hides breaches.
questions.pre_read: Ask who decided what counts toward the six-hour limit.
questions.correct_explanation: The board set the tolerance in terms of customers being unable to order, so slowdowns that halt ordering count against it. Dropping them from the count loosens the board's limit without its approval and hides a breach. The analyst reports downtime on the board's measure, slowdowns included, so the breach reaches the owner and the board. Logging the slowdowns as a separate risk is the runner-up: it records them, but outside the limit they breach.

wrong_explanations.A: Adding capacity picks a treatment before the breach is even reported; the owner chooses the response, and the board would still see a limit met that was not.
wrong_explanations.C: A separate register entry records the slowdowns but keeps them outside the board's tolerance, so the breach they cause stays hidden from those who set the limit.
wrong_explanations.D: Half-weighting slowdowns is another redefinition, this time by the analyst; what counts toward a tolerance is decided by the level that set it.

tips: Eliminate: A picks a treatment before the breach is even reported, and D changes what counts toward the tolerance, which is for the level that set it.
Final two: B beats C because slowdowns that halt ordering are what the tolerance limits; a separate entry records them but keeps the breach out of the board's view.
Exam cue: when an owner narrows what counts toward a tolerance, report against the measure the limit-setter defined; changing what counts is the limit-setter's decision.

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. Where to begin with NIST's RMF
questions.question: A probation service adopting NIST's Risk Management Framework plans to begin with categorizing its case-management system, though senior leaders have not yet stated the service's risk tolerance. What is the risk analyst's BEST advice?

options.A: Categorize the case-management system by the impact of its loss
options.B: Have the system owner pick its controls from the SP 800-53 baselines
options.C: Start with the organization-level Prepare tasks, such as roles and strategy
options.D: Adopt the framework's tasks as published across its systems

questions.key_concept: In NIST's RMF, organization-level preparation, including a risk management strategy that states risk tolerance, comes before system-level steps such as categorization.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the framework's system-level steps rely on being in place.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST's RMF opens with a Prepare step at the organization level, where leaders assign risk roles and set a risk management strategy that includes the organization's risk tolerance. The system steps that follow, such as choosing and authorizing controls, work within those limits. Categorizing the system is the runner-up: it is the first step after Prepare, but starting there leaves later choices with no stated tolerance to meet.

wrong_explanations.A: Categorizing is the first step after Prepare, but the RMF puts organization-level preparation first; without stated tolerance, the controls and decisions that follow have no agreed limit.
wrong_explanations.B: Picking baseline controls before the system is categorized skips steps, and the owner would choose without the tolerance that should bound the choice.
wrong_explanations.D: The RMF is meant to be tailored; adopting its tasks as published across every system ignores the service's own risks, size and priorities.

tips: Eliminate: B picks controls before the system is even categorized, and D adopts the tasks as published instead of tailoring them to the service.
Final two: C beats A because the RMF prepares at the organization level first; categorizing now leaves later choices with no stated tolerance to meet.
Exam cue: when adopting a risk framework, settle organization-level roles, strategy and risk tolerance before system-level steps; those steps rely on them.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Strategy, goals and objectives. Where objectives are taken from
questions.question: Which of the following should a sauce maker's risk analyst use as the PRIMARY source of the business objectives against which IT risks are rated?

options.A: Technology objectives in the IT department's roadmap
options.B: Objectives set out in the board-approved strategic plan
options.C: Priorities that unit managers describe in interviews
options.D: Weaknesses ranked in the latest vulnerability scan

questions.key_concept: IT risks are rated against business objectives as the approved strategic plan states them, the authoritative record of what the enterprise aims to achieve.
questions.pre_read: Before reading the options, name who sets the enterprise's objectives.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk is the effect of uncertainty on objectives, so the analyst needs the objectives the sauce maker's leaders have committed to. The board-approved strategic plan states them with authority, so ratings measured against it reflect what the enterprise has promised. Priorities unit managers describe in interviews are the runner-up: they add useful detail, but they are personal views that can drift from what the board approved. IT roadmaps and scan findings sit further down.

wrong_explanations.A: An IT roadmap sets IT's own targets, which should serve the enterprise's objectives; rating risks against it treats technology goals as ends in themselves.
wrong_explanations.C: Interviews help interpret objectives, but they record individual managers' views; the approved strategic plan is the authoritative statement to rate against.
wrong_explanations.D: A vulnerability scan lists technical weaknesses, which are causes inside risk scenarios; it says nothing about what the business is trying to achieve.

tips: Eliminate: A rates risk against IT's own roadmap targets, and D offers technical weaknesses, which are causes of risk, not objectives.
Final two: B beats C because the board-approved plan states the objectives the enterprise has committed to; managers' interview priorities add detail but carry no approval.
Exam cue: when asked where the objectives behind risk ratings come from, choose the approved enterprise strategy over IT plans, individual views or technical findings.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Organizational structure, roles and responsibilities. An IT risk committee with no business members
questions.question: A candle maker's IT risk committee, made up of the CIO and four IT managers, oversees risks to production and online sales, though no business leader attends. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Give production and sales leaders seats on the committee
options.B: Send minutes of the committee to production and sales leaders
options.C: Submit the committee's decisions to internal audit for approval
options.D: Hand the committee's oversight work to the risk team

questions.key_concept: A committee overseeing risks to business objectives includes leaders from the business it covers, not IT alone, so business impact shapes its decisions.
questions.pre_read: Check who sits on the committee and whose objectives it oversees.
questions.correct_explanation: A committee overseeing risks to production and online sales needs the leaders responsible for those objectives at the table: they judge the business impact, challenge IT's view and carry decisions back to their units. With IT managers alone, IT judges business risk for itself. Sending the minutes to production and sales leaders is the runner-up: it keeps them informed, but only after decisions are made, when their input can no longer shape them.

wrong_explanations.B: Minutes tell production and sales leaders what was decided after the fact; the committee still weighs their risks without the people whose objectives are at stake.
wrong_explanations.C: Internal audit gives independent assurance; approving committee decisions would make it part of choices it later audits, and still adds no business voice.
wrong_explanations.D: The risk team advises and challenges; handing it the committee's oversight leaves business leaders out of decisions on their own risks.

tips: Eliminate: C has internal audit approve decisions it must later assess independently, and D hands oversight of business risks to the risk team, which advises rather than decides.
Final two: A beats B because no business leader attends a committee overseeing production and sales risks; minutes inform them after decisions, while seats let them shape decisions.
Exam cue: when a committee oversees business risks without business members, look for the option that brings those leaders into its membership; minutes and reports inform but do not involve.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Organizational culture and ethics. A fix demanded with every problem raised
questions.question: An employment service's caseworkers left a fault that wrongly closed claims unreported for months; their managers require a proposed fix with any system problem raised. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Pay caseworkers a bonus for the problems they report
options.B: Issue a policy requiring staff to report system problems
options.C: End the rule that problems must come with a solution
options.D: Discipline the caseworkers who knew about the fault but stayed silent

questions.key_concept: A rule that makes raising a problem costly, such as demanding a proposed fix first, silences early warnings; removing it restores reporting.
questions.pre_read: Look for what stands between seeing a problem and reporting it.
questions.correct_explanation: Caseworkers saw the fault but could not offer a fix, and their managers require one with any problem raised, so the fault stayed hidden for months. Ending that rule removes the barrier between seeing a problem and reporting it. Paying a bonus for reported problems is the runner-up: it adds a reason to report, but the managers' rule still stands in the way, and paying per report rewards volume over early, honest warnings.

wrong_explanations.A: A bonus pulls against the rule without removing it; caseworkers still need a fix before they can raise a problem, and paying per report invites volume over quality.
wrong_explanations.B: A policy says problems must be reported, but managers would still demand a fix first; behavior follows what leaders require in practice more than a document.
wrong_explanations.D: Punishing people for silence teaches others that raising issues is risky; the aim is earlier reporting, so remove what delayed it.

tips: Eliminate: B answers a culture barrier with a policy statement, and D punishes people for staying silent, which teaches everyone else to stay quiet.
Final two: C beats A because the managers require a proposed fix with any problem raised; a bonus adds a reason to report but leaves that barrier standing.
Exam cue: when people stay silent about problems because raising one demands a ready fix, drop that demand before adding rewards or policies; a warning without a fix still has value.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Policies and standards. A policy rule with no written steps
questions.question: A wealth manager's policy requires a call-back check before client-service staff change payment details, but no procedure says who calls or which number to use. Which of the following is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Task the client-service team with a written call-back procedure
options.B: Remind client-service staff of the call-back requirement in the policy
options.C: Write who calls and which number into the policy itself
options.D: Treat staff's current call-back methods as the procedure

questions.key_concept: A policy requirement is carried out through a procedure giving the steps, owned by the team that performs it; without one, practice varies.
questions.pre_read: Note what the stem says exists and what it says is missing.
questions.correct_explanation: The policy sets the requirement, but nothing tells staff how to meet it: who makes the call, and to which number. Procedures supply those steps and are owned by the team that performs them, so the client-service team writes one, approved by its manager, and the check becomes consistent. Reminding client-service staff of the requirement is the runner-up: it restates the rule, but leaves each person to decide how to carry it out.

wrong_explanations.B: Staff already know a call-back is required; a reminder repeats the rule without saying who calls or which number to use, so practice stays uneven.
wrong_explanations.C: A policy states intent and changes rarely; step-by-step call-back details belong in a procedure owned by the team that performs the check.
wrong_explanations.D: Staff's own methods were never defined or approved, so they may differ in ways that weaken the check; adopting them as they stand leaves the gap unexamined.

tips: Eliminate: C writes the call-back steps into the policy, which states intent, and D adopts whatever methods staff use, though nobody has defined how the check should run.
Final two: A beats B because no procedure says who calls or which number to use; a reminder restates the requirement but leaves those steps undefined.
Exam cue: when a policy requirement is carried out unevenly because nobody has written the steps, look for a procedure owned by the team that performs the work.

questions.subtopic: 1B1 Enterprise risk management (ERM). AI use inventory kept outside ERM
questions.question: A paving contractor's innovation team keeps its inventory of 15 AI uses, such as bid pricing, outside ERM, so their risks never reach the enterprise register. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Name the innovation team owner of the AI uses' risks
options.B: Build risk ratings into the team's own AI inventory
options.C: Rate the AI uses' risks within the enterprise register
options.D: Make the CIO owner of an AI section in the enterprise register

questions.key_concept: An AI use inventory lists what exists; each use's risks are rated in the enterprise register under business owners, so ERM compares and reports them.
questions.pre_read: Check where the AI uses' risks are rated and who sees them.
questions.correct_explanation: AI risks are enterprise risks: they belong in the enterprise register, rated like any other risk and owned by the managers whose processes use each tool, such as bid pricing, so leaders can compare, combine and report them against appetite. Making the CIO owner of an AI section is the runner-up: the risks reach the register, but under IT, though they fall on the business processes that use the tools.

wrong_explanations.A: The innovation team builds and runs the tools; the risks fall on the processes that use them, such as bid pricing, so ownership sits with those business managers.
wrong_explanations.B: Scoring the uses' risks in the team's own inventory still leaves them outside ERM, unowned by business managers and not compared with other risks or reported against appetite.
wrong_explanations.D: The entries reach the register, but under the CIO; AI uses such as bid pricing serve business processes, whose managers own the risks they create.

tips: Eliminate: A gives the risks to the team that builds the tools, and B rates them in the team's own inventory, which still sits outside ERM.
Final two: C beats D because AI uses such as bid pricing serve business processes; D brings the risks into the register but makes IT their owner.
Exam cue: when AI uses sit in a separate inventory, bring their risks into the enterprise register, owned by the managers whose processes use them, not by IT or the tools' builders.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. Owner steps back once a risk reaches the board's profile
questions.question: Once pump-control ransomware entered a sewer authority's board risk profile as a top risk, its owner, the operations director, stopped reviewing it, saying the board now manages it. What is the risk analyst's BEST advice?

options.A: Make the board's risk committee owner of the ransomware risk
options.B: Keep the risk with the director to treat and track
options.C: Report to the board's risk committee that the director withdrew
options.D: Take the risk off the operations unit's register

questions.key_concept: Listing a risk in the board's profile adds board oversight but does not move ownership; the owner keeps treating and tracking it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what changes, and what does not, when a risk appears in the board's profile.
questions.correct_explanation: A place in the board's profile gives the board oversight of the risk; it does not move ownership. The operations director still treats and tracks the ransomware risk, and the profile depends on that work to stay current. Reporting the step back to the board's risk committee is the runner-up: escalation suits an owner who will not act, but this director misread what the profile means, so the analyst corrects that with the owner first.

wrong_explanations.A: Committees oversee and challenge; making one the owner leaves nobody in operations accountable for a risk that sits in the pumping systems the director runs.
wrong_explanations.C: Escalation suits an owner who refuses to act; this director misread what the profile means, and advice to the owner can fix that before the board steps in.
wrong_explanations.D: The board's profile is drawn from register entries; removing the entry cuts the profile off from the record that keeps the risk current and owned.

tips: Eliminate: A makes a committee the owner, though committees oversee rather than own, and D removes the register entry the board's profile is drawn from.
Final two: B beats C because the director stepped back on a misreading of the profile, not a refusal; the owner is advised first, and escalation follows if they still will not act.
Exam cue: when an owner steps back because a risk entered the board's profile, the listing has not moved ownership; the board oversees while the owner keeps treating and tracking it.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 Organizational structure, roles and responsibilities. What a control owner answers for
questions.question: At a plywood mill, the production systems manager owns the backup control for kiln-drying settings. Which of the following is the manager MOST responsible for as control owner?

options.A: Deciding whether to retain the residual risk
options.B: Giving independent assurance that the backups work
options.C: Setting the outage tolerance the backups support
options.D: Making sure the backups exist and restore as intended

questions.key_concept: A control owner answers for the control being in place and working as intended; whether the risk left is acceptable is the risk owner's decision.
questions.pre_read: Separate decisions about a control from decisions about the risk it reduces.
questions.correct_explanation: In the ISACA Glossary, a control owner holds authority and accountability for decisions about the control and answers for it being implemented and operating effectively. For the kiln-drying settings, the manager answers for backups that exist and restore as designed. Deciding whether to retain the residual risk is the runner-up: owners do make decisions, but that one belongs to the risk owner, the business manager whose objective bears the loss.

wrong_explanations.A: Retaining residual risk is a risk decision; it belongs to the risk owner, whose objective bears the loss, while the control owner answers for the control itself.
wrong_explanations.B: Independent assurance comes from a function outside the management that runs the control; the manager who owns the backups cannot independently assure them.
wrong_explanations.C: Leaders set tolerances from appetite and the impact on objectives; a control owner runs controls that keep risk inside those limits, not the limits themselves.

tips: Eliminate: B has the owner of a control give independent assurance over it, and C has the control owner set the tolerance the control serves, which leaders set.
Final two: D beats A because a control owner answers for the control being in place and working; whether to retain the residual risk is the risk owner's call.
Exam cue: control owners answer for controls working as intended; risk owners decide whether the risk left after those controls is acceptable.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Business processes and resilience. A long outage with the plan never invoked
questions.question: An orthodontic group's booking system failed for nine hours; the operations director, empowered to invoke the continuity plan, awaited IT's fix estimates, so clinics never switched to paper. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Add invocation criteria tied to the booking system's RTO
options.B: Give clinic managers authority to invoke the continuity plan
options.C: Train IT staff on the clinics' paper booking steps
options.D: Shorten the booking system's RTO for faster recovery

questions.key_concept: A continuity plan states in advance when it is invoked, such as an outage reaching a set point inside the RTO with no confirmed fix.
questions.pre_read: Note who could have invoked the plan, and what they were waiting for.
questions.correct_explanation: The director could invoke the plan but had no rule for when, so each hopeful fix estimate pushed the decision back while clinics stood idle. Criteria set in advance, such as an outage reaching a set point inside the booking system's RTO with no confirmed fix, turn invocation into a check, not a wait. Giving clinic managers authority is the runner-up: it spreads the decision, but none of them would know when to act.

wrong_explanations.B: Authority already sat with the director, who was there to use it; more people able to invoke the plan still have no point at which an outage calls for it.
wrong_explanations.C: IT restores the system during an outage while clinics run the paper workaround; the gap was that nobody triggered the workaround, not how it runs.
wrong_explanations.D: The RTO comes from the business impact of the outage; a shorter target does not make anyone invoke the plan while fix estimates keep slipping.

tips: Eliminate: C trains IT on a workaround the clinics run, and D tightens a recovery target, though the failure was that nobody invoked the plan.
Final two: A beats B because the empowered director still waited on fix estimates; more people with authority would lack the same rule for when to invoke.
Exam cue: when someone empowered to invoke a plan is present but waits as an outage drags on, look for activation criteria set in advance with triggers inside the RTO, not more people with authority.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 4.2.1 (Activation Criteria and Procedure: the plan is activated when stated criteria are met, which may include the extent of damage, the system's criticality and an outage expected to last longer than the RTO); COBIT 2019 DSS04 (Managed Continuity)

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Organizational asset management. Sizing a provider's breach from the inventory
questions.question: A SaaS provider's breach took a jam maker's risk analyst a week to size, working from an inventory entry giving the service's owner, provider and contract. Which of the following is the analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Note the price paid for the service in the entry
options.B: List the provider's breach-notice time alongside its contract
options.C: Log the provider's security certifications in the entry
options.D: Record the types and class of data the service holds

questions.key_concept: An inventory entry for a SaaS service records the types and class of data it holds, so impact can be judged quickly.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the analyst had to find out before the breach could be sized.
questions.correct_explanation: Sizing a breach means knowing what was exposed: which kinds of data, whose, and how sensitive. An entry that records the types and class of data the service holds lets the analyst judge impact in hours, and it feeds classification and risk ratings before any breach. Listing the provider's breach-notice time is the runner-up: it shows how soon the jam maker hears of a breach, but not what the breach touched.

wrong_explanations.A: The price paid measures cost, not exposure; a cheap service can hold the most sensitive data, so the figure does nothing to size a breach.
wrong_explanations.B: A notice deadline tells the jam maker when it will hear of a breach; the week went on finding what the service held, which the entry still would not show.
wrong_explanations.C: Certifications speak to how well the provider protects the service, which bears on likelihood; once a breach happens, they do not show what was exposed.

tips: Eliminate: A records what the service cost, not what it exposes, and C records the provider's certifications, which bear on likelihood rather than the size of a breach.
Final two: D beats B because the week went on learning what the service held; a notice time speeds the alert but still leaves the analyst asking what was exposed.
Exam cue: for a SaaS or cloud service, the inventory records what data it holds and how it is classed; impact, breach sizing and protection start there.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM-07 (inventories of data and corresponding metadata for designated data types are maintained); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM-04 (inventories of services provided by suppliers are maintained)

questions.subtopic: 1B2 Lines of defense. Ratings that settle under the challenge cut-off
questions.question: A gas network operator's risk team challenges only risks that units rate 15 or more of 25; since then, most units' ratings have settled between 12 and 14. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Move the challenge threshold down to ratings of 12
options.B: Challenge a sample of ratings below the threshold as well
options.C: Train units on the rating method's impact scale
options.D: Rate the units' risks within the risk team on their behalf

questions.key_concept: A fixed cut-off for second-line challenge invites ratings just under it; sampled challenge below the cut-off keeps ratings honest.
questions.pre_read: Compare when the ratings moved with when the challenge rule began.
questions.correct_explanation: A fixed cut-off for challenge rewards ratings just under it, and the bunching at 12 to 14 since the rule began suggests units rate to avoid scrutiny. Challenging a sample below the threshold as well leaves no rating safe from review, removing the reward and showing whether ratings are understated. Moving the threshold down to 12 is the runner-up: it widens coverage but keeps a fixed line, inviting the same bunching below it.

wrong_explanations.A: A lower cut-off widens coverage for now, but it keeps a line that units can rate under, so the bunching is likely to move below 12.
wrong_explanations.C: Training helps units who misread the scale; ratings that settled just under the cut-off once it began point to avoiding scrutiny, not to confusion.
wrong_explanations.D: Units own their risks and know them best; the second line challenges their ratings, and rating in their place would take ownership away from the first line.

tips: Eliminate: C treats the bunching as a misreading of the scale, and D has the second line rate the units' risks, taking over what the first line owns.
Final two: B beats A because ratings settled just under the cut-off once it began; any fixed line can be rated under, while sampling below it removes the reward.
Exam cue: when ratings bunch just under the cut-off for second-line review, suspect the cut-off is steering them; add sampled challenge below it rather than moving the line.

questions.subtopic: 1B3 Risk profile. AI features vendors switched on by default
questions.question: A custodian bank's board profile reports AI risk from its in-house models; no register entry covers AI features SaaS vendors switched on by default, two used in reconciliations. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Switch off the vendors' AI features the bank did not approve
options.B: Add the vendors' AI features to the AI count in the profile
options.C: Rate the vendors' AI features in the register behind the profile
options.D: Record the SaaS vendors in the register as owners of the features

questions.key_concept: Vendor-enabled AI features in services the enterprise uses are its own AI risk; rating them in the register brings them into the profile.
questions.pre_read: Ask where the board's profile gets its figures from.
questions.correct_explanation: The board's profile is built from rated register entries, so AI that never reaches the register is missing from it. Features vendors switch on inside services the bank uses bring new data uses and harms, and two already support reconciliations, so they are rated in the register like in-house models. Switching off unapproved features is the runner-up: it acts before anyone knows the risk and would disrupt those reconciliations.

wrong_explanations.A: Switching off before rating acts ahead of analysis and would disrupt the two reconciliations that use the features; the services' business owners decide that once the risk is rated.
wrong_explanations.B: A count tells the board how many features exist, not how much risk they carry; the profile reports rated exposure against appetite.
wrong_explanations.D: A vendor supplies the feature but does not bear the bank's loss; risk from the bank's use sits with the business owners of the services using it.

tips: Eliminate: B adds a count of features to the board's figure in place of rated exposure, and D makes the vendors owners of risks that fall on the bank.
Final two: C beats A because two features already support reconciliations; rating them in the register brings the risk into the profile before anyone decides to switch features off.
Exam cue: AI a vendor switches on inside a service the enterprise uses is enterprise AI risk; it reaches the profile through rated register entries, whoever built the model.

questions.subtopic: 1B4 Risk appetite and risk tolerance. Two appetites for one pilot
questions.question: Citing a high appetite for innovation risk, a drywall contractor's team skips data review for a pilot app storing clients' floor plans; the firm's breach appetite is low. What is the risk analyst's BEST advice?

options.A: Judge the app's data risk against the breach appetite
options.B: Run the pilot app under the innovation appetite with monitoring
options.C: Merge the data breach and innovation appetites into one
options.D: Take the pilot's risk to the board as an exception

questions.key_concept: Appetite is set by type of risk; an initiative's data breach risk is judged against the breach appetite, even when its innovation risk is welcome.
questions.pre_read: Name what the pilot could gain and what it could expose.
questions.correct_explanation: Appetite sets the amount and type of risk a firm will take, and one initiative can carry several types. The innovation appetite covers the chance the pilot fails to deliver; clients' floor plans bring breach risk, which the firm wants low, so it is judged against the breach appetite, starting with the skipped review. Running the pilot under the innovation appetite with monitoring is the runner-up: monitoring watches the data, but against the wrong limit.

wrong_explanations.B: Monitoring adds sight of the data, but the decision still rests on the innovation appetite; exposing clients' floor plans is breach risk, which the firm wants low.
wrong_explanations.C: The firm set two appetites on purpose; one merged level would either block innovation or loosen data protection, and the analyst cannot rewrite the appetite statement.
wrong_explanations.D: An exception asks the board to accept more risk than its appetite; nobody yet knows whether the app's data risk falls outside the breach appetite.

tips: Eliminate: C merges two appetites the firm set apart, and D seeks a board exception before anyone knows whether the app's data risk breaks the breach appetite.
Final two: A beats B because the clients' floor plans bring breach risk; monitoring under the innovation appetite still judges that risk against the wrong limit.
Exam cue: when an initiative claims a generous appetite, sort its risks by type; each is judged against the appetite for that type, not the initiative's label.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286 Rev. 1 Section 2.1 (Overview of ERM: risk appetite is the amount and type of risk that an organization is willing to take in meeting its objectives); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-02 (risk appetite and risk tolerance statements are established, communicated and maintained)

questions.subtopic: 1B5 Risk frameworks, legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. Target Profile tailored by IT
questions.question: A housing authority's IT team has tailored its NIST CSF 2.0 Target Profile and will use it to set three years of cybersecurity priorities and spending. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Seek internal audit's sign-off on the Target Profile
options.B: Submit the Target Profile to senior management for approval
options.C: Gather business owners' comments on the Target Profile
options.D: Reshape the profile to look like other authorities' profiles

questions.key_concept: A tailored framework profile that sets enterprise priorities and spending is approved by senior management, not finalized by IT.
questions.pre_read: Note who shaped the profile and what it will commit the authority to.
questions.correct_explanation: A Target Profile states the outcomes the authority will pursue and, here, three years of priorities and spending. NIST CSF 2.0 starts Organizational Profiles by gathering priorities and risk direction from executives, and senior management's approval makes the tailored profile the authority's target, not IT's. Gathering business owners' comments is the runner-up: their input improves the content, but the profile would still commit spending without senior management, which answers for it.

wrong_explanations.A: Internal audit gives independent assurance and may later audit the profile; signing it off would make audit part of a management decision it should assess.
wrong_explanations.C: Owners' comments improve the content, but comments are not approval; the profile would still commit three years of spending without senior management's risk direction.
wrong_explanations.D: Other authorities' profiles reflect their own risks and priorities; copying them skips the tailoring to this authority's risks that the framework expects.

tips: Eliminate: A has internal audit sign off a management decision it may later audit, and D copies peers' profiles in place of tailoring to the authority's own risks.
Final two: B beats C because the profile will set three years of priorities and spending; owners' comments add content, while senior management's approval makes it the authority's target.
Exam cue: a tailored framework or Target Profile that commits the enterprise's priorities is approved by senior management, not finalized by IT; others' input improves it but does not approve it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 Section 5.1 (Improving Risk Management Communication: preparing to create and use Organizational Profiles involves gathering organizational priorities, resources and risk direction from executives); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-01 (organizational leadership is responsible and accountable for cybersecurity risk and fosters a culture that is risk-aware, ethical and continually improving)
